context: Marie Tharp arrived at Columbia University in 1948 «with two master’s degrees, and almost no prospect» of going to sea.

choices.text: with two master’s degrees and almost no prospect
with two master’s degrees; and almost no prospect
with two master’s degrees and, almost no prospect

why.A: "almost no prospect of going to sea" is not an independent clause, so comma + FANBOYS is illegal here.
why.B: Correct — two compound objects of the same preposition need no comma.
why.C: A semicolon requires a complete sentence on both sides.
why.D: A comma cannot separate a conjunction from what follows it.

context: Research vessels of the era «do not accept» women aboard, so Tharp worked from a drafting table.

why.A: Present tense clashes with the past-tense "worked" later in the same sentence.
why.B: Future tense is impossible for a historical fact.
why.C: Correct — matches the established past tense of the surrounding narrative.
why.D: Present progressive contradicts the historical setting.

context: For four years she plotted depth readings, «one single line at a time, one after another.»

choices.text: OMIT the underlined portion, ending the sentence after "readings."

why.A: "one single" is redundant and "one after another" repeats "at a time."
why.B: Cuts past the redundancy into the meaning: she plotted thousands of lines over four years, not one, and "at a time" is what says so.
why.C: Correct — the shortest phrasing that keeps the full meaning.
why.D: This removes the redundancy by removing the information. The sentence exists to say how slowly the plotting went, and "one line at a time" is the only place it says it.

context: «Plotting depth readings for four years, the drafting paper revealed» a mountain range running down the center of the Atlantic.

choices.text: Plotting depth readings for four years, Tharp saw emerge on her drafting paper
Plotted over four years, the depth readings on her drafting paper eventually revealed
After four years of plotting depth readings, the drafting paper showed

why.A: Dangling modifier — drafting paper cannot plot readings.
why.B: Correct — places Tharp, the actual plotter, immediately after the modifier.
why.C: Readings do not plot themselves either; the actor is still missing.
why.D: "the paper" still did not do the four years of plotting.

context: Splitting that range lengthwise was a deep V-shaped notch «— a rift valley.»

why.A: Correct — a single dash after a complete clause may introduce an appositive for emphasis.
why.B: With no punctuation at all, "a rift valley" runs straight into "notch" and the sentence reads as nonsense.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it.
why.D: A closing dash at the end of a sentence is not a real construction.

context: Tharp recognized what the valley implied. If the seafloor was pulling apart along that seam, then continents were moving, «a idea» then associated with Alfred Wegener.

why.A: "a" cannot precede a vowel sound.
why.B: Correct — "an" before the vowel sound in "idea."
why.C: "and" creates a nonsensical list.
why.D: "ideal" changes the meaning entirely.

context: Heezen dismissed her interpretation as "girl talk" and asked her to redraw the maps. «Similarly,» she redrew them. The rift valley appeared again.

why.A: "Similarly" signals a parallel between two things, but her redrawing was a response to the request, not something like it.
why.B: "Nevertheless" wrongly signals that she redrew them despite being asked to.
why.C: The redrawing is not an example of anything.
why.D: Correct — the two-word sentence lands hardest with no connector, and the sequence is already clear.

context: It appeared in the North Atlantic, «in profiles from the Indian Ocean, and the Pacific was another place it appeared.»

choices.text: in profiles from the Indian Ocean, and in the Pacific.
the Indian Ocean profiles, and appearing in the Pacific.
in the Indian Ocean, also the Pacific.

why.A: The third item switches to a full clause, breaking parallel structure.
why.B: Correct — three parallel prepositional phrases beginning with "in."
why.C: Mixes a noun phrase with a participial phrase.
why.D: "also the Pacific" is not parallel and creates a comma splice feel.

context: When Heezen overlaid the locations of recorded undersea earthquakes onto Tharp’s maps, the pattern of epicenters «trace» the rift valley almost exactly.

why.A: The subject is "pattern," singular, and the passage is in past tense.
why.B: Still plural, and the added pronoun is redundant.
why.C: Correct — singular subject "pattern" plus past tense to match the narrative.
why.D: Present perfect breaks the established past-tense sequence.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence "Heezen dismissed her interpretation as ‘girl talk.’" If deleted, the paragraph would primarily lose:

choices.text: a specific detail about the professional resistance that Tharp’s discovery met at the time.
evidence that Heezen was not a competent scientist.
a transition to the paragraph about plate tectonics.
nothing of significance, since the resistance is stated elsewhere in the essay.

why.A: Correct — the quotation is the paragraph’s only concrete evidence of the dismissal Tharp faced.
why.B: The passage never evaluates Heezen’s competence; it later credits his earthquake overlay.
why.C: The sentence does not function as a transition.
why.D: No other sentence states the resistance in specific terms.

context: The maps «Tharp’s and Heezen’s» published in 1957 changed how the public pictured the planet.

why.A: Nothing is possessed here — they are the subject of "published."
why.B: Correct — a compound subject with no possession requires no apostrophe.
why.C: Adds incorrect plurals to proper names.
why.D: Introduces a possessive where none belongs.

context: Plate tectonics, the framework that now organizes all of geology, «rests substantially on» the seafloor she drew.

why.A: Correct — matches the passage’s measured, formal register.
why.B: "totally built off of" is colloquial and overstated.
why.C: "kind of" is vague and informal.
why.D: "a whole lot" clashes with the surrounding academic prose.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to write an essay explaining how one scientist’s work contributed to a major shift in scientific understanding. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it traces Tharp’s mapping from her drafting table to the acceptance of plate tectonics.
Yes, because it describes several women who worked in mid-century geology.
No, because it focuses on the obstacles Tharp faced rather than on her scientific contribution.
No, because it does not explain the mechanism of plate tectonics in detail.

why.A: Correct — the essay follows exactly that arc: her method, her discovery, and its role in tectonic theory.
why.B: Only one woman is discussed.
why.C: The obstacles are secondary; the contribution is the spine of the essay.
why.D: A detailed mechanism was never part of the stated goal.

context: They are met by a dozen volunteers with soldering irons, sewing machines, and «a rule; nobody repairs anything for you.»

choices.text: a rule: nobody repairs anything for you.
a rule, nobody repairs anything for you.
a rule nobody repairs anything for you.

why.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause before it; "...and a rule" is not one.
why.B: Correct — a colon announces the rule that follows, and the clause before it is complete.
why.C: A comma cannot join a full statement to another full statement. "Nobody repairs anything for you" could stand alone, which is what makes this a splice.
why.D: Runs two statements together with no punctuation.

context: «I starting coming two years ago» with a toaster that had stopped toasting.

choices.text: I started coming two years ago
Starting to come two years ago
Having started coming two years ago

why.A: "starting" is a participle, not a conjugated verb.
why.B: Correct — supplies a real past-tense main verb.
why.C: Leaves the sentence with no main verb at all.
why.D: Also a participial phrase, producing a fragment.

context: Ellis, «a retired elevator mechanic handed» me a screwdriver and waited.

why.A: The nonessential appositive opens with a comma but never closes.
why.B: Correct — matched pair of commas around the appositive.
why.C: A semicolon cannot close an appositive.
why.D: A dash cannot close what a comma opened.

context: Inside was not the mysterious machinery I expected, «it was a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal.»

choices.text: but a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal.
a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal it was.
it being a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal.

why.A: Comma splice — two independent clauses joined by only a comma.
why.B: Correct — "not X but Y" is parallel and eliminates the second clause entirely.
why.C: Awkward inversion that still leaves a splice.
why.D: A participial phrase that garbles the sentence.

context: We cleaned the contact. The toaster «has worked» for another three years.

why.A: Present perfect implies the toaster is still working, but "another three years" is a closed period.
why.B: Present tense contradicts the completed span.
why.C: Correct — simple past for a finished duration.
why.D: Future tense is impossible for an event already described.

context: A toaster costs sixteen dollars, and I «had been prepared and ready to throw one away in the garbage» rather than spend twenty minutes with a screwdriver.

choices.text: had been prepared to throw one away
had been ready to throw one away in the trash

why.A: "prepared and ready" is redundant, as is "away in the garbage."
why.B: Correct — removes both redundancies without losing meaning.
why.C: Shorter, and it reports something that never happened. He was willing to throw the toaster out; the sentence goes on to say he did not.
why.D: "throw away in the trash" repeats itself.

context: The economics were not the point; the habit was. «In addition,» the Repair Café movement began in Amsterdam in 2009 and has since spread to more than two thousand locations.

why.A: "In addition" implies the new paragraph adds to the previous point, but it shifts to background information.
why.B: The movement’s founding is not a consequence of the writer’s realization.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph turns to context and needs no connector.
why.D: There is no contrast between the two ideas.

context: Its organizers keep careful records: what came in, what was fixed, what could not be. «Roughly two-thirds of items leaves» working.

choices.text: Roughly two-thirds of items is leaving
Roughly two-thirds of items has left

why.A: With fractions, the verb agrees with the object of "of" — "items" is plural.
why.B: Correct — plural verb for a plural object.
why.C: Singular and needlessly progressive.
why.D: Singular and shifts tense.

context: The remaining third leave with an explanation, «which the volunteers insist it is also a kind of success.»

choices.text: which the volunteers insist is also a kind of success.
that the volunteers insist it is also a kind of success.
and the volunteers insist is also a kind of success.

why.A: "which" already serves as the clause’s subject, so "it" is a redundant second subject.
why.B: Correct — removes the doubled subject.
why.C: Same doubled-subject error, and "that" would require no comma.
why.D: Leaves the clause without a clear subject.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence "He never once took the screwdriver out of my hand." Where would it most logically be placed?

choices.text: In paragraph 1, after the rule that nobody repairs anything for you.
In paragraph 2, after "Ellis... handed me a screwdriver and waited."
In paragraph 3, after the discussion of disposability.
In the final paragraph, after Ellis’s death is mentioned.

why.A: The rule is stated abstractly there; the sentence is about Ellis specifically.
why.B: Correct — it directly extends the image of Ellis handing over the screwdriver and waiting.
why.C: Paragraph 3 is about economics and habit, not about Ellis.
why.D: Placing it after his death breaks the chronology of the toaster scene.

context: The café now runs a small-appliance table «in his name, staffed from three people» he taught.

choices.text: in his name, staffed by three people
on his name, staffed by three people
in his name, staffed of three people

why.A: "staffed from" is not idiomatic English.
why.B: Correct — "in his name" and "staffed by" are both standard.
why.C: "on his name" is not idiomatic.
why.D: "Staffed of" is not idiomatic; a table is staffed by the people who run it.

stem: Which choice best concludes the essay by tying back to its opening image of broken things?
context: Final sentence options:

choices.text: I am not a good repairer. I am a patient one, which he told me is most of the job.
Repair Cafés can be found in over two thousand locations worldwide.
Ellis was seventy-eight when he died, and he had worked on elevators for forty years.
Everyone should learn to use a screwdriver at some point in their life.

why.A: Correct — returns to the essay’s personal thread and to Ellis’s lesson about the nature of repair.
why.B: A statistic already given, with no connection to the closing image.
why.C: Biographical detail that does not resolve the essay’s idea.
why.D: A generic moral that abandons the specific voice of the piece.

context: The trees grew a hundred feet tall «and eight feet across, produced reliable annual nut crops, and yielded» straight, rot-resistant timber.

choices.text: and eight feet across produced reliable annual nut crops and yielded
and eight feet across; produced reliable annual nut crops; and yielded
and eight feet across, produced reliable annual nut crops and, yielded

why.A: Correct — three parallel verbs in a series, properly separated by commas.
why.B: Removing the commas fuses the list into unreadable prose.
why.C: Semicolons are only for list items that themselves contain commas.
why.D: Places a comma between the conjunction and its verb.

context: «Cryphonectria parasitica, a fungus that had arrived on imported Japanese chestnut stock.» Asian chestnuts had coevolved with it and tolerated it.

choices.text: The cause was Cryphonectria parasitica, a fungus that had arrived on imported Japanese chestnut stock.
Cryphonectria parasitica being a fungus that had arrived on imported Japanese chestnut stock.
Cryphonectria parasitica, a fungus, having arrived on imported Japanese chestnut stock.

why.A: A noun followed by an appositive with no main verb is a fragment.
why.B: Correct — supplies subject and verb ("The cause was").
why.C: "being" is not a conjugated main verb.
why.D: Still a fragment, now with an extra dangling appositive.

context: Asian chestnuts had coevolved with the fungus and tolerated it. American chestnuts had not. «This» moved outward at roughly twenty-four miles a year.

why.A: "This" has no clear antecedent — it could point to the fungus, the tolerance, or the whole situation.
why.B: Plural and equally vague.
why.C: Correct — naming the noun removes the ambiguity.
why.D: "It" could refer to the fungus or to either chestnut species.

context: Within forty years an estimated four billion trees «are» dead.

why.A: Present tense clashes with the completed historical span.
why.B: Correct — simple past matches the narrative of the blight’s spread.
why.C: Present perfect suggests the dying continues into the present.
why.D: Future tense is impossible for a completed event.

context: Most Americans alive today have never seen a mature chestnut. The species, «therefore,» is not extinct.

why.A: Extinction does not follow from people not having seen the tree.
why.B: Correct — signals the contrast between apparent total loss and continued survival.
why.C: Survival is not an addition to the loss; it opposes it.
why.D: The survival is not an example of the loss.

context: Millions of these stump sprouts «persists» across the Appalachians.

why.A: "Millions" is plural, so the singular verb is wrong.
why.B: Correct — plural subject takes a plural verb.
why.C: Singular and shifts the tense unnecessarily.
why.D: Singular and needlessly progressive.

context: «Girdling trunks and cutting off nutrient flow, an estimated four billion trees were killed by the blight.»

choices.text: Girdling trunks and cutting off nutrient flow, the blight killed an estimated four billion trees.
Girdled trunks and cut nutrient flow killed an estimated four billion trees.
An estimated four billion trees, girdling trunks and cutting off nutrient flow, died across the range.

why.A: Dangling modifier — the trees did not girdle themselves.
why.B: Correct — places "the blight," which does the girdling, right after the modifier.
why.C: Changes the meaning and drops the blight as the agent.
why.D: Attaches the modifier to the trees, repeating the original error.

context: Breeders cross American chestnuts with Chinese varieties and then «backcrossing the hybrids» repeatedly toward American characteristics.

why.A: "cross... and backcrossing" mixes a conjugated verb with a participle.
why.B: Correct — both verbs share the subject "Breeders" in the same form.
why.C: An infinitive does not parallel "cross."
why.D: The past tense breaks the match with the present "cross" that the two verbs share.

stem: The writer is considering adding: "Chestnut wood was also prized by furniture makers in the nineteenth century." Should the sentence be added to the final paragraph?

choices.text: Yes, because it explains why the chestnut was economically valuable.
Yes, because it provides a transition to the restoration efforts.
No, because the final paragraph concerns restoration research, not the tree’s historical uses.
No, because the essay has already stated that chestnut timber was rot-resistant and durable.

why.A: True but irrelevant to the paragraph’s subject.
why.B: It does not transition to anything; it interrupts.
why.C: Correct — identifies the actual mismatch between the detail and the paragraph’s focus.
why.D: The essay mentions rot resistance but not furniture makers, so the stated reason is inaccurate.

context: None has yet produced a tree that can be planted at scale, and «due to the fact that» any restored forest will take a century to grow, patience is required.

why.A: "due to the fact that" is a five-word way of saying one word.
why.B: Correct — the concise standard form.
why.C: "Though" sets the century of growth against the need for patience, when the long growth is the reason patience is required.
why.D: "Owing to the fact that" is the same padding with a different opening word.

context: A third group works with hypovirulence, a virus that weakens the «fungus’s own ability» to kill tissue.

why.A: Correct — singular noun ending in -s takes apostrophe + s for possession.
why.B: A plural with no apostrophe cannot show possession.
why.C: No possessive marker at all.
why.D: Shifts to plural, contradicting the single fungus under discussion.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to argue that genetic engineering is the most promising way to restore the American chestnut. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it describes researchers inserting a wheat gene that neutralizes the fungus’s acid.
Yes, because it explains that Asian chestnuts tolerate the fungus while American ones do not.
No, because it presents the gene work as one of three approaches and favors none of them.
No, because it never mentions any attempt to change the chestnut’s genes.

why.A: Describing the wheat-gene work is not the same as ranking it; the essay gives it one sentence among three approaches.
why.B: That explains why the American tree was vulnerable, which is not an argument for any one restoration method.
why.C: Correct — breeding, the wheat gene, and hypovirulence are listed side by side, and the essay says none has yet produced a tree that can be planted at scale.
why.D: The essay does mention one: researchers inserted a wheat gene into the tree.

context: Other researchers have inserted «a wheat gene, that neutralizes the acid, the fungus uses» to kill tissue.

choices.text: a wheat gene that neutralizes the acid the fungus uses
a wheat gene, that neutralizes the acid the fungus uses
a wheat gene that neutralizes the acid, the fungus uses

why.A: Both commas are illegal — one precedes "that," the other splits the noun from its modifying clause.
why.B: Correct — essential clauses take no commas at all.
why.C: A comma before "that" is essentially always wrong.
why.D: Separates "acid" from the clause identifying it.

context: My grandmother’s bakery opened at six, «which meant: her day began at one.»

choices.text: which meant her day began at one.
which meant; her day began at one.
which meant, that her day began at one.

why.A: A colon cannot follow an incomplete clause like "which meant."
why.B: Correct — no punctuation is needed inside the relative clause.
why.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause before it.
why.D: A comma before "that" is wrong and "that" is unnecessary here.

context: My mother, out of options and patience, sent «I» to Queens for eight weeks.

why.A: "I" is a subject pronoun; this is the object of "sent."
why.B: Correct — object pronoun receiving the action.
why.C: Reflexives require the subject and object to be the same person.
why.D: "mine" is possessive and ungrammatical here.

context: She moved between the mixer, the proofing cabinet, and the oven «in a sequence, that had no visible logic.»

choices.text: in a sequence that had no visible logic.
in a sequence; that had no visible logic.
in a sequence — that had no visible logic.

why.A: A comma before "that" is wrong; the clause is essential.
why.B: Correct — no punctuation before an essential relative clause.
why.C: A semicolon requires a complete sentence after it.
why.D: A dash also wrongly separates the noun from its essential modifier.

context: At three in the morning she «hands» me a bench scraper and pointed at a mound of dough.

why.A: Present tense conflicts with "pointed" in the same compound predicate.
why.B: Correct — both verbs must be past tense.
why.C: Present perfect breaks parallel structure with "pointed."
why.D: Present progressive clashes with the past-tense narrative.

context: I ruined the first four batches, «the rolls came out dense, or flat, or fused into a single continental mass.»

choices.text: the rolls came out dense, flat, or they fused into a single continental mass.
which the rolls came out dense, or flat, or fused into a single continental mass.
and the rolls came out dense, or flat, or fused into a single continental mass.

why.A: Comma splice — two independent clauses joined by a comma alone.
why.B: The comma still joins two independent clauses on its own, and "or they fused" breaks the list of three outcomes.
why.C: "Which" has no job in what follows — "the rolls came out dense" is already a complete clause — so the relative pronoun is left dangling and the sentence falls apart.
why.D: Correct — comma + FANBOYS legally joins the two independent clauses.

context: She did not scold me, «it was somehow worse.»

choices.text: a silence that was somehow worse.

why.A: A comma alone joins two complete sentences, and "it" has no clear antecedent.
why.B: Correct — names the referent, eliminating the vague pronoun.
why.C: "Being" is not a finished verb, so the clause has no verb and cannot stand.
why.D: "it" still lacks a clear antecedent.

context: By the fourth week I could shape a roll that held its form. «By the sixth, understanding why she touched the dough constantly.»

choices.text: By the sixth I understood why she touched the dough constantly.
By the sixth, an understanding of why she touched the dough constantly.
The sixth week, understanding why she touched the dough constantly.

why.A: Fragment — no conjugated verb.
why.B: Correct — parallels the preceding sentence’s structure with a real main verb.
why.C: A noun phrase, still a fragment.
why.D: Also a fragment with no subject-verb pair.

context: There was no recipe «in the sense that I had previously believed in recipes in the past.»

choices.text: in the sense I had believed in recipes.
OMIT the underlined portion, ending the sentence after "recipe."

why.A: "previously" and "in the past" say the same thing twice.
why.B: Correct — removes the redundancy while keeping the meaning.
why.C: "As I had believed" means the narrator had expected this, which is the opposite of the paragraph. The original phrase names a sense of the word recipe, not an expectation.
why.D: "There was no recipe" flatly contradicts the paragraph, which has just described one. The qualification is the sentence’s point, so it cannot be cut to fix its wordiness.

context: There «was only conditions, and adjustments, and forty years of adjustments remembered in her hands.»

choices.text: were only conditions, and adjustments, and forty years of adjustments remembered in her hands.
is only conditions, and adjustments, and forty years of adjustments remembered in her hands.
was only conditions, adjustments, and forty years of adjustments remembering in her hands.

why.A: In "there ___" constructions the subject follows the verb; "conditions... adjustments" is plural.
why.B: Correct — plural verb agreeing with the compound plural subject, in past tense.
why.C: "Is" is singular, which disagrees with the plural subject, and the present tense breaks the narrative’s past.
why.D: Keeps the singular verb and misuses "remembering."

context: The rolls came out even and golden. «Similarly,» she looked at the tray for a long moment.

why.A: "Similarly" implies a comparison that does not exist between the rolls and her looking.
why.B: Correct — the relationship is simple sequence.
why.C: There is no contrast to signal.
why.D: Her looking at the tray is not an example of anything in the sentence before.

stem: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence "I had never opened an appliance before" would best be placed in this essay:

choices.text: in paragraph 1, after the mention of the eight weeks in Queens.
nowhere — it belongs to a different essay entirely.
in paragraph 2, after she hands the narrator the bench scraper.

why.A: The detail concerns appliances, not baking, and paragraph 1 sets up the summer.
why.B: Correct — this sentence belongs to the Repair Café essay; nothing in the bakery narrative involves opening an appliance.
why.C: Paragraph 3 is about the ruined batches of rolls; nothing in it involves opening an appliance.
why.D: A bench scraper is a baking tool, not an appliance.

stem: The final paragraph is primarily intended to:

choices.text: reveal that the grandmother had never approved of the narrator’s work.
reinterpret a gesture the narrator had previously misunderstood.
explain the technical process of running a bakery oven.
describe the narrator’s decision to become a baker.

why.A: The point is precisely that the nod was never about approval at all.
why.B: Correct — the closing lines redefine the nod as recognition rather than judgment.
why.C: No technical process is described.
why.D: The narrator never states such a decision.

context: Forty years of adjustments were remembered in «her’s hands.»

why.A: "her’s" is never a word; possessive pronouns take no apostrophe.
why.B: "hers" stands alone and cannot modify a noun.
why.C: Correct — "her" is the possessive adjective form.
why.D: "Her’" puts an apostrophe on a possessive pronoun, which never takes one — the same error as "her’s" with the s removed.

context: She was reading the humidity, which changed the flour, which «in turn changed on everything.»

why.A: "changed on" is not idiomatic in this sense.
why.B: Correct — "changed everything" takes a direct object with no preposition.
why.C: "changed for" alters the meaning to substitution.
why.D: "changed with" implies simultaneous variation, not causation.

context: The tower is a fourteen-foot-square room on stilts, «ringed by windows furnished with a bed, a stove, and an Osborne Firefinder.»

choices.text: ringed by windows, furnished with a bed, a stove, and an Osborne Firefinder.
ringed by windows; furnished with a bed, a stove, and an Osborne Firefinder.
ringed by windows and furnished, with a bed, a stove, and an Osborne Firefinder.

why.A: Two parallel participial phrases need a comma between them.
why.B: Correct — separates the two descriptive phrases modifying "room."
why.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it.
why.D: Splits the verb from its objects.

context: an Osborne Firefinder «— a rotating brass sighting device, essentially unchanged since 1915,» that lets an observer report a bearing.

choices.text: — a rotating brass sighting device, essentially unchanged since 1915 —
, a rotating brass sighting device, essentially unchanged since 1915 —
a rotating brass sighting device essentially unchanged since 1915

why.A: The description opens with a dash and closes with a comma. The sentence then has no mark telling the reader where the interruption ended and the main clause resumed.
why.B: Correct — the interrupter is set off by a matched pair of dashes, and the dash is the right choice here because the description already contains a comma of its own.
why.C: Mixes an opening comma with a closing dash.
why.D: Removes all punctuation, fusing the appositive into the sentence.

context: She «is hired» in 1974, when the Forest Service still staffed more than five thousand towers.

why.A: Present tense contradicts the 1974 date.
why.B: Correct — simple past matches "staffed" in the same sentence.
why.C: Present perfect implies an ongoing or unspecified time.
why.D: Future tense is impossible for a past event.

context: By the time she retired, fewer than three hundred «towers remains» active.

why.A: "towers" is plural and the passage is in past tense.
why.B: Correct — plural subject with past-tense verb.
why.C: "has remained" is singular and present perfect, and the subject is plural and the passage past.
why.D: "three hundred tower" is ungrammatical.

context: Satellites detect heat signatures from orbit; aircraft fly grid patterns; «lightning-strike sensors are triangulating ground contacts» within minutes.

choices.text: ground contacts are triangulated by lightning-strike sensors
the triangulation of ground contacts by lightning-strike sensors

why.A: Shifts to progressive while the other two clauses use simple present.
why.B: Correct — matches "detect" and "fly" in form.
why.C: Shifts to passive voice, breaking the parallel.
why.D: A noun phrase, producing a fragment.

context: The technology is genuinely better at finding fires that have already grown. «Similarly,» what the technology is not better at is seeing the fire that has not started yet.

why.A: "Similarly" signals likeness where the sentence draws a contrast.
why.B: The limitation is not a consequence of the strength.
why.C: Correct — the sentence’s own structure ("What the technology is not better at") already carries the contrast.
why.D: The limitation is not an example of the strength.

context: She knew which drainages held humidity into August and which slopes cured early, and «this» let her predict ignitions.

why.A: "this" vaguely refers to the whole preceding clause.
why.B: "That" points at the whole preceding clause exactly as "this" does, so the referent is still unnamed.
why.C: Correct — naming the referent removes the ambiguity.
why.D: "it" has no clear antecedent.

context: Her successors are cameras. Six of them «now currently cover at the present time» the Bearpaw district.

why.A: "now," "currently," and "at the present time" all say the same thing.
why.B: Correct — one time marker is enough.
why.C: Still doubles the time reference.
why.D: The shortest option here is also the wrong tense: the cameras are the successors, watching the district now, and the past tense retires them.

context: The system misses less than the towers did, «it also knows nothing about the ridge.»

choices.text: but it also knows nothing about the ridge.
however, it also knows nothing about the ridge.
it knows also nothing about the ridge.

why.A: Comma splice joining two independent clauses.
why.B: Correct — comma + FANBOYS, and "but" captures the contrast.
why.C: "However" is an adverb rather than a conjunction, so the comma in front of it is still joining two clauses alone.
why.D: Leaves the splice unfixed and garbles word order.

context: Vance «isn’t all sappy about» the work. The tower leaked. The radio failed.

why.A: "all sappy" is colloquial and clashes with the profile’s measured tone.
why.B: Correct — maintains the passage’s restrained register.
why.C: "Get all mushy over" is further from the profile’s measured register than the original, not closer to it.
why.D: Changes the meaning and adds slang.

context: She keeps a bound notebook of every ignition she called in, and she can still name «each ones drainage.»

why.A: Possession requires an apostrophe.
why.B: Correct — singular "one" takes apostrophe + s.
why.C: Places the apostrophe as if "one" were plural.
why.D: This closes the space between the two words and still supplies no apostrophe, so it fails on spacing and on possession both.

stem: The final paragraph most directly supports which idea from earlier in the essay?

choices.text: That satellite detection has entirely replaced the human lookout in the towers.
That Vance’s value lay in accumulated knowledge of a specific landscape.
That the Forest Service should rehire tower observers.
That the tower was uncomfortable to live in.

why.A: The essay says cameras miss less, but the paragraph is about her memory of the terrain.
why.B: Correct — recalling every drainage without checking demonstrates the local knowledge the essay contrasts with cameras.
why.C: No such recommendation appears.
why.D: True but incidental; the leaking tower is mentioned only to show she is unsentimental.

context: Anyone who has stood on a busy street knows the sound of a city: a low continuous roar, «punctuated by horns, and sirens.»

why.A: With only two items, no comma precedes "and."
why.B: Correct — a two-item list takes no comma.
why.C: Separates the participle from its prepositional phrase.
why.D: Splits the preposition from its objects.

context: «An internal combustion engine being loud at every speed.» An electric motor is nearly silent below twenty miles per hour.

choices.text: An internal combustion engine is loud at every speed.
An internal combustion engine, loud at every speed.
Being loud at every speed, an internal combustion engine.

why.A: "being" is not a conjugated main verb.
why.B: Correct — supplies a real verb.
why.C: A noun plus modifier with no verb.
why.D: Still a fragment, now with a dangling modifier.

context: In dense urban traffic, the average speed of most vehicles «rarely exceed» fifteen miles per hour.

why.A: The subject is "speed," singular, not "vehicles."
why.B: Correct — singular subject takes a singular verb.
why.C: The present perfect is plural here and also wrong about time: the sentence describes what average speed does in dense traffic, not what it has done up to now.
why.D: Plural and needlessly progressive.

context: Four decibels sounds modest. «Therefore,» because the decibel scale is logarithmic, it represents a reduction of well over half the sound energy.

why.A: "Therefore" makes the second sentence a consequence of the first, when it actually corrects it.
why.B: Correct — the first sentence says four decibels sounds modest, and the second turns against that impression.
why.C: There is no similarity being drawn.
why.D: "In other words" promises a restatement, and the second sentence overturns the first instead of repeating it.

context: It falls in the range that studies associate with «measurable outcomes; fewer sleep disturbances, lower reported annoyance, and reduced stress hormones.»

choices.text: measurable outcomes: fewer sleep disturbances, lower reported annoyance, and reduced stress hormones.
measurable outcomes, fewer sleep disturbances, lower reported annoyance, and reduced stress hormones.
measurable outcomes fewer sleep disturbances, lower reported annoyance, and reduced stress hormones.

why.A: A semicolon cannot introduce a list that is not an independent clause.
why.B: Correct — a colon after a complete clause announces the list.
why.C: Makes "measurable outcomes" look like a list item.
why.D: Runs the list into the clause with no punctuation.

context: «Relying for a century on engine noise as a warning, the requirement now mandates an artificial sound.»

choices.text: Because pedestrians had relied on engine noise as a warning, regulators now require an artificial sound.
Relying for a century on engine noise as a warning, an artificial sound is now required of manufacturers.
Having relied on engine noise, the regulation now mandates an artificial sound.

why.A: Dangling modifier — a requirement cannot rely on engine noise.
why.B: Correct — names pedestrians as the ones who relied, and regulators as those who act.
why.C: A sound cannot rely on noise either.
why.D: A regulation cannot have relied on noise.

context: Manufacturers have treated this requirement «to a design opportunity,» commissioning composers to produce signature tones.

why.A: "Treat to" means to give someone a pleasure, as in treating a friend to dinner; it cannot introduce what the requirement was regarded as.
why.B: Correct — "treated X as Y" is the idiomatic construction.
why.C: "treat for" means to give medical care.
why.D: "Treat in" is not an English idiom. The preposition has to be "as" to link the thing to what it is being treated as.

stem: The writer wants to add: "The two vehicle types sound essentially identical on a highway." Where should it go?

choices.text: In the opening paragraph, after the description of the urban roar.
At the very end of the essay, as its closing line.

why.A: Correct — it restates and reinforces the convergence point just established.
why.B: The opening has not yet introduced electric vehicles.
why.C: The Oslo paragraph concerns urban, low-speed noise, where electric and combustion vehicles do not sound alike.
why.D: The closing concerns acoustic planning policy.

context: Noise has always been treated as an unavoidable byproduct of urban life «rather than as something that was designed by design.»

choices.text: OMIT the underlined portion, ending the sentence after "urban life."

why.A: "designed by design" repeats itself.
why.B: Correct — removes the redundancy.
why.C: Drops the "rather than" and with it the comparison. The sentence stops contrasting two ways of treating noise and simply asserts that urban life is undesigned.
why.D: The contrast between byproduct and design is what the paragraph goes on to argue about. Cutting it leaves a sentence nobody would disagree with and nothing to develop.

context: A handful of municipalities «have begun writing acoustic standards into their planning codes.»

choices.text: has begun writing acoustic standards into its planning codes.
have begun writing acoustic standards into its planning codes.
has begun writing acoustic standards into their planning codes.

why.A: Correct — "a handful of municipalities" is plural, and "their" agrees.
why.B: Treats a plural subject as singular.
why.C: Mismatched verb and pronoun number.
why.D: Mismatched in the other direction.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence about pedestrians with limited vision. If deleted, the essay would primarily lose:

choices.text: the explanation for why artificial vehicle sounds are now required.
a transition into the Oslo measurements.
nothing, since the requirement is already stated in the opening paragraph.

why.A: Correct — that sentence supplies the causal reason for the regulation described next.
why.B: No accident statistics appear.
why.C: The Oslo paragraph precedes it.
why.D: The requirement is stated, but its rationale appears only here.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to persuade city governments to write acoustic standards into their planning codes. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it says cities could specify sound the way they specify building height.
Yes, because it shows that quieter streets in Oslo meant fewer sleep disturbances.
No, because it reports the planners’ proposal and leaves its future an open question.
No, because it never mentions any city that has written such standards.

why.A: That sentence reports what acoustic planners argue; the writer never adopts it as a recommendation.
why.B: The Oslo evidence is about the effect of electric vehicles, not a case for planning codes.
why.C: Correct — the essay ends by saying that whether such standards survive budget committees remains open, which is description rather than persuasion.
why.D: It does: a handful of municipalities have begun writing acoustic standards into planning codes.

context: Four hundred feet inside a sandstone mountain «on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, at seventy-eight degrees north, sits» a room kept far below freezing.

choices.text: on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen at seventy-eight degrees north sits
on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, at seventy-eight degrees north sits
on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen at seventy-eight degrees north, sits

why.A: Correct — the nonessential locating phrase is bracketed by a matched pair of commas.
why.B: Removes both commas, fusing three modifiers together.
why.C: Opens the interruption without closing it.
why.D: Closes it without opening it.

context: It holds roughly 1.3 million seed samples, sealed in foil packets inside black plastic boxes, that «is stacked» on steel shelving.

why.A: The relative pronoun refers to plural "boxes."
why.B: Correct — plural antecedent takes a plural verb.
why.C: Singular and shifts tense.
why.D: Active voice reverses the meaning.

context: Svalbard simply holds a copy in case a working bank fails. «Nevertheless,» banks do fail.

why.A: "Nevertheless" implies a contrast that does not exist — the next sentence confirms the premise.
why.B: Correct — the blunt two-word sentence lands hardest with no connector.
why.C: Failures are not an example of holding a copy.
why.D: The sentences agree rather than contrast.

context: In 2015, researchers «make» the vault’s first withdrawal, retrieving samples deposited by a bank in Aleppo.

why.A: Present tense contradicts the 2015 date.
why.B: Correct — simple past for a dated completed event.
why.C: Present perfect conflicts with a specified past year.
why.D: Future tense is impossible here.

context: The material was regenerated in Lebanon and Morocco and «then they redeposited it» in Svalbard three years later.

why.A: Shifts from passive to active with a new subject, breaking the parallel.
why.B: Correct — shares the subject and the passive "was" with "regenerated."
why.C: Needlessly progressive and wordy.
why.D: A noun phrase that garbles the sentence.

context: The site was chosen «due to the fact that it offered redundancy» rather than convenience.

choices.text: owing to the fact of redundancy

why.A: "due to the fact that" is five words for one.
why.B: Correct — the concise phrasing keeps the contrast with "convenience" parallel.
why.C: "Redundantly" describes how the choosing was done, which changes the meaning, and it leaves "rather than convenience" with nothing to contrast against.
why.D: "Owing to the fact of" keeps the padding and loses the verb, so the sentence no longer says what redundancy was offered by.

context: The permafrost would hold the seeds frozen for decades, «the refrigeration and the power grid could both fail permanently.»

choices.text: even if the refrigeration and the power grid both failed permanently.
the refrigeration and power grid both failing permanently.
; the refrigeration and the power grid both failing permanently

why.A: Comma splice between two independent clauses.
why.B: Correct — subordinating the second clause fixes the splice and states the intended condition.
why.C: A participial phrase that obscures the conditional meaning.
why.D: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and "failing" leaves this one without a finite verb.

context: Meltwater flowed partway in. «It» froze before reaching the seed room, and no material was damaged.

why.A: Correct — "it" clearly refers to the singular meltwater in the preceding sentence.
why.B: Plural, with no plural antecedent.
why.C: Vaguer than "it" and points to the whole situation.
why.D: "Which" cannot begin an independent sentence.

context: Norway has since spent roughly twenty million dollars «waterproofing the tunnel and relocating» heat-generating equipment outside the mountain.

choices.text: to waterproof the tunnel and relocating
waterproofing the tunnel and to relocate
for the waterproofing of the tunnel and relocating

why.A: Correct — two parallel gerunds follow "spent."
why.B: Mixes an infinitive with a gerund.
why.C: Mixes them in the other order.
why.D: Mixes a noun phrase with a gerund and adds padding.

stem: The writer is considering adding: "Spitsbergen has a population of roughly 2,500 people." Should it be added to the paragraph about site selection?

choices.text: Yes, because it explains why the location is politically quiet and geologically stable.
Yes, because it provides useful geographic background.
No, because population size is unrelated to the redundancy criteria the paragraph lists.
No, because the essay has already given the island’s population.

why.A: The paragraph attributes political quiet to Norway, not to population.
why.B: Interesting but not responsive to the paragraph’s focus.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph lists permafrost, geology, sea level, and politics; population is not among them.
why.D: No population figure appears anywhere in the essay.

stem: The final paragraph opens "The incident is often reported as a near-disaster." For this to make sense, it must follow:

choices.text: the paragraph describing the 2016 meltwater event.
the paragraph about the Aleppo withdrawal.
the opening description of the vault.
the paragraph listing the number of gene banks.

why.A: Correct — "the incident" is a backward-pointing phrase requiring a specific event already described.
why.B: The Aleppo withdrawal is presented as a success, not an incident.
why.C: No incident has occurred yet at that point.
why.D: That paragraph describes the network, not an event.

stem: The last sentence of the essay primarily serves to:

choices.text: argue that the vault should be relocated.
reframe the 2016 event as evidence the backup system worked as intended.
criticize the press for its inaccurate reporting of the 2016 meltwater flooding.
introduce a new threat to the vault.

why.A: Relocation is never proposed.
why.B: Correct — it redefines a "near-disaster" as a backup doing its job by exposing a flaw harmlessly.
why.C: It contrasts framings without attacking reporters.
why.D: Nothing new arrives in the last sentence. It reinterprets the 2016 meltwater that the essay has already described rather than introducing a further danger.

context: He talked about the walk-in cooler, the third burner that never lit properly, «and the only one of his produce vendors, who shorted him on tomatoes for two years.»

choices.text: and the only one of his produce vendors who shorted him on tomatoes for two years.
and the only one of his produce vendors, who shorted him on tomatoes, for two years.
and the only one of his produce vendors; who shorted him on tomatoes for two years.

why.A: "The only one of his produce vendors" needs the clause to say which one, so the clause is essential and takes no comma.
why.B: Correct — essential relative clauses are not set off.
why.C: Adds a comma that severs the time phrase from its verb.
why.D: A semicolon cannot precede a dependent clause.

context: «I working there the summer before college,» mostly on the dish pit.

choices.text: I worked there the summer before college,
Working there the summer before college,
Me working there the summer before college,

why.A: "working" is a participle, not a conjugated verb.
why.B: Correct — supplies a past-tense main verb.
why.C: Leaves the sentence with no subject or main verb.
why.D: Uses an object pronoun and still lacks a verb.

context: By eight o’clock my shirt «will be» soaked through and my hands would have gone pink.

why.A: Future tense conflicts with the past-tense narration.
why.B: Correct — "would be" matches "would have gone" and conveys habitual past action.
why.C: Present perfect breaks the sequence.
why.D: Present tense clashes with the memoir’s past frame.

context: «Leaning against the ice machine, a minute or two would pass before he went back out.»

choices.text: Leaning against the ice machine, he said nothing for a minute or two before going back out.
Leaning against the ice machine, nothing was said for a minute or two before he went back out.
A minute or two, leaning against the ice machine, would pass.

why.A: Dangling modifier — a minute cannot lean against a machine.
why.B: Correct — places "he," the one leaning, right after the modifier.
why.C: "nothing" cannot lean either.
why.D: Buries the modifier without supplying an actor.

context: On the Friday of the Fourth of July weekend we did two hundred and eleven covers, «which was the most and highest number the room had ever done before previously.»

choices.text: the most the room had ever done.
OMIT the underlined portion, ending the sentence after "covers."

why.A: "most and highest" and "ever before previously" each repeat themselves.
why.B: Correct — a tight appositive with no redundancy.
why.C: Cuts the room out of the claim, so the sentence now says two hundred and eleven covers is a record for anyone anywhere rather than for this kitchen.
why.D: Two hundred and eleven covers means nothing to a reader who does not know the room. The clause is redundant in its wording, not in its work.

context: He took the panel off with a butter knife and cleared a lodged bottle cap out of «the drains» opening.

why.A: Possession requires an apostrophe.
why.B: Correct — one drain, so apostrophe before the s.
why.C: Marks a plural possessive, but only one drain is described.
why.D: This adds a plural possessive apostrophe and then a second s on top of it, which no possessive form in English uses.

context: He had it running in under four minutes. «However,» he stood up, looked at the stack of pans, and started washing.

why.A: There is no contrast between fixing the machine and washing pans.
why.B: Correct — the relationship is simple sequence.
why.C: Also signals a contrast that does not exist.
why.D: Washing the pans is not an instance of fixing the machine.

context: He worked the sink and I worked the machine, and «us two» cleared the stack in twenty minutes.

why.A: "us" is an object pronoun but this is the clause’s subject.
why.B: Correct — subject pronoun performing the action.
why.C: Both are object pronouns.
why.D: A reflexive cannot serve as a subject.

context: It was the only time I remember working beside him at something we «were equally able to do and that was shared between us.»

choices.text: both were able and it was shared.

why.A: The added clause repeats the idea and breaks the sentence’s rhythm.
why.B: Correct — one clean relative clause carries the meaning.
why.C: Mixes a verb with a gerund.
why.D: Shifts subject mid-clause.

context: The station was six feet of stainless steel and a machine that ran a ninety-second cycle at «a temperature of one hundred and eighty degrees of heat.»

choices.text: a hot temperature of one hundred and eighty degrees.
one hundred and eighty degrees of temperature.

why.A: "a temperature of" and "of heat" both restate what degrees already convey.
why.B: Correct — the unit alone is sufficient.
why.C: "hot temperature" is redundant.
why.D: "degrees of temperature" repeats itself.

stem: The writer is considering deleting "which is where you put a seventeen-year-old who has never worked in a kitchen." If deleted, the essay would primarily lose:

choices.text: a wry explanation of why the narrator was assigned to that particular station.
a description of how the industrial dishwasher actually operated.
evidence that the father was a demanding employer.
nothing, since the narrator’s age is given elsewhere.

why.A: Correct — the aside supplies both the reason for the assignment and the narrator’s self-deprecating voice.
why.B: The machine is described in the next sentence.
why.C: The clause implies kitchen convention, not the father’s character.
why.D: The narrator’s age appears only in this clause.

stem: The closing sentence is primarily intended to:

choices.text: explain why the narrator decided against ever taking a restaurant job of his own.
reveal how little his father ever shared.
describe the physical difficulty of working the dish pit.
criticize the father for having missed so many family birthdays over the years.

why.A: No career decision is stated.
why.B: Correct — the narrator recognizes the father spent every birthday in a room he never described.
why.C: The physical detail appears earlier and serves a different purpose.
why.D: The tone is recognition, not blame.

context: Which choice correctly punctuates the underlined portion at [4]?

choices.text: drill, which is the most requested item in the collection,
drill which is the most requested item in the collection,
drill, which is the most requested item in the collection

why.B: 'which is the most requested item in the collection' is a nonrestrictive clause: remove it and 'Members who arrive for a drill often leave...' still names the same members. A nonrestrictive clause takes a comma on both sides.
why.A: Leaves the clause unpunctuated, so the sentence runs on and the reader loses the main verb.
why.C: Closes the clause but never opens it, so only one of the two required commas is present.
why.D: Opens the clause but never closes it, leaving 'often leave' stranded outside the interruption.

context: Which choice best replaces the underlined portion at [3] without losing meaning?

choices.text: The reason for the library working so well and continuing to work is that

why.B: 'The reason that ... is that' is a long frame around a simple causal claim, and 'works so well and continues to work well' says one thing twice. 'The library works because' keeps the meaning in four words.
why.A: Keeps both the padded frame and the redundant pair of verbs.
why.C: Removes the wordiness and the connective with it, leaving "The library works most tools sit idle" — two clauses with nothing joining them.
why.D: Is longer than the original and adds a nominalization on top of the redundancy.

context: «Its» been three months since I first found the bike behind the paint cans.

why.C: "It's" is the contraction of "it has" and is needed here; "Its" without an apostrophe is the possessive form, and "Its'" is not a correct spelling of either.
why.A: Uses "Its," the possessive form, where the contraction "It's" ("it has") is needed.
why.B: Adds a second, unnecessary apostrophe after the contraction.
why.D: Places the apostrophe after the s, a placement that is never correct for this word.

context: My «grandfathers» old toolbox held every wrench I needed.

why.A: One grandfather possesses the toolbox, so the singular possessive "grandfather's" is correct — apostrophe before the s.
why.B: Leaves out the apostrophe needed to show that the toolbox belongs to one grandfather.
why.C: Places the apostrophe after the s, which would indicate the toolbox belongs to more than one grandfather.
why.D: Adds a second possessive marker that doesn't belong.

context: «Bikes' from the 1970's» often used steel frames instead of aluminum.

why.B: Neither "bikes" nor "1970s" is possessive — both are simple plurals, and plain plurals never take an apostrophe, including plural decades.
why.A: Adds an apostrophe to both "Bikes" and "1970s," though neither is possessive — both are simple plurals.
why.C: Fixes "Bikes'" but still incorrectly adds an apostrophe to the plural decade "1970s".
why.D: Fixes "1970s" but still incorrectly adds an apostrophe to the plural "Bikes".

context: «After three weekends of scrubbing» I finally saw the bicycle's original blue paint beneath the grime.

why.A: "After three weekends of scrubbing" is an introductory phrase and needs a comma before the main clause begins.
why.B: Leaves out the comma needed after the introductory phrase "After three weekends of scrubbing".
why.C: Places a comma in the middle of the introductory phrase itself instead of after it.
why.D: Adds an unnecessary comma directly after "After" in addition to the one after the phrase.

context: I replaced the rusted «chain the cracked seat and» both flat tires before testing the brakes.

why.B: "The rusted chain," "the cracked seat," and "both flat tires" are three items in a series and each needs a comma separating it from the next, including one before "and."
why.A: Has no commas at all separating the three items in the list, leaving them run together.
why.C: Leaves "chain" and "the cracked seat" run together with no comma between the first two items in the series.
why.D: Adds a stray extra comma directly after "and" that doesn't belong.

context: Which choice provides the correct punctuation for this sentence that opens Paragraph 3? "Maple Street Books a single-room shop in a midsized city offers a case study in what changed."

choices.text: Maple Street Books a single-room shop in a midsized city offers a case study in what changed.
Maple Street Books, a single-room shop in a midsized city offers a case study in what changed.
Maple Street Books a single-room shop, in a midsized city, offers a case study in what changed.
Maple Street Books, a single-room shop in a midsized city, offers a case study in what changed.

why.D: "A single-room shop in a midsized city" is a nonessential appositive describing Maple Street Books — it needs a comma both before and after it to be set off correctly from the rest of the sentence.
why.A: Leaves the nonessential appositive phrase completely unset off, making the sentence hard to parse.
why.B: Opens the appositive with a comma but never closes it, leaving the sentence unbalanced.
why.C: Sets off the wrong words — "in a midsized city" is not the nonessential phrase that needs framing.

context: The «bicycle my grandfather had ridden every summer for two decades,» finally looked new again.

choices.text: bicycle, my grandfather had ridden every summer for two decades,
bicycle my grandfather had ridden, every summer for two decades,
bicycle my grandfather had ridden every summer for two decades

why.D: "The bicycle my grandfather had ridden every summer for two decades" is the complete subject, and "finally looked new again" is the verb phrase. A single comma should never separate a subject from its verb, no matter how long the subject is.
why.A: Places a single comma between the sentence's subject and its verb, which is never correct.
why.B: Sets off "my grandfather had ridden every summer for two decades" as if it were nonessential, but it's a restrictive clause identifying which bicycle, so this changes the sentence's meaning.
why.C: Splits "every summer for two decades" off with commas in a spot that awkwardly separates it from the verb it modifies.

context: Which choice most effectively completes this sentence from Paragraph 4, keeping its structure parallel? "Volunteering at the clinic taught me patience, humility, and ___."

choices.text: how to trust people I had just met
to trust people I had just met
trust in people I had just met
how trusting people I had just met

why.C: "Patience" and "humility" are both simple noun phrases, so the third item in the list needs to match that pattern. "Trust in people I had just met" continues the noun-phrase structure; the other options shift to a different grammatical form.
why.A: Breaks the parallel structure by switching from a noun phrase ("patience, humility") to a "how to" clause.
why.B: Still switches to an infinitive clause rather than continuing the noun-phrase pattern of "patience, humility".
why.D: An awkward gerund construction that still doesn't match the simple noun form of "patience" and "humility".

context: Which choice most effectively revises this sentence from Paragraph 4 to fix its misplaced modifier? "Exhausted after a sixteen-hour shift, the walk back to the volunteer house felt endless."

choices.text: Exhausted after a sixteen-hour shift, I found the walk back to the volunteer house felt endless.
Exhausted after a sixteen-hour shift, the volunteer house's walk felt endless to me.
Being exhausted after a sixteen-hour shift, the walk back to the volunteer house felt endless.

why.A: "Exhausted after a sixteen-hour shift" logically describes the narrator, not the walk itself. The sentence needs a subject capable of being exhausted — "I" — immediately after the introductory phrase.
why.B: The opening phrase "Exhausted after a sixteen-hour shift" describes a person, but the sentence's actual subject is "the walk," which cannot be exhausted.
why.C: Still attaches "Exhausted" to "the volunteer house's walk" rather than to a person, leaving the same underlying problem.
why.D: Adding "Being" doesn't fix the core issue — "the walk" is still the thing being described as exhausted.

context: Which choice most clearly conveys that the narrator gave the last of the bandages to the child with the deepest cut and to no one else? "During a shortage in July, I only gave the last of the bandages to the child with the deepest cut."

choices.text: During a shortage in July, I gave only the last of the bandages to the child with the deepest cut.
During a shortage in July, only I gave the last of the bandages to the child with the deepest cut.
During a shortage in July, I gave the last of the bandages only to the child with the deepest cut.

why.D: The intended meaning is that the bandages went to one specific child and no one else. "Only" needs to sit directly before "to the child with the deepest cut" to restrict the recipient rather than the action, the item given, or the giver.
why.A: As placed, "only" modifies "gave," suggesting giving was the sole action taken, rather than restricting who received the bandages.
why.B: Places "only" so it modifies "the last of the bandages," implying just those bandages (not other supplies) were given, a different meaning.
why.C: Places "only" so it modifies "I," implying the narrator was the sole person who gave out bandages, a third distinct meaning.

context: Which choice most clearly completes this sentence from Paragraph 3? "I set the clinic's spare thermometer next to the donated stethoscope one afternoon, and then I accidentally dropped ___ into a bin of gauze."

why.B: With two singular objects mentioned in the same sentence, "it" could refer to either one. Naming the specific object directly removes the ambiguity.
why.A: Could refer to either the thermometer or the stethoscope, since both are singular nouns mentioned just before it.
why.C: "them" is plural and doesn't clearly match either singular antecedent, so it doesn't resolve the ambiguity.
why.D: Still doesn't specify which of the two objects was dropped.

context: Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Paragraph 4? "The head nurse thanked my fellow volunteers and ___ for staying late every night that week."

why.D: "Volunteers and ___" is the object of the verb "thanked," so it needs an object pronoun. "Myself" is reflexive and requires the subject to be "I" in the same clause, which isn't the case here, so "me" is correct.
why.A: A reflexive pronoun like "myself" needs an antecedent in the same clause referring to the same person as the subject — here, the subject is "the head nurse," not "I".
why.B: Uses the subject form of the pronoun where an object form is needed, since "volunteers and ___" is the object of "thanked".
why.C: Still misuses "myself" as an object pronoun, just in a different position in the sentence.

context: Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Paragraph 4? "The doctor ___ I most admired at the clinic was the one ___ stayed latest every single night."

why.C: The first blank is the object of "admired" (I admired whom), so it needs "whom." The second blank is the subject of "stayed" (who stayed), so it needs "who."
why.A: Reverses both blanks: the first is the object of "admired" and needs "whom," and the second is the subject of "stayed" and needs "who."
why.B: Correctly fixes the first blank but "whom" still cannot serve as the subject of "stayed" in the second blank.
why.D: Correctly fixes the second blank but "who" is still incorrect as the object of "admired" in the first blank.

context: The garage held everything I «needed» old rags, a can of chain oil, and a wire brush.

why.C: A colon is the conventional mark for introducing a list after a complete independent clause like "The garage held everything I needed."
why.A: Has no punctuation at all introducing the list that follows.
why.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and "old rags, a can of chain oil, and a wire brush" is not an independent clause.
why.D: Uses a comma to introduce the list where a stronger mark is conventional after a complete independent clause.

context: The «wheels—warped from years in a damp garage, spun» unevenly even after truing.

choices.text: wheels—warped from years in a damp garage—spun
wheels—warped from years in a damp garage; spun
wheels warped from years in a damp garage—spun

why.A: "Warped from years in a damp garage" interrupts the sentence and needs matching punctuation on both sides. A pair of dashes, opening and closing, is the consistent fix.
why.B: Opens the interrupting phrase with a dash but closes it with a comma, an inconsistent pair.
why.C: Opens with a dash but closes with a semicolon, an inconsistent pair.
why.D: Includes only a closing dash with no matching opening punctuation, leaving the interruption unbalanced.

context: The frame was «solid however» the fork had bent just enough to throw off the steering.

why.B: "However" here is a conjunctive adverb joining two independent clauses; that combination needs a semicolon before it and, conventionally, a comma after it.
why.A: Has no punctuation at all around "however," fusing two independent clauses into a run-on.
why.C: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses, even with a conjunctive adverb like "however" between them.
why.D: Commas on both sides of "however" still leave a comma holding two independent clauses together, which is a comma splice.

context: What I loved about restoring the bike «was:» the slow return of small details, like the manufacturer's decal, that I'd assumed were gone forever.

why.D: A colon, semicolon, or dash used this way must follow a complete independent clause. "What I loved about restoring the bike was" is incomplete without its complement, so none of them belong — the sentence just continues directly.
why.A: A colon should not follow "was" — "What I loved about restoring the bike was" is not a complete independent clause on its own.
why.B: A semicolon has the same requirement as a colon here — an independent clause before it — and "was" alone still doesn't complete one.
why.C: A dash used this way has the same underlying problem: "was" is not a complete clause for it to follow.

context: The bike had not been ridden in ten «years,» the tires were flat as pancakes.

why.A: "The bike had not been ridden in ten years" and "the tires were flat as pancakes" are both independent clauses. A semicolon correctly joins them without a conjunction.
why.B: Joins two independent clauses with only a comma, a comma splice.
why.C: Removes the comma entirely, fusing two independent clauses into a run-on with no punctuation between them.
why.D: "However" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma on each side of it still leaves two independent clauses spliced together.

context: Which choice best joins these two word groups from Paragraph 1? "My grandfather taught me to ride on this same bike. Back when the chain still turned freely and the paint still held its shine."

choices.text: My grandfather taught me to ride on this same bike, back when the chain still turned freely and the paint still held its shine.
My grandfather taught me to ride on this same bike; back when the chain still turned freely and the paint still held its shine.
My grandfather taught me to ride on this same bike. And back when the chain still turned freely and the paint still held its shine.

why.B: "Back when the chain still turned freely and the paint still held its shine" is a dependent clause with no subject-and-verb main clause of its own — it can't stand alone. Attaching it to the sentence before it with a comma fixes the fragment.
why.A: Leaves "Back when the chain still turned freely and the paint still held its shine" standing alone as a sentence fragment — it has no independent clause.
why.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and "back when..." is a dependent clause, not an independent one.
why.D: Still leaves the second word group as a fragment — adding "And" doesn't give it an independent clause.

context: Rust had crept along the handlebars and eaten into the gear «housing, that» was the part that worried me most.

why.D: "Rust had crept along the handlebars and eaten into the gear housing" and "that was the part that worried me most" are both independent clauses, so they need a period, a semicolon, or a comma with a coordinating conjunction — not a bare comma.
why.A: Joins two independent clauses with only a comma, a comma splice.
why.B: The comma after "and" separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and "which was..." is a dependent relative clause, not independent.

context: Which choice is the most effective version of this sentence from Paragraph 3? "Once the wheels spun true again, I moved on to the brakes, which had seized entirely."

choices.text: Once the wheels spun true again I moved on to the brakes, which had seized entirely.
Once the wheels spun true again, I moved on to the brakes; which had seized entirely.
Once the wheels spun true again, I moved on to the brakes. Which had seized entirely.

why.C: The sentence as written is already correct: an introductory dependent clause followed by a comma, an independent clause, and a nonessential relative clause. Every alternative introduces a new error instead of fixing one.
why.A: Removes the comma that should follow the introductory dependent clause "Once the wheels spun true again".
why.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and "which had seized entirely" is a dependent relative clause.
why.D: Turns "Which had seized entirely" into a sentence fragment with no independent clause of its own.

context: Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Paragraph 2? "The old clinic, along with its two overworked nurses, ___ to keep up with the number of patients each week."

why.D: "Along with its two overworked nurses" is a prepositional phrase, not part of the subject. The true subject is the singular "clinic," and the essay is told in the past, so the verb is the singular past "struggled."
why.A: Agrees with the plural-sounding "nurses," but the sentence's actual subject is the singular "clinic".
why.B: Uses a plural auxiliary that doesn't agree with the singular subject "clinic".
why.C: Uses a plural verb form that doesn't agree with the singular subject "clinic".

context: Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Paragraph 1? "Neither the doctor nor the volunteers ___ prepared for how many families would arrive that first week."

why.C: In a "neither...nor" construction, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it — here, the plural "volunteers" — so the correct verb is "were," not "was."
why.A: With "neither...nor," the verb should agree with the nearer subject, the plural "volunteers," not the singular "doctor".
why.B: Uses a singular-implying form that doesn't agree with the nearer plural subject "volunteers".
why.D: Besides being the wrong number, this is also the wrong tense for a sentence describing a past event.

context: Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Paragraph 3? "Each of the children who visited the clinic that week ___ a small paper bracelet with the child's name written on it."

why.A: Correct — "Each" is the subject and is always singular, whatever plural noun follows it in the prepositional phrase, and the sentence is set in the past ("visited ... that week"), so the verb is the singular past "carried."
why.B: Agrees with the plural "children," but the subject is the singular "Each" — and the present tense clashes with "visited."
why.C: Uses a plural, past-progressive form that doesn't agree with the singular subject "Each".
why.D: Uses a plural auxiliary that doesn't agree with the singular subject "Each".

context: Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Paragraph 1? "On my first day, I ___ into the clinic not knowing a single word of the local language."

why.A: The essay narrates events from a completed summer using simple past tense throughout. "Walked" matches that established tense; the other options shift to present, present perfect, or future.
why.B: Present tense, inconsistent with the simple past tense the rest of the essay's narrative uses.
why.C: Present perfect, still inconsistent with the essay's simple past narrative tense.
why.D: Future tense, which doesn't fit an event the essay describes as already having happened.

context: Which choice most precisely completes this sentence from Paragraph 1? "By the time I arrived, the morning line of patients ___ around the building."

why.B: "By the time I arrived" sets a past reference point, and the line had already formed before that point — the past perfect ("had already stretched") is the tense built for exactly this sequence.
why.A: Present tense clashes with the past "arrived" that sets the time of the sentence.
why.C: Present perfect is inconsistent with the essay's simple past narrative tense.
why.D: Present progressive clashes with the past "arrived" and describes a line still forming rather than one already formed.

context: Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Paragraph 2? "Each morning I unlocked the supply closet, sorted the donated medicine by expiration date, and ___ the waiting room chairs into neat rows before the doors opened."

why.D: The sentence lists three actions that all happened each morning, and the first two ("unlocked," "sorted") are past tense. The third verb must match: "organized."
why.A: Present tense, breaking the parallel past-tense list started by "unlocked" and "sorted".
why.B: Present progressive, still breaking the parallel past-tense list.
why.C: Future tense, still breaking the parallel past-tense list.

context: Which choice most effectively eliminates the redundancy in this sentence from Paragraph 2? "Turning a slab of concrete into a garden meant starting with almost nothing at all, starting from a place with no plants, no soil, and nothing green anywhere in sight."

choices.text: , beginning from a completely bare and empty space,
, which is to say a place utterly without plants or soil,
(Omit the underlined portion, ending the sentence after "almost nothing at all.")

why.D: "Almost nothing at all" already conveys the idea completely; the added clause listing plants, soil, and greenery just restates it. The cleanest fix is to cut the restatement entirely.
why.A: Leaves the redundant restatement of "almost nothing at all" in place.
why.B: Still restates the same idea in different words instead of cutting the redundancy.
why.C: Adds a third restatement of the same idea rather than removing the redundant ones.

context: Which choice most effectively eliminates the redundancy in this sentence from Paragraph 3? "The store survived its worst year, a year that was the hardest one it had faced, by turning its aisles into a weekly meeting place rather than a pure point of sale."

choices.text: (Omit the underlined portion, ending the clause after "worst year".)
during a time period that was tough,

why.B: "Worst year" and "a year that was the hardest one it had faced" say the same thing twice. Since "worst year" already conveys the idea completely, the clause adds no new information and should be cut.
why.A: Leaves the redundant restatement of "worst year" in place.
why.C: Still restates the same idea in different words rather than removing the redundancy.
why.D: Adds a third, equally redundant restatement of the same idea.

context: Which choice most effectively eliminates the wordiness in this sentence from Paragraph 5, without losing any of its meaning? "The lot at Fifth and Poplar will never make anyone rich due to the fact that it only produces a few hundred pounds of vegetables a year, which is not enough to matter to anyone's grocery bill in a significant way."

choices.text: The lot at Fifth and Poplar will never make anyone rich; it produces only a few hundred pounds of vegetables a year.
The lot at Fifth and Poplar will never make anyone rich; it produces only a few hundred pounds of vegetables a year, not enough to matter to anyone's grocery bill.

The lot at Fifth and Poplar will never make anyone rich because it only produces a few hundred pounds of vegetables a year, which is not enough to matter to anyone's grocery bill in a significant way.

why.C: "Due to the fact that" can be cut to "because" — or, as here, to a semicolon linking two related independent clauses — and "in a significant way" adds nothing "not enough to matter" doesn't already say. Fixing only one of the two leaves the sentence still needlessly wordy.
why.A: Keeps both wordy constructions, "due to the fact that" and "in a significant way," that the sentence doesn't need.
why.B: The shortest version on offer, and it drops the clause that tells the reader why a few hundred pounds is a small amount. The question asks for concision without loss of meaning.
why.D: Fixes "due to the fact that" but leaves "in a significant way" in place.

context: Which choice is most consistent with the tone established elsewhere in the essay for this sentence from Paragraph 5? "By the end of the summer, the clinic's tiny staff had become like family to me, and leaving them was totally a bummer."

choices.text: and leaving them was super sad
and leaving them was kind of a drag
and leaving them was more difficult than I had expected

why.D: The essay's voice throughout is reflective and personal but not slangy. "Totally a bummer" breaks that register; "more difficult than I had expected" keeps the same sincerity without the clashing slang.
why.A: "totally a bummer" is casual slang that clashes with the essay's consistently reflective, personal tone.
why.B: "Super" as an intensifier is spoken slang. It swaps one casual register for another instead of fixing it.
why.C: "A drag" is the same kind of slang idiom as "a bummer" — a synonym for the problem, not a repair.

context: Which choice is most consistent with the tone of the rest of this sentence from Paragraph 5? "I will never forget the day a mother grabbed my hand and thanked me, her eyes wet with relief, for basically not letting her kid die."

choices.text: for saving her kid, like, basically
for staying by her son's side through the worst night of his illness
for doing my job that night
