why.C: The sentence builds toward genuine emotional weight ("grabbed my hand," "eyes wet with relief"), and its ending needs to match that register. "Staying by her son's side through the worst night of his illness" is sincere and specific; the other options are either too casual or too flat.
why.A: "basically not letting her kid die" is jarringly blunt and casual next to the sentence's otherwise formal, emotional phrasing ("her eyes wet with relief").
why.B: Still casual, and adds a filler word ("like") that makes the register clash even worse.
why.D: Too flat and dismissive for the context, undercutting the emotional weight the rest of the sentence is building rather than matching it.

context: Which choice most precisely conveys the scale described by the rest of this sentence from Paragraph 2? "The clinic was very busy every single morning, with lines of patients waiting before the doors even opened."

why.C: The detail that follows — lines forming before the doors even opened — describes a clinic struggling to keep pace with demand, not just generally "busy." "Overwhelmed" precisely matches that scale.
why.A: "very busy" is vague and doesn't capture the specific scale suggested by lines forming before the doors even opened.
why.B: Even vaguer and more informal than "very busy," moving further from precision rather than closer to it.
why.D: Doesn't convey a sense of busyness at all, leaving the sentence's own supporting detail unexplained.

context: Which choice most precisely describes the effect of the nurse's calm instructions in this sentence from Paragraph 3? "The nurse's calm instructions kept the frightened children ___ during their shots, no matter how loudly they had been crying moments before."

why.A: The sentence is describing a change from frightened and crying to soothed and cooperative — an emotional state, not just a noise level. "Calm" precisely matches that intended meaning and echoes the "calm instructions" that caused it.
why.B: "Kept the children ___" needs an adjective describing the children; "quietly" is an adverb.
why.C: Overshoots the effect: children getting shots can be soothed, but nothing in the sentence says they became happy.
why.D: Describes physical stillness, not the calming emotional effect the nurse's instructions produced.

context: The four sentences in Paragraph 2 are numbered [1] through [4]. For the paragraph to proceed in the most logical order, how should the sentences be arranged?

why.D: The paragraph moves logically from general framing [1], to demolition [2], to soil delivery [3], to the planting result [4] — each step depends on the one before it, so the written order is already correct.
why.A: Opening with the sledgehammer work before the general framing sentence leaves the reader without context for why demolition was happening.
why.B: Places the topsoil delivery before the pavement removal it depends on, reversing the actual construction sequence.
why.C: Opens with the June planting result before any of the preparation work is described, undercutting the paragraph's step-by-step structure.

context: If the writer were to delete Sentence 3 from Paragraph 3 ("None of these events sold many books outright."), the paragraph would primarily lose:

choices.text: a concession that sets up the contrast completed by the paragraph's final sentence.
a transition that connects Paragraph 3 to Paragraph 4.
evidence that the book club at Maple Street Books was profitable.
the paragraph's only reference to Maple Street Books by name anywhere in the whole essay.

why.A: Sentence 3 concedes that the events didn't drive direct sales, which sets up Sentence 4's contrast: the events mattered for a different reason, customer loyalty. Removing it would make the final sentence's "Together" feel unearned.
why.B: Sentence 3 doesn't reference Paragraph 4 or curated selection at all.
why.C: The sentence says the opposite — that the events did not sell many books.
why.D: The store is named in Sentence 1, not Sentence 3.

context: The writer is considering moving Paragraph 4 so that it appears immediately after Paragraph 1, before the current Paragraph 2. Would this be a logical change?

No, because Paragraph 4 responds to the specific example in Paragraph 3, and moving it earlier would break that connection.
Yes, because Paragraph 4's discussion of curated selection is unrelated to the Maple Street Books example, so its position doesn't matter.

why.A: Paragraph 4 discusses curated selection, not background needed to understand the growth statistics in Paragraph 2.
why.C: The two paragraphs are related — Paragraph 4 adds a second reason alongside the community programming shown in Paragraph 3.
why.D: Paragraph 1 discusses price competition and shipping speed, not curated selection.

context: The writer is considering moving Paragraph 4 (beginning "Poplar Street's garden is not unusual") so that it appears immediately after Paragraph 1, before the current Paragraph 2. Would this be a logical change?

choices.text: Yes, because readers need to know gardens are a national pattern before reading about one specific garden.
Yes, because Paragraph 4 and Paragraph 1 both mention the lot's location, so they belong together.
No, because Paragraph 4 generalizes from the Poplar Street example that Paragraphs 2 and 3 build.
No, because Paragraph 1 already discusses the composting classes in some detail.

why.C: Paragraph 4 opens by generalizing ("is not unusual") from the specific Poplar Street story just told in Paragraphs 2 and 3. Moving it before that story would leave the generalization referring to an example the reader hasn't read yet.

why.B: Paragraph 4 never mentions the lot's location — it discusses land trusts and agriculture programs nationally.
why.D: Paragraph 1 discusses the lot's neglected condition and the city's permission, not composting classes.

context: The writer is considering adding the following true sentence to the end of Paragraph 1: "The fence itself had rusted through in three places, and one panel had fallen over completely." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: Yes, because it explains why the city eventually agreed to let residents use the lot.
No, because the paragraph already contains enough descriptive detail and does not need any more.
No, because Paragraph 1 is focused on the neighbors' opinions, not on physical descriptions of the lot.
Yes, because it adds a concrete detail that reinforces the paragraph's picture of a neglected lot.

why.A: The sentence describes the fence's condition, not the city's reasoning for granting permission.
why.B: Isn't a real reason to reject true, on-topic, concrete supporting detail — vague sufficiency isn't a relevance test.
why.C: Misstates the paragraph's focus — it already describes the fence, the slab, and the trash directly.

context: The writer is considering adding the following true statement to the end of Paragraph 1: "Many analysts also blamed the trend on falling literacy rates among young readers." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: Yes, because it identifies literacy rates as the primary cause of the closures the paragraph describes.
No, because the paragraph's focus is price competition and the sentence adds an unrelated claim.
Yes, because any true statement about the bookselling industry strengthens the paragraph's argument.
No, because the paragraph never mentions young readers anywhere else in the essay.

why.B: Paragraph 1 builds a specific case: price competition and fast shipping explain the decline. A new, undeveloped cause introduced in the final sentence breaks that focus rather than supporting it, so the addition should not be made.
why.A: Overstates the sentence's role — the paragraph never treats literacy as a cause at all, let alone the primary one.
why.C: Confuses factual accuracy with relevance — a true statement can still be off-topic.
why.D: Gives the right answer for the wrong reason — the issue is relevance to this paragraph's focus, not whether the topic recurs elsewhere.

context: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after Sentence 3 in Paragraph 3: "The book club now has a two-year waiting list for new members." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: Yes, because it shows that Maple Street Books also raised its book prices during this period.
No, because the sentence contradicts the paragraph's earlier claim that the events did not sell many books directly.
Yes, because it gives a concrete detail supporting the claim that programming created loyalty.
No, because the essay does not mention Maple Street Books' book club anywhere else in the passage.

why.A: The sentence says nothing about prices — this reasoning invents a connection that isn't there.
why.B: A waiting list for a club is not a book sale — there is no contradiction to avoid.
why.D: The book club is introduced in this very paragraph, so recurrence elsewhere isn't the relevant test.

context: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the sentence about the retired mechanic in Paragraph 3: "The classes were free, and anyone who wanted to attend was welcome, whether or not they had ever grown anything before." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: Yes, because it explains how the retired mechanic learned to compost in the first place.
No, because the paragraph already states that a retired mechanic taught the classes.
Yes, because it develops the point about openness with a concrete detail about the people who attended.
No, because the sentence shifts focus toward a discussion of teaching methods.

why.B: Naming who taught the classes and describing who could attend them are different, complementary details, not a repeated one.
why.D: The sentence describes who could attend the classes and says nothing about how they were taught.

An essay arguing survival was about matching prices would need different evidence than the one given here.

why.B: Explaining the cause of the decline is not the same as arguing that price competition also explains the recovery.

context: Suppose the writer wants to add one more sentence to the end of Paragraph 4 to best strengthen its claim that gardens matter more for social reasons than for the food they produce. Which true statement would accomplish this most effectively?

choices.text: "Raised garden beds are typically built from untreated lumber so that no chemicals leach into the soil."
"In surveys, members name the friendships they've formed as their top reason for returning, even after a poor harvest."
"Community gardens have existed in some form in the United States since at least the closing decades of the nineteenth century."

A survey result showing members return even when the harvest fails directly isolates and confirms that comparison — the other options are on-topic facts about gardens that don't address the social-versus-produce comparison at all.

why.C: A historical fact about how long gardens have existed doesn't support the specific claim that social reasons outweigh produce.
why.D: Restates what kinds of vegetables are common without addressing why people actually return to the garden.

context: Which choice would most logically complete the underlined portion of this sentence from Paragraph 3? "A retired mechanic started teaching Saturday composting classes to anyone who showed up, mostly kids. ___ the garden was hosting a potluck every other Sunday, and the dishes people brought said as much about the block as the produce did."

why.A: The potlucks are a second, parallel example of community activity building on the first (the composting classes), not a contrast or a result. A time-based transition like "By summer's end" connects them without implying a relationship that isn't there.
why.B: Signals a contrast that isn't there — the potlucks are another example of the same trend as the composting classes, not an opposing one.
why.C: Implies the composting classes directly caused the potlucks, a causal link the paragraph never claims.
why.D: Signals a contrast the sentence doesn't have, for the same reason "However" doesn't fit.

context: Which choice would most logically complete the underlined portion of this sentence from Paragraph 2? "That extinction never finished. ___ the American Booksellers Association has recorded slow, steady growth in independent store membership since 2010."

why.C: The second sentence confirms and elaborates the claim that the extinction never finished, rather than contrasting with it or following from it causally. "In fact" signals exactly that kind of confirming elaboration.
why.A: "Otherwise" introduces what would follow if the first statement were false, but the second sentence supports the first.
why.B: Signals a contrast the sentence doesn't have — the second sentence confirms the first, it doesn't oppose it.
why.D: Implies the closures caused the growth, which reverses the essay's actual claim.

context: Which choice would provide the most effective transition from Paragraph 3 to Paragraph 4?

choices.text: Large retailers have always stocked more inventory than small stores can.
Public libraries also compete with bookstores for readers' attention.
Books remain a popular form of entertainment despite streaming services.
Curated selection mattered just as much as community programming.

why.D: This opening explicitly ties the new topic (curated selection) to the one just discussed (community programming) with "just as much as," giving the reader a clear bridge between the two ideas.
why.A: Opens with a fact about large retailers rather than bridging to the paragraph's actual subject, curated selection.
why.B: Introduces libraries, a topic the essay never returns to.
why.C: Introduces a comparison to streaming that has no connection to either paragraph.

context: Given that all the choices are true, which one most logically completes this sentence from Paragraph 4, given the essay's argument that curated selection is distinct from algorithmic recommendation? "A good independent bookseller stocks what sells here, recommending titles a regular customer would not have found through an algorithm, ___ browsing shelf after shelf on a website that has never met them."

why.A: The sentence's entire point is a contrast: a human recommendation versus an anonymous website's shelf. "Rather than" is the only option that expresses that contrast correctly.
why.B: Reverses the sentence's meaning — the essay contrasts human recommendation with algorithmic browsing, it doesn't equate them.
why.C: Suggests the bookseller offers both experiences, which the sentence doesn't support.
why.D: Implies the website caused the recommendation, which doesn't fit the sentence's logic.

context: Which choice would most logically complete the underlined portion of this sentence from Paragraph 5? "The lot at Fifth and Poplar will never make anyone rich; it produces only a few hundred pounds of vegetables a year, not enough to matter to anyone's grocery bill. ___, what it produces instead is harder to put in a ledger."

why.B: The sentence needs to concede the lot's low material output while pivoting to a different kind of value it does have. "Still" is the concessive pivot that does exactly that; the other options imply a causal or comparative relationship that isn't present.
why.A: Implies the lot's other value is a result of its low vegetable yield, a causal link the sentence doesn't support.
why.C: The second sentence isn't an example of the low yield discussed in the first sentence — it introduces a separate kind of value entirely.
why.D: The sentence introduces something different from vegetable yield (social and communal value), not something comparable to it.

context: Which choice, placed at [2], best signals the contrast between the collection's beginning and its present size?

why.A: The sentence before describes a single donated wheelbarrow; the sentence at [2] describes more than nine hundred items. The relationship is one of time and contrast, and 'Today' marks both without overstating the logical connection.
why.B: Signals an illustration, but nine hundred items is not an example of one wheelbarrow.
why.C: Signals likeness, which is the opposite of the contrast the two sentences set up.
why.D: Signals restatement, but the second sentence adds new information rather than rephrasing the first.

context: The entries were «spare: wind» direction, cloud cover, the hour the lamp was lit, and whatever else struck her as worth recording.

why.A: Correct — "The entries were spare" is a complete sentence, and a colon is the right mark to introduce the list that explains it.
why.B: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and the list of items that follows is not one.
why.C: A comma is too weak to announce a list, and here it would read as though "wind direction" were simply one more thing the entries were.
why.D: A list following a colon does not begin with a capital letter unless it starts an independent clause.

context: Pell had no training as a «scientist, she had been hired» in 1889 because her husband held the post.

why.A: This is a comma splice: two complete sentences joined by a comma alone.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon properly joins two closely related independent clauses.
why.C: Removing the comma produces a fused sentence, which is worse than the splice.
why.D: The tense change does nothing to fix the splice, and "had been hiring" wrongly suggests Pell was doing the hiring.

context: The almanac «— a ledger she kept for fifty-one years,» sat in a county archive for most of a century.

choices.text: — a ledger she kept for fifty-one years —
, a ledger she kept for fifty-one years —
- a ledger she kept for fifty-one years -

why.A: A dash opens the description and a comma closes it. An interrupter has to be bracketed by two of the same mark, whichever mark is chosen.
why.B: Correct — both ends of the description now carry a dash, so "The almanac sat in a county archive" reads straight through with the ledger held aside.
why.C: Same mismatch in the other direction: a comma cannot be closed by a dash.
why.D: These are hyphens, not dashes. A hyphen joins parts of a word; it cannot set off a phrase.

context: Alcantara «— who had come looking for shipping records,» spent two years transcribing the almanac.

choices.text: — who had come looking for shipping records —
, who had come looking for shipping records —
who had come looking for shipping records

why.A: The interrupter opens with a dash and closes with a comma, so the pair does not match.
why.B: Correct — matching dashes on both sides cleanly enclose the aside.
why.C: This reverses the same mismatch rather than fixing it.
why.D: With no punctuation at all, the clause runs into the main verb and the sentence loses its subject boundary.

context: «Looking for shipping records, the ledger was opened» instead.

choices.text: Looking for shipping records, Alcantara opened the ledger
The ledger, looking for shipping records, was opened
Looking for shipping records, the opening of the ledger happened

why.A: This dangles the modifier: as written, the ledger is doing the looking.
why.B: Correct — the person who was looking, Alcantara, now follows the modifier directly.
why.C: Moving the phrase inside the sentence still attaches it to the ledger.
why.D: An event cannot look for records either, and the phrasing is needlessly heavy.

context: Every evening at sunset she «only wrote a single line» in the ledger.

why.A: Before the verb, "only" limits the act of writing — as though writing were the single thing she did that evening — rather than limiting how much she wrote.
why.B: Correct — "only" belongs directly before "a single line," the amount it actually restricts.
why.C: Trailing "only" attaches loosely and could modify the ledger instead of the line.
why.D: This inverts the subject and verb for no reason and reads as though the line did the writing.

context: The inspectors found the brass polished, the wicks trimmed, and «the ledger was current».

why.A: The first two items are noun-plus-participle phrases; a full clause breaks the pattern.
why.B: Correct — "the ledger current" matches "the brass polished" and "the wicks trimmed" exactly.
why.C: Adding "that" turns the third item into a subordinate clause, which the first two are not.
why.D: "Being" adds a word the other two items do not have, so the three no longer match.

context: Pell's almanac recorded when the ice broke, when the ducks arrived, and «the running of the herring».

why.A: A noun phrase cannot sit in a series whose other members are "when" clauses.
why.B: Correct — "when the herring ran" matches the two clauses before it in both structure and tense.
why.C: This is a noun phrase with a relative clause, still not parallel to "when the ice broke."
why.D: "How" changes the meaning from timing to manner, and the progressive tense breaks the pattern too.

context: That trend has since been «corroborated with» three other regional records.

why.A: "Corroborated with" names an instrument rather than a source. The records are what do the corroborating.
why.B: Correct — evidence is corroborated by whatever supplies the confirmation, which is the idiom English settled on.
why.C: "From" would name an origin, which is not the relationship between evidence and the claim it supports.
why.D: "Through" implies a route or a means, not the agent doing the corroborating.

context: In 1994 a graduate student named Teodoro Alcantara, «looking for» shipping records, opened it instead.

why.A: Correct — "look for" means to search for something, which is what he was doing in the archive.
why.B: "Look after" means to care for or supervise, which makes no sense applied to records he had not found.
why.C: "Look up to" means to admire someone, which makes no sense applied to records.
why.D: "Look at" means to direct your eyes toward something already in front of you.

context: Pell's ledger reached back into the «1880s, it was» continuous.

why.A: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma make a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — adding the coordinating conjunction "and" makes the comma legal.
why.C: With no punctuation the two sentences fuse, which is a worse version of the same error.
why.D: "Being" creates a dangling fragment rather than joining the clauses.

context: Every evening Pell «recorded: wind» direction, cloud cover, and the hour the lamp was lit.

why.A: A colon must follow a complete sentence. "Every evening Pell recorded" is missing its object, so the colon cuts the verb off from what it acts on.
why.B: Correct — with no mark at all, the verb runs straight into its list of objects, which is what the grammar requires.
why.C: A comma between a verb and its direct object is not allowed either.
why.D: A semicolon has the same problem as the colon, and it additionally requires a full sentence on both sides.

context: Two things made the almanac «valuable: its» daily entries and its unbroken span.

why.A: Correct — a complete sentence precedes the colon, and the two noun phrases after it name the "two things" just promised.
why.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause on the right, but "its daily entries and its unbroken span" is only a phrase.
why.C: A comma cannot introduce an explanatory list after a complete statement like this one.
why.D: The material after a colon is capitalized only when it is itself a full sentence.

context: Three regional records «— one from a lightship, one from a cannery, and one from a ferry line,» have since corroborated the trend.

choices.text: , one from a lightship, one from a cannery, and one from a ferry line,
— one from a lightship, one from a cannery, and one from a ferry line —
one from a lightship, one from a cannery, and one from a ferry line

why.A: The list opens behind a dash and closes with a comma, which leaves the reader unable to see where the list stops and the verb picks up.
why.B: Commas here compete with the three commas inside the list, leaving the reader unsure where the aside ends.
why.C: Correct — a matched pair of dashes. Dashes rather than commas, because the list being set off has commas inside it already.
why.D: With no punctuation the list collides with the main verb, and the sentence reads as though the records themselves were the three items.

context: The city expected complaints about three «things: the» view, the lighting, and the price.

why.A: Correct — a complete sentence precedes the colon, and the three items after it deliver exactly what the sentence promised.
why.B: A semicolon requires a complete sentence after it, and a list of noun phrases is not one.
why.C: A comma turns the sentence into a four-item list, so "three things" becomes one of the things.
why.D: Material after a colon is capitalized only when it is itself a complete sentence.

context: Each synchronized step «feeds: the» motion that produced it, and the sway grows.

why.A: A colon can only follow a complete sentence, and "Each synchronized step feeds" is missing the object of the verb.
why.B: Correct — nothing should separate a verb from its direct object.
why.C: A comma between a verb and its object is not allowed either.
why.D: A semicolon has the same defect as the colon, and it also demands a full sentence on each side.

context: The answer depended on a single «measurement: the» number of walkers on the deck at once.

why.A: Correct — the colon follows a complete sentence and introduces the phrase that identifies the measurement.
why.B: What follows is a noun phrase, not an independent clause, so a semicolon cannot join it.
why.C: A period leaves "The number of walkers on the deck at once" standing alone as a fragment.
why.D: Capitalizing after a colon is reserved for material that is a complete sentence.

context: The bridge still «flexes, it no longer» amplifies.

why.A: Two complete sentences joined by a comma alone form a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon is the right mark for two short, sharply contrasted independent clauses.
why.C: With no punctuation the clauses fuse into a run-on.
why.D: "No more" does not fix the splice, and it is the wrong idiom for describing an ongoing state.

context: Ordinarily those pushes are «scattered, they» cancel.

why.A: This is a comma splice: a comma cannot by itself join two independent clauses.
why.B: Correct — a comma plus the coordinating conjunction "and" is a standard way to join them.
why.C: Dropping the comma produces a fused sentence rather than repairing the splice.
why.D: A semicolon already does the joining, so adding "and" after it is redundant and incorrect.

context: The knowledge «existed, the codes» had simply not caught up to it.

why.A: Both halves are complete sentences, so a comma alone splices them.
why.B: Correct — the semicolon joins two independent clauses whose contrast is the point of the sentence.
why.C: Removing the comma fuses the two sentences together.
why.D: The extra comma sets off "the codes" as though it were an interrupter, leaving the second clause without a subject.

context: Adding stiffness would have raised the bridge's natural frequency, but it would also «have cost» more than the bridge did.

why.A: Correct — "would also have cost" matches the "would have raised" construction in the first half of the sentence.
why.B: The past participle of "cost" is "cost"; "costed" is used only for the separate sense of estimating a price.
why.C: Dropping "have" breaks the match with "would have raised" and changes the time frame.
why.D: The progressive form does not pair with "would also" here and abandons the parallel structure entirely.

context: The dampers absorb energy rather than «resisting force».

why.A: "Rather than" joins two comparable elements, and an -ing form does not match the plain verb "absorb."
why.B: Correct — "absorb energy rather than resist force" puts both verbs in the same form.
why.C: The infinitive does not match "absorb" either, and it adds a word the first half lacks.
why.D: Adding a subject turns the second half into a clause, which cannot be paired with a bare verb phrase.

context: «Gripping the rails, the movement grew» until the crossing ended.

choices.text: Gripping the rails, pedestrians felt the movement grow
The movement, gripping the rails, grew
Gripping the rails, the growth of the movement continued

why.A: As written the movement is doing the gripping, which is impossible.
why.B: Correct — the pedestrians are the ones gripping, so naming them right after the modifier fixes the attachment.
why.C: Moving the phrase into the middle still attaches it to "the movement."
why.D: An abstract growth cannot grip a rail either, so the modifier still dangles.

context: «Tuned to the frequency the crowd had found, the city installed» dampers beneath the deck.

choices.text: Tuned to the frequency the crowd had found, the dampers were installed
The city, tuned to the frequency the crowd had found, installed
Tuning to the frequency the crowd had found, the city installed

why.A: The opening phrase describes whatever noun follows it, so this says the city was tuned to a frequency.
why.B: Correct — the dampers are what was tuned, so they belong directly after the modifier.
why.C: Relocating the phrase still attaches it to "the city."
why.D: Changing the participle to "tuning" makes the city perform the tuning of itself, which is still wrong.

context: A person walking pushes sideways a little «with» every step.

why.A: Correct — "with every step" is the standard phrasing for something that accompanies each repetition of an action.
why.B: "By every step" would name a means, as though the steps caused the push from outside.
why.C: "In every step" would place the push inside the step rather than alongside it.
why.D: "From every step" names a source and does not fit the repeated-action sense the sentence needs.

context: The bridge was strong enough «for holding» many times the crowd standing on it that morning.

why.A: "Strong enough" takes an infinitive, not a gerund phrase: enough to do something, never enough for doing it.
why.B: Correct — "strong enough to hold" is the idiom, and the infinitive is what "enough" is looking for.
why.C: "To" here is part of the infinitive, so it must be followed by the base verb "hold," not "holding."
why.D: "In holding" describes a circumstance and does not complete the "strong enough" construction.

context: Pedestrian lock-in «depends of» the number of walkers rather than their weight.

why.A: Nothing depends "of" anything in English; the verb has never taken that preposition.
why.B: Correct — the verb is fixed to "on", whatever the thing being depended upon happens to be.
why.C: "Depends from" appears only in the unrelated architectural sense of hanging from something.
why.D: "Depends in" is not an accepted pairing for this verb.

context: What it got instead were «complaints about» the walking.

why.A: Correct — a complaint is about its subject; that is the standard pairing.
why.B: "Complaints on" suggests a report delivered on a topic rather than an objection to it.
why.C: "Complaints for" would name a reason or a recipient, not the thing objected to.
why.D: "Complaints to" names the person receiving the complaint, not its subject.

context: The «keepers logbooks» went back to the 1880s, four entries a day in a hand that changed as the decades passed.

why.A: The books belong to the keepers, and a possessive has to be marked.
why.B: Singular possessive, but the passage describes generations of keepers, not one.
why.C: Correct — a plural noun already ending in s takes the apostrophe after the s.
why.D: Marks the thing owned instead of the owner.

context: «Its» beam never changed; what changed was that nobody was there to watch it.

why.A: Correct — the possessive of "it" is the one possessive in English that takes no apostrophe.
why.B: Contracts "it is," which turns the opening into "it is beam."
why.C: Not a form English has; "it" has no plural possessive.
why.D: Plural, but the beam belongs to a single lamp.

context: She left at fifty-one with two suitcases and a barometer. «Which she had been told she could keep.»

choices.text: which she had been told she could keep.
She had been told she could keep it.
Having been told she could keep it.

why.A: A relative clause standing alone is a fragment; there is no main verb governing it.
why.B: Lowercasing does not help while the period before it still cuts the clause off from its noun.
why.C: Correct — it becomes an independent clause with its own subject and verb.
why.D: A participial phrase, which is still not a sentence.

context: «Recorded four times a day, every day, in books going back to the 1880s by keepers who had no particular choice but to be looking.»

choices.text: The weather was recorded four times a day, every day, in books going back to the 1880s by keepers who had no particular choice but to be looking.
Recorded four times a day, every day, in books going back to the 1880s, by keepers who had no particular choice but to be looking.
Recording it four times a day, every day, in books going back to the 1880s by keepers who had no particular choice but to be looking.

why.A: A long participial phrase is still a phrase; nothing here is being said about anything.
why.B: Correct — supplying a subject and a finite verb turns the phrase into a sentence.
why.C: Adds a comma to a fragment, which leaves it a fragment.
why.D: Swaps one participle for another without ever reaching a main verb.

context: Keepers logged the things nobody had asked them to log «— fog banks, bird strikes, the first gannets,» and they logged them four times a day.

choices.text: — fog banks, bird strikes, the first gannets —
, fog banks, bird strikes, the first gannets —
; fog banks, bird strikes, the first gannets;

why.A: The interruption opens with a dash and closes with a comma; a pair has to match.
why.B: Correct — an interrupter that contains its own commas is set off by a matching pair of dashes.
why.C: Still mismatched, with the dash and the comma simply swapped.
why.D: Semicolons join independent clauses, and this is a list rather than a clause.

context: Three things kept her on the rock «, the work, the weather, and a stubbornness she never explained,» far longer than she had planned.

choices.text: — the work, the weather, and a stubbornness she never explained —
— the work, the weather, and a stubbornness she never explained,
: the work, the weather, and a stubbornness she never explained:

why.A: Commas cannot mark the edges of an interruption that already contains commas of its own.
why.B: Correct — dashes are the one pair strong enough to enclose a list that is itself comma-separated.
why.C: Opens with a dash and closes with a comma, so the reader never learns where the interruption ended.
why.D: A colon cannot close anything, and nothing before it announces a list.

context: The job came down to one thing «, maintenance:» brass, glass, damp, and rust.

why.A: Announces the list with a comma and then punctuates the apposition with a colon, which is backwards.
why.B: Correct — a colon introduces the word the sentence has been building toward, and a dash then opens the list that expands it.
why.C: Two colons in one sentence leave the reader unsure which one is doing the announcing.
why.D: Sets the word off as an aside and leaves the list with nothing to attach to.

context: The radio link reports exactly one «fact; lamp» on or lamp off, and it reports that fact perfectly.

why.A: "Lamp on or lamp off" is the fact being named rather than a second statement about it, so it cannot sit on the far side of a semicolon.
why.B: Correct — the colon names the one fact the link reports, which is what the first half of the sentence has promised.
why.C: A comma is too weak to carry the announcement the sentence has set up.
why.D: Runs the announcement into its own answer with no punctuation at all.

context: «The light never went out, the keeper simply stopped being there to watch it.»

choices.text: The light never went out; the keeper simply stopped being there to watch it.
The light never went out the keeper simply stopped being there to watch it.
The light never went out, and, the keeper simply stopped being there to watch it.

why.A: Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone is a splice.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon joins two complete clauses that belong in one sentence.
why.C: Removing the comma makes a fused sentence, which is worse than the splice.
why.D: The conjunction would fix it, but the comma after it cuts the second clause off from its own joint.

context: «She is not sentimental about the rock, however, she still writes the pressure down every morning.»

choices.text: She is not sentimental about the rock; however, she still writes the pressure down every morning.
She is not sentimental about the rock however she still writes the pressure down every morning.
She is not sentimental about the rock, however she still writes the pressure down every morning.

why.A: "However" is an adverb rather than a conjunction, so a comma in front of it still leaves two clauses spliced.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon carries the joint and the following comma marks the adverb as an aside.
why.C: Stripping the punctuation fuses the two clauses outright.
why.D: Moves the splice rather than repairing it; a comma is still the only thing between two sentences.

context: The automated lamp switched itself on with more «preciseness» than any keeper had ever managed.

why.A: A real word, but a clumsy one where the ordinary noun exists and is shorter.
why.B: Correct — the standard noun, and the one a reader expects after "more."
why.C: Inflates the phrase and then leaves the trailing words doing no work.
why.D: An adjective where the comparison needs a noun.

context: None of it was science exactly; it was «attention», recorded by someone who had no particular choice but to be looking.

why.A: Correct — the essay's point is that the keepers were looking rather than measuring, and this is the only choice that says so.
why.B: Carries a sense of watching people under suspicion, which the passage never suggests.
why.C: Curiosity is voluntary, and the sentence insists the looking was not.
why.D: Data is what the attention produced, not what the looking itself was.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence "The lamp had never once failed under her." Where would it most logically be placed?

choices.text: In the opening paragraph, before Aird Rock is named.
In the paragraph describing the 1998 automation, before the equipment is listed.
In the paragraph about Muir's departure, after her years on the rock are described.
In the final paragraph, after the barometer on the windowsill.

why.A: The opening has not yet introduced a keeper for the pronoun to refer to.
why.B: That paragraph is about the machinery replacing her, and the pronoun would still have no antecedent.
why.C: Correct — it belongs where her record as keeper is being summarised, and the pronoun has a clear referent there.
why.D: The closing has moved off the rock entirely and onto her life afterwards.

stem: For the sake of the logic of this essay, the sentence "When the rock was automated, the logbooks stopped." should be placed:

choices.text: where it is now, opening the paragraph about what automation cost.
in the second paragraph, immediately after the solenoid and photocell are installed.
in the opening paragraph, as the essay's first sentence.
in the final paragraph, just before the barometer is mentioned.

why.A: Correct — it lands after the reader has been shown what the logbooks contained, so the loss means something.
why.B: Moving it there states the loss before the logbooks have been described, and the sentence falls flat.
why.C: Opening on it would give away the essay's conclusion before its subject is introduced.
why.D: The barometer is the private echo of the logbooks, so the loss has to be established well before it.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence describing the winters as worse than anyone who has not spent one there can understand. If this sentence were deleted, the essay would primarily lose:

choices.text: a detail that keeps the closing from reading as simple nostalgia for the job.
the essay's only factual information about North Atlantic weather.
an explanation of why the harbour authority chose to automate the light.
the transition between the logbooks and the barometer.

why.A: Correct — it is the line that stops the ending being sentimental, which the essay has been careful to avoid throughout.
why.B: The weather appears elsewhere, and this sentence offers no facts about it in any case.
why.C: The authority's reasoning is never given, and this sentence does not supply it.
why.D: That transition is carried by the sentence about her living within sight of the water.

stem: Suppose the writer's goal had been to argue that automating the light was a mistake. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it shows that the logbooks ended when the keeper left.
Yes, because it describes the automated equipment as unable to notice the gannets.
No, because it concedes that the automated light works better and never asks to undo the change.
No, because it provides no information at all about what the automation cost the harbour authority.

why.A: The ending of the logbooks is presented as a loss, not as grounds for reversing the decision.
why.B: That observation describes a limit of the equipment; the essay never argues the trade was wrong.
why.C: Correct — the essay grants that the lamp is more reliable than any keeper and stops at describing what went with the keeper.
why.D: Cost is not the measure the essay uses, so its absence is not what keeps this from being an argument.

context: The «seeds» survival depended on how little moisture the cave allowed it to keep.

why.A: The survival belongs to the seed, and an unmarked plural cannot show possession.
why.B: Correct — one seed is under discussion, so the singular possessive is what the sentence needs.
why.C: Plural possessive, but the verb and the later pronoun both treat this as a single seed.
why.D: Adds a second possessive ending to a form that already has one.

context: Two thousand «years worth» of damage had accumulated, and enough of the instructions still survived to build a tree.

why.A: An expression of measure like this is possessive in form and has to be marked.
why.B: Singular, which contradicts the two thousand years the sentence has just counted.
why.C: Correct — a plural measure ending in s takes the apostrophe after the s.
why.D: Attaches the possessive to the wrong word entirely.

context: They soaked the seed in water and then in hormones. «Then setting it in a pot of ordinary soil.»

choices.text: Then they set it in a pot of ordinary soil.
Then setting it in a pot of ordinary soil, and waiting.
Then, setting it in a pot of ordinary soil.

why.A: A participle is not a verb a sentence can be built on, so nothing here is asserted.
why.B: Correct — a subject and a finite verb make it a sentence; without "they," it would read as an instruction to the reader.
why.C: Adds a second participle, which doubles the problem rather than solving it.
why.D: A comma changes the rhythm and leaves the fragment exactly as it was.

context: «A library with the lights off, whose single design goal is that nothing inside it should ever happen.»

choices.text: A library with the lights off; whose single design goal is that nothing inside it should ever happen.
It is a library with the lights off, and its single design goal is that nothing inside it should ever happen.
Being a library with the lights off, whose single design goal is that nothing inside it should ever happen.

why.A: A noun phrase trailing a relative clause has no main verb, however long it runs.
why.B: A semicolon needs a complete clause on each side and there is not one on either.
why.C: Correct — it supplies a subject and a verb and turns the relative clause into a second independent clause.
why.D: Opening with a participle moves the fragment further from being a sentence.

context: The vault does the one thing it was built to do «— nothing.»

why.A: Correct — a single dash before a one-word ending gives it the pause the joke needs and is standard for an abrupt appositive.
why.B: A closing dash needs more sentence after it; here it is followed only by the full stop, so the pair fences off nothing.
why.C: A semicolon promises a second independent clause, and a single word is not one.
why.D: With no punctuation the word collides with the verb and the sentence stops making sense.

context: The others «— kept in a university drawer for thirty years,» were never planted because nobody expected anything to happen.

choices.text: — kept in a university drawer for thirty years —
kept in a university drawer for thirty years —
— kept in a university drawer for thirty years;

why.A: The opening dash is never answered. A comma cannot close what a dash opened, and the subject is left waiting for its verb.
why.B: Correct — the modifier is fenced off at both ends by dashes, so "The others were never planted" survives intact underneath it.
why.C: Drops the opening mark, so the reader cannot tell where the interruption began.
why.D: A semicolon cannot close an interruption; it can only join clauses.

context: The chemistry has been slowed almost to a «stop, water» removed, enzymes immobilised, the whole machine held still.

why.A: A comma cannot announce the list that spells out what the slowing consists of.
why.B: Correct — the clause before the colon is complete and what follows itemises it.
why.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, and these are phrases.
why.D: Runs two ideas together with no mark at all.

context: The result was «: a shoot», eight weeks after the seed went into the pot.

why.A: A colon cannot separate a linking verb from the thing it links to; the clause before it is incomplete.
