why.B: An infinitive on one side of the contrast and a gerund on the other.
why.C: "But" after a semicolon, and an infinitive set against a gerund.
why.D: A participial phrase with no subject or verb, which cannot follow a semicolon.

context: A system that reports on itself will report that «it’s» fine right up until it cannot.

context: For the first few months this struck me as an elaborate way of proving that a thermometer works. «Then» a storage manager from another seed bank came through on a tour.

why.B: The visit is not another instance of the job feeling pointless; it is what stopped it feeling that way.
why.C: A visiting manager is not an example of an elaborate proof.
why.D: A contrast marker would set the visit against the first few months, but the sentence is simply what happened after them.

context: The job posting said "facility technician"« and» did not mention that the facility was kept at minus eighteen degrees.

why.A: Correct — one subject with two verbs, "said" and "did not mention", and a compound predicate takes no comma before the conjunction.
why.B: The comma suggests a second independent clause, but what follows has no subject of its own.
why.C: Supplying "it" creates a second clause, which changes the sentence rather than punctuating it.

context: Nobody expected a mismatch, and in eleven months I «found» two.

why.B: The present perfect keeps the period open, but the narrator says elsewhere that the year ended.

context: Walter Ostrowski, who is ninety-one and does not drive, had built his day «around» walking out to the box at one o’clock.

why.C: "Build a day about" is not English; "about" would mean concerning, which is not the sense here.

context: Her successor said he had not known there was anything «for knowing» about the Ostrowski box.

context: Within the fourth paragraph, the sentence "A route is a route" belongs where it is because it:

context: The writer is considering moving the sentence about the 2009 call to the end of the final paragraph. This move would:

context: The writer is considering deleting the detail that the new order ran 4.2 miles shorter and saved eleven minutes a day. Should it be kept?

why.B: The passage argues the opposite; conceding a saving is not the same as endorsing the decision.

context: The writer is considering adding the following sentence to the second paragraph: "Software of this kind is now used by most rural districts in the state." Should it be added?

context: Reyes had been the one to notice that the box had not been emptied in nine days, and «it was her who» called it in.

why.B: Correct — "she" follows "was" as a predicate nominative, and "who" then introduces the clause about her.
why.C: This keeps the object form and swaps the relative pronoun, so the one real error is left in place.
why.D: A participial phrase leaves the clause with no verb of its own and cannot join what comes before it.

context: The district’s position was that this is not a carrier’s concern, and as a matter of policy «they were» right.

why.B: Correct — the antecedent is "the district", a singular noun, which takes the singular "it was".
why.C: This corrects nothing about number and adds a past perfect the sentence has no earlier event to need.
why.D: "Those" is a plural demonstrative and points at nothing in the sentence that could be plural.

context: The software was not wrong about distance. «Therefore,» Reyes drove the new order for three weeks and then stopped.

weeks and then stopped and her
weeks, and then stopped, and her

context: The software plans the route by the minute, reorders the ninety-eight boxes, and «it saves eleven minutes a day».

Having been reordered by the software, Reyes found

why.B: Correct — turning the phrase into a clause gives "reordered" its own subject, so nothing is left dangling.
why.C: This makes Reyes the one doing the reordering, and it was the software that reordered the route.

context: For two weeks his mail «sat in the box overnight and remained there through the night until morning».

why.C: This cuts one repetition and keeps the other, so the sentence still says the night twice.
why.D: Cutting to "sat" loses where the mail sat, which is the detail the sentence exists to report.

context: In the third week he stopped coming out at «all, Reyes found» four days of it.

why.A: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses, which is what stands on either side of it here.
why.B: Correct — the coordinating conjunction after the comma is what licenses joining the two clauses.
why.C: Removing the comma turns a comma splice into two clauses with no punctuation at all between them.
why.D: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and "Reyes finding four days of it" has no finite verb.

context: Suppose the writer had intended to show that a job can contain work its own description leaves out. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because the one record of the 2009 call sits in a file no route description mentions.
Yes, because it gives the length of the loop and the number of addresses along it.
No, because the district was right about the policy as the writer concedes.
No, because Reyes retired before the reordered route could be judged fairly.

why.A: Correct — the call is work no route plan asked for, and the passage says it is the only reason the date is known.
why.B: The mileage and the address count are exactly the part of the job its description does cover.
why.C: The writer grants the policy and then argues that something real falls outside it, so the concession is part of the case.
why.D: When she retired has no bearing on whether the passage shows uncounted work, which it does through the 2009 call.

context: The records of every earlier retuning «is» kept in the parish book.

why.A: The subject is "records", not "retuning", so a singular verb has no plural noun to agree with.
why.B: Correct — "records" is the plural subject, and the phrase between it and the verb does not change that.
why.C: This is singular as well, and it adds a perfect tense the sentence gives no reason to shift into.
why.D: A singular past verb repeats the agreement error and moves a standing fact into the past.

context: Neither the historical society nor the parish trustees «was» willing to pay for a new bell.

why.A: With "neither...nor" the verb agrees with the nearer subject, and "trustees" is plural.
why.B: Correct — "trustees" sits closest to the verb, so the plural is the form the rule calls for.
why.C: This is singular and also shifts into the present perfect, which the surrounding past tense does not support.
why.D: A present singular verb is wrong on both counts, in number and in time.

context: The foundry proposed to tune the bell «by means of removing» metal from the inside.

why.A: "By means of" is a roundabout way to say "by"; it adds three words and nothing else.
why.B: Correct — "by" plus a gerund is the ordinary way English names the method of an action.
why.C: "Through removing of" mixes two constructions and leaves the "of" with nothing to attach to.
why.D: "With" names an instrument rather than a method, so it cannot introduce the removing itself.

context: Nkemelu was not indifferent «to» the objection; she had grown up under the same bell.

why.A: Correct — "indifferent to" is the fixed pairing when the adjective takes what is being disregarded.
why.B: "Indifferent about" is not idiomatic; "about" follows verbs of opinion rather than this adjective.
why.C: "From" would suggest distance or origin, neither of which is the relationship being described.
why.D: "Indifferent with" is not English, and "with" would imply accompaniment rather than attitude.

context: Within the fourth paragraph, the sentence listing the cuttings of 1854, 1901 and 1963 belongs where it is because it:

choices.text: supplies the record that turns the objection back against the society itself.
introduces Nkemelu to the reader before her apprenticeship is described.
explains why a bell has to be cast thick and then cut on a lathe.
concedes that the bell in the tower is no longer the bell of 1817.

why.A: Correct — the sentence after it draws the conclusion, and it can only be drawn once the three dates are on the table.
why.B: Nkemelu is introduced in the sentence before this one, together with her apprenticeship.
why.C: How a bell is tuned is explained in the second paragraph, not here.
why.D: The paragraph uses the earlier cuttings to answer that claim rather than to grant it.

context: The writer is considering moving the sentence "A bell is tuned by taking metal away, never by adding it" to the opening paragraph. This move would:

choices.text: weaken the passage, because it is what makes the proposal beside it make sense.
strengthen the passage, because the opening paragraph is where the crack is described.
weaken the passage, because the opening paragraph is already the longest of the five.
strengthen the passage, because a reader needs to know how bells work before the date.

why.A: Correct — it explains why cutting is the only remedy available, and the proposal it explains is the sentence directly before it.
why.B: The crack is what creates the problem; the method of tuning belongs with the proposed answer to it.
why.C: Paragraph length is not what governs placement, and the opening paragraph is not the longest anyway.
why.D: The first paragraph asks the reader to understand a silent bell, which needs no account of tuning at all.

context: The writer is considering deleting the detail that the bell went unrung for eleven of its two hundred and six years. Should it be kept?

choices.text: Kept, because it measures the cost of the decade the parish spent arguing.
Kept, because it establishes that the crack made the bell unsafe to ring.
Deleted, because the passage is about the objection rather than about silence.
Deleted, because the figure conflicts with the date the bell was hung again.

why.A: Correct — eleven years against two hundred and six is what makes the delay register as a loss rather than a pause.
why.B: The passage never says the crack made the bell unsafe, only that it killed the note.
why.C: The silence is what the objection cost, so it is part of the subject rather than a departure from it.
why.D: The figures agree: silent from 2009, cut in 2020 and hung again that July.

context: The writer is considering adding the following sentence to the second paragraph: "Foundries in several countries have experimented with welding cracked bells instead." Should it be added?

choices.text: No, because the paragraph is establishing that cutting is the remedy a bell allows.
No, because the passage does not name the countries where this has been tried.
Yes, because it shows the foundry had an alternative it declined to offer.
Yes, because it supports the claim that a bell is never tuned by adding metal.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph turns on there being one remedy, and a second one contradicts the sentence it sits beside.
why.B: Naming the countries would not repair the problem, which is that the addition undercuts the paragraph.
why.C: The passage gives no sign that welding was available or declined, so the sentence would imply what it cannot show.
why.D: Welding adds metal, so the sentence would tell against that claim rather than support it.

context: By the time the crack was found, the bell «has rung» for nearly two centuries.

why.A: The present perfect reaches up to now, but the ringing had already finished by a point in the past.
why.B: Correct — the past perfect places the two centuries of ringing before the moment the crack was found.
why.C: A present-tense verb puts the ringing in the present, while the clause beside it is plainly in the past.
why.D: The present progressive says the ringing is going on as we read, which the crack ended in 2009.

context: The foundry proposed the only remedy a bell allows «— cutting the inside on a lathe —» and the trustees agreed to it.

choices.text: — cutting the inside on a lathe,
, cutting the inside on a lathe —

why.A: Correct — a pair of dashes sets off an interruption, and both ends of this one are dashes.
why.B: Opening with a dash and closing with a comma leaves the interruption with two different marks around it.
why.C: This is the same mismatch the other way round, opening with a comma and closing with a dash.
why.D: A parenthesis has to be closed by a parenthesis; a dash cannot finish what a bracket started.

context: The historical society announced that «they» would not pay for any cutting.

why.A: A society is a single body, so a plural pronoun has no plural antecedent to point back to.
why.B: Correct — "the historical society" is singular, and "it" is the pronoun that matches.
why.C: "Those" is a demonstrative and points at nothing in the sentence that could be plural.
why.D: "Them" is an object pronoun standing where the subject of the clause has to go.

context: The «founders» intention in 1817 is the one thing nobody can now establish.

why.A: Without an apostrophe this reads as a plural noun, and the intention plainly belongs to somebody.
why.B: Correct — one founder cast the bell in 1817, so the apostrophe goes before the s.
why.C: This makes the intention belong to several founders, and the passage describes a single casting.
why.D: A plural already ending in s never takes a second s after the apostrophe.

context: Nkemelu names what the ten years were really «about: who in a town gets to decide» what it sounds like.

choices.text: about; who in a town gets to decide
about, and who in a town gets to decide
about who in a town gets to decide

why.A: Correct — a complete sentence precedes the colon and what follows delivers the thing it promised to name.
why.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and a noun clause beginning "who" is not one.
why.C: "And" makes the question a second thing Nkemelu names rather than the answer to what the years were about.
why.D: With no mark at all the clause runs into the verb and the announcement the sentence was making is lost.

context: The parish book records every earlier cutting in the same hand. «Which the society had never read.»

choices.text: a book the society had never read.
The society had never read it, though.
Never having been read by the society.

why.A: A clause opening with "which" is subordinate, so standing alone it is a fragment with no main verb of its own.
why.B: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence, and it would need to be joined to the sentence before it.
why.C: Correct — this is a complete sentence with its own subject and verb, and it keeps the contrast intact.
why.D: A participial phrase cannot stand as a sentence, and this one names nobody who did the not-reading.

context: The crack had no visible «affect» on the bell, but the note went dead.

why.A: "Affect" is ordinarily the verb; the sentence needs the noun that follows "no visible".
why.B: Correct — "effect" is the noun for a result, which is what the crack did or did not produce.
why.C: An affectation is a put-on manner, which a crack in a bell cannot have.
why.D: "Effecting" is a participle of the verb meaning to bring about, and no verb form fits after "no visible".

context: The state has spent four decades trying to «substitute the tube with» an automatic sensor.

why.A: "Substitute" takes the new thing as its object: you substitute a sensor for a tube, not the reverse.
why.B: Correct — "replace X with Y" is the idiom that names the old thing first, which is the order here.
why.C: "Substitute by" is not English, and the tube and the sensor are still the wrong way round.
why.D: "Replace" pairs with "with"; "by" after it would name whoever did the replacing.

context: Fenn does not object «to» the pillow so much as to the single number the state reports.

why.A: Correct — "object to" is the fixed pairing when what follows names the thing opposed.
why.B: "Object against" doubles a sense of opposition the verb already carries on its own.
why.C: "Object about" is not idiomatic; "about" follows verbs of complaining rather than this one.
why.D: "From" marks a source, which is not the relationship between Fenn and the pillow.

context: A crusted layer can span the pillow, «carrying part of the load onto» the ground around it.

choices.text: carrying part of the load at
carrying part of the load in
carrying part of the load through

why.A: Correct — "onto" carries the sense of the load transferring out to the ground beside the pillow.
why.B: "At the ground" treats the ground as a point rather than a surface taking weight.
why.C: "In the ground" would put the load below the surface instead of pressing on it.
why.D: "Through the ground" would send the load down into the earth rather than onto its surface.

context: Within the third paragraph, the sentence explaining that crust layers can span the pillow the way an arch spans a doorway belongs where it is because it:

choices.text: names the mechanism whose cost the rest of the paragraph measures.
introduces Blue Lake to the reader for the first time in the passage.
explains how a snow pillow turns a pressure reading into a water figure.
concedes that the manual snow course is the less accurate of the two.

why.A: Correct — the sentences after it report what bridging costs, and that cost is unreadable without the arch.
why.B: Blue Lake is named in the first paragraph and again in the sentence that opens this one.
why.C: How the pillow works is the business of the second paragraph, not this one.
why.D: The paragraph is an objection to the pillow, so it concedes nothing about the tube.

context: The writer is considering moving the sentence "Blue Lake is not flat or sheltered" to the end of the second paragraph. This move would:

choices.text: weaken the passage, because it is the turn the third paragraph is built on.
strengthen the passage, because the second paragraph is where the pillow is described.
weaken the passage, because the second paragraph already runs longer than the third.
strengthen the passage, because the reader first meets Blue Lake in the opening paragraph.

why.A: Correct — the second paragraph ends by granting that the pillow works, and this sentence takes that grant back.
why.B: The pillow is described there in general; the sentence is about one site where the description fails.
why.C: Paragraph length does not govern placement, and the third paragraph is the longer of the two.
why.D: Blue Lake appearing earlier is why the sentence needs no introduction, not a reason to move it.

context: Which of the following sentences, if added at the start of the fourth paragraph, would most logically introduce it?

choices.text: Fenn has walked the Blue Lake line in every kind of January weather.
None of this makes the pillow the wrong instrument to have.
The state has published both records side by side since 2019.
A snow pillow costs far less to read than a snow course does.

why.A: The sentence naming Fenn already gives her years on the line, so this only repeats it.
why.B: Correct — the paragraph opens by refusing to call for the pillow to be removed, and this concedes that first.
why.C: The side-by-side publication is the subject of the final paragraph, and moving it here spoils that.
why.D: Cost arrives at the end of the paragraph as a criticism, so leading with it gives the point away.

context: Since 1938 someone «walks» the same line up the slope above Blue Lake each winter.

why.A: A simple present does not reach back to 1938, and "since" needs a tense that spans the years.
why.B: Correct — the present perfect covers an action begun in 1938 and still going on now.
why.C: A simple past closes the walking off, but it continues every winter.
why.D: The past perfect places the walking before some other past event, and none is named.

context: By the time the state began publishing both records in 2019, Fenn «walks» the course for more than twenty years.

why.A: The present cannot describe a stretch of time completed before a named point in the past.
why.B: Correct — the past perfect puts the twenty years inside the period before 2019.
why.C: The present perfect measures back from now, not from the moment the sentence names.
why.D: A simple past sets the two actions side by side instead of nesting one inside the other.

context: Laid on bare ground in autumn, «the winter snow buries the pillow» without anyone returning to the site.

choices.text: the pillow is buried by the winter snow
burying the pillow is what winter snow does

why.A: The opening phrase describes the pillow, but this makes the snow the thing laid on the ground.
why.B: Correct — the pillow is what was laid down, so it belongs directly after the opening phrase.
why.C: This makes an action the subject, which leaves the opening phrase attached to nothing at all.
why.D: A pronoun subject still leaves the phrase modifying the snow, and "it" arrives before its noun.

context: «Fenn only weighed the tube at ten marked points», not at every step along the line.

choices.text: Fenn weighed the tube only at ten marked points
Only Fenn weighed the tube at ten marked points
Fenn weighed only the tube at ten marked points

why.A: "Only" sits beside the verb, so it limits the weighing rather than the places it happened.
why.B: Correct — "only" belongs immediately before what it limits, and here that is the ten points.
why.C: This limits the person, claiming nobody else weighed the tube, which is not the contrast drawn.
why.D: This limits the object, claiming she weighed nothing but the tube, which the sentence never says.

context: The spread between the two records «— nineteen percent in 2023,» is now published as a figure of its own.

why.A: A dash cannot be closed by a comma; an interrupter takes the same mark at both ends.
why.B: Correct — a matching pair of dashes sets the interrupting figure off from the sentence around it.
why.C: This opens with a comma and closes with a dash, so the two ends still fail to match.
why.D: An opening parenthesis has to be answered by a closing one, not by a dash.

context: Two instruments «— the tube and the pillow, —» have measured the same slope since 1996.

why.A: A comma sitting just inside the closing dash leaves two marks doing a single job.
why.B: Correct — matching dashes on both sides set the pair of names off from the main clause.
why.C: This closes with a comma where the opening dash needs another dash to answer it.
why.D: This opens with a comma and closes with a dash, so the two ends do not match.

context: The pillow and the tube each have a job, and «they are» better at telling you what changed since yesterday.

why.A: "They" points at both instruments, but only one of the two is being credited in this clause.
why.B: Correct — naming the pillow removes an ambiguity no pronoun can clear up in this sentence.
why.C: "It" has two singular nouns to reach back to, so the reader cannot tell which is meant.
why.D: "This" is vaguer still, pointing at a whole clause rather than at either instrument.

context: The disagreement was between the state and «she», and it went on for thirty years.

why.A: A pronoun after a preposition takes the object form, and "she" is the subject form.
why.B: Correct — "between" is a preposition, so the pronoun that follows it has to be "her".
why.C: A reflexive needs a matching subject earlier in the clause, and the subject here is the disagreement.
why.D: "Hers" is possessive, which would make the sentence say the disagreement belonged to something of hers.

context: The «sensors» reading is lighter than the snowpack standing on top of it.

why.A: With no apostrophe this is a plural noun, and the sentence needs a possessive instead.
why.B: Correct — one sensor owns the reading, so the apostrophe goes in front of the s.
why.C: This is the plural possessive, but the rest of the sentence treats the sensor as singular.
why.D: A plural already ending in s takes an apostrophe alone; a second s is never added.

context: A truck comes over the pit, you take a probe sample, and «reading the moisture».

why.A: A gerund phrase breaks a series whose other members are full clauses beginning with "you".
why.B: Correct — the series runs on parallel clauses, and this one matches the two in front of it.
why.C: A passive clause changes who is doing the work, so it no longer matches the pattern.
why.D: An infinitive turns the third item into a purpose rather than a third step in the sequence.

context: The job is mostly arithmetic, paperwork, and «you have to keep the scale clean».

choices.text: the scale must be kept clean

why.A: A full clause cannot sit in a list beside two bare nouns; the three items have to match.
why.B: Correct — a gerund phrase works as a noun, which is what the other two items already are.
why.C: An infinitive is not a noun of the same kind, so the third item still stands apart.
why.D: This is a clause again, and a passive one, which pulls further from the two nouns.

context: He would run the sample, note the dial, and «then he squeezed a handful» of corn from the hopper.

why.A: The first two verbs follow "would" directly, so a separate past-tense clause breaks the pattern.
why.B: Correct — "would run, note, squeeze" keeps all three verbs under the same auxiliary.
why.C: A gerund cannot follow "would", so the third action no longer attaches to the auxiliary.
why.D: A passive clause moves the subject from the uncle to the handful of corn.

context: The argument at the scale house always came down to one thing«:» how wet the corn was.

why.A: Correct — a colon delivers the thing an independent clause has just promised to name.
why.B: "And" makes the wetness of the corn a second thing alongside the "one thing" rather than naming it.
why.C: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and what follows here is not one.
why.D: "That is" would need punctuation of its own and still not do the introducing.

context: The office kept two records for every load«;» the dial reading and the weight ticket.

why.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and a pair of nouns is not one.
why.B: Correct — a colon introduces the items an independent clause has just announced.
why.C: ", and" adds the dial reading and the ticket as further items rather than naming the two records.
why.D: A dash could work on its own, but "namely" after it repeats the job the mark already does.

context: There was only one reason to run a second sample«:» doubt about the first.

why.A: Correct — a colon introduces the noun phrase the clause before it has led the reader to expect.
why.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, and "doubt about the first" is a phrase.
why.C: ", and" makes the doubt a second item after the reason rather than the reason itself.
why.D: "That is" needs its own punctuation and still does not perform the introduction.

context: He was slower than the man who replaced him«. By about ninety seconds a truck.»

choices.text: , by about ninety seconds a truck.
; by about ninety seconds a truck.
by about ninety seconds a truck.

why.A: The second group has neither a subject nor a verb, so it cannot stand as a sentence.
why.B: Correct — a comma attaches the measuring phrase to the clause it modifies.
why.C: A semicolon promises an independent clause on the right, and a phrase is not one.
why.D: With no mark the phrase attaches to "replaced him," as though the man had been replaced by ninety seconds.

context: Corn out of a dry August behaves differently in the hand than corn out of a wet one«. Even at the same reading on the dial.»

choices.text: , even at the same reading on the dial.
; even at the same reading on the dial.
: even at the same reading on the dial.

why.A: The group beginning "Even at" has no subject and no verb, which makes it a fragment.
why.B: Correct — a comma joins the qualifying phrase to the sentence it qualifies.
why.C: A semicolon promises an independent clause on the other side, and none arrives.
why.D: A colon announces something the clause has led the reader to expect, and nothing here does.

context: In the last week of October, ninety seconds a truck is a line of trucks out to the county road«. Which nobody wanted to see.»

choices.text: , which nobody wanted to see it.

why.A: A clause beginning with "which" is subordinate and cannot stand as a sentence by itself.
why.B: Correct — a comma attaches the relative clause to the noun it describes.
why.C: A semicolon calls for an independent clause, and a "which" clause is not one.
why.D: The relative pronoun already stands in for the line of trucks, so "it" repeats the object.

context: The difference between the two weights «are» somebody’s year.

why.A: The subject is "difference", and the plural noun sitting between it and the verb does not govern it.
why.B: Correct — "difference" is singular, so the verb agrees with it rather than with "weights".
why.C: This is plural as well, and it moves a standing fact into the past for no reason.
why.D: A plural perfect verb repeats the agreement error and adds a tense the sentence does not need.

context: Neither the dial nor the two weight tickets «tells» the whole story of a load.

why.A: With "neither...nor" the verb agrees with the nearer subject, and "tickets" is plural.
why.B: Correct — "tickets" sits closest to the verb, so the plural is the form the rule calls for.
why.C: This is singular and also shifts into the perfect, which nothing in the sentence supports.
why.D: A singular progressive is wrong in number and turns a standing fact into a passing moment.

context: The writer is considering deleting the detail that the uncle would have been fired if he had ever overruled the dial. Should it be kept?

choices.text: Kept, because it shows the limits he worked inside, and so what the second sample cost.
Kept, because it proves the elevator was wrong to write the rule the way it did.
Deleted, because the passage is about the uncle rather than about company policy.
Deleted, because it contradicts the claim that he wrote the dial’s number every time.

why.A: Correct — a man who cannot act on what he learns is doing something stranger than second-guessing.
why.B: The passage never faults the rule; it says the elevator paid for something it never priced.
why.C: The policy is the thing the uncle is working inside, so it is not a departure from the subject.
why.D: There is no contradiction: the rule and his practice agree, which is the whole of the point.

context: The writer is considering adding a sentence at the end of the fourth paragraph reporting that the meter was recalibrated twice a season. Should it be added?

choices.text: No, because the paragraph is about what the meter could not measure, not about its accuracy.
Yes, because it would show that the uncle’s suspicion of the meter was well founded.
No, because the passage has already given the meter’s reading to one decimal place.
Yes, because a reader needs to know how often the equipment was maintained.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph turns on a difference the meter reads correctly and still cannot explain.
why.B: The passage says he wrote the dial’s number every time, so it never claims the meter was wrong.
why.C: The decimal place appears two paragraphs earlier and settles nothing about this one.
why.D: Maintenance is never at issue, and nothing in the passage turns on the meter drifting.

context: The elevator paid that price without ever being told what it was paying «for».

why.A: Correct — "pay for" is the fixed pairing when what follows names the thing being bought.
why.B: "Pay of" is not English, and "of" cannot introduce what a payment buys.
why.C: "Pay about" would concern a topic rather than a purchase.
why.D: "Pay with" names the means of payment rather than the thing paid for.

context: Corn out of a dry August behaves differently «in comparison to» corn out of a wet one.

why.A: "In comparison to" pads the sentence, since "differently" has already set up the comparison.
why.B: Correct — "differently from" is the standard pairing when a noun phrase follows.
why.C: "Differently than" is widely objected to and wants a clause after it, not a noun phrase.
why.D: "As" would say the dry-August corn behaves in the role of the other corn rather than unlike it.

context: A young male learns «his fathers song» only if he hears it during his first summer.

why.A: With no apostrophe at all, "fathers" is a plain plural and nothing shows possession.
why.B: Correct — one father owns the song, so the apostrophe goes in front of the s.
why.C: The plural possessive would mean several fathers share the one song between them.
why.D: This makes both words plain plurals, which leaves the possession unmarked again.

context: The basement archive is older than «it’s» nearest rival by about fifteen years.

why.A: Read out in full this says "older than it is nearest rival", which is not English.
why.B: Correct — the possessive form of "it" never takes an apostrophe.
why.C: There is no such form; the possessive of "it" carries no apostrophe in any position.
why.D: Spelling the contraction out only makes the broken sentence easier to hear.

context: The line where the buzz gives way to the whistle has «moved» twice since the first tapes were cut.

why.A: Correct — "moved" is the plain verb for a line shifting position on a map.
why.B: "Emigrated" means people leaving their own country to live in another, not a line shifting on a map.
why.C: "Transferred" needs someone to hand a thing over from one place to another.
why.D: "Relocated" suggests a deliberate move made by somebody in charge of it.

context: The song is learned rather than inherited, which «infers» that a boundary can move in one generation.

why.A: "Infer" is what a listener does with evidence; a fact cannot infer anything itself.
why.B: Correct — the fact leads straight to the conclusion, which is what "means" says.
why.C: "Implicates" is used for involving someone in wrongdoing, not for drawing conclusions.
why.D: "Alludes" needs "to" after it and names an indirect reference, not a consequence.

context: The tapes cut in the 1960s differ «with» the ones made last spring in a way anyone can hear.

why.A: "Differ with" means to disagree with a person, not to be unlike another thing.
why.B: Correct — English pairs "differ" with "from" when two things are unlike.
why.C: "Than" follows a comparative such as "more" or "louder", and none appears here.
why.D: "Differ against" is not an English pairing in any sense of the verb.

context: Field workers must be «capable to distinguish» the two dialects by ear before they work alone.

why.A: "Capable" is followed by "of" and an -ing verb, never by an infinitive.
why.B: Correct — "capable of" takes the -ing form of the verb that follows it.
why.C: "Capable in" is not an English pairing, whatever verb form comes after it.
why.D: This keeps the wrong preposition and adds the wrong verb form on top of it.

context: By the time the second survey began in 1979, the northern dialect «had already crossed» the ridge.

why.A: Correct — the past perfect marks the crossing as finished before the 1979 survey.
why.B: The present perfect cannot describe something completed before a past event.
why.C: A present-tense verb puts the crossing in the reader’s own time rather than in 1979.
why.D: The past progressive leaves the crossing still under way when the survey began.

context: «Listening to the two dialects side by side, the difference is obvious» even to a beginner.

choices.text: Listening to the two dialects side by side, a beginner hears the difference
Listening to the two dialects side by side, the difference can be heard
The difference, listening to the two dialects side by side, is obvious

why.A: The opening phrase describes a listener, but the sentence supplies "the difference" instead.
why.B: Correct — the beginner is the one listening, so the beginner has to follow the comma.
why.C: The passive still leaves no listener in the main clause for the phrase to describe.
why.D: Moving the phrase into the middle does not change what it is attached to.

context: One tape from 1968 «— cut during a thunderstorm —» is still the clearest in the basement.

why.A: Correct — a pair of dashes fences off the aside with the same mark at each end.
why.B: An interrupter cannot open with a dash and close with a comma; the marks must match.
why.C: This mixes the two marks in the other order, which fails for the same reason.
why.D: Semicolons separate independent clauses and cannot fence off a phrase like this one.

context: Neither of the two surveys published «their» recordings in full.

why.A: "Neither" is singular, so a plural pronoun does not agree with it.
why.B: Correct — "neither" takes a singular pronoun, and the possessive form is "its".
why.C: This is the contraction of "it is", which cannot show possession of anything.
why.D: Adding "own" leaves the pronoun plural and the disagreement entirely untouched.

context: The archive of field tapes, along with the notebooks kept beside the machines, «are» stored in a basement.

why.A: The subject is "archive", and the phrase fenced off by commas cannot change its number.
why.B: Correct — "archive" is singular, so the verb that follows it is "is".
why.C: This is plural as well as past, so it disagrees with the singular subject twice over.
why.D: A plural auxiliary still fails to match the singular subject "archive".

context: Suppose the writer wanted to add a sentence stressing that the dialect boundary is not fixed. Which of the following would best accomplish that goal?

choices.text: The line has shifted twice since the first surveys, and no one expects it to hold.
The recordings are catalogued by date, by location and by the initials of the recordist.
A white-crowned sparrow weighs about as much as a small handful of paper clips.
Reel-to-reel tape was the standard recording medium throughout the 1960s.

why.A: Correct — a line that has already shifted twice is plainly not a fixed one.
why.B: Cataloguing practice says nothing about whether the boundary stays where it is.
why.C: The bird’s weight is a physical detail unrelated to where the two dialects meet.
why.D: The recording medium is background, and it leaves the boundary entirely unaddressed.

context: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to establish which explanation for the moving boundary is correct. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it explains that a buzz carries better through dense coastal scrub.
Yes, because it says the line has moved more than once since the 1960s.
No, because it sets out two explanations and says they are hard to separate.
No, because it never offers any explanation for why the boundary moves.

why.A: That is one side’s argument, and the essay sets a second argument beside it.
why.B: That establishes that the boundary moves, not why it moves.
why.C: Correct — the vegetation account and the cultural account are both given, and the essay says cover and culture move together.
why.D: It offers two, one about vegetation and one about which adults the young males heard.

context: The writer is considering deleting the statement that a male raised where he hears no adult singer invents a song of his own. Should it be kept?

choices.text: Kept, because it shows that the song has to be learned from another bird.
Kept, because it names the month in which young males first begin to sing.
Deleted, because the essay is about boundaries rather than about single birds.
Deleted, because the opening paragraph has already made the same point.

why.A: Correct — the invented song is the evidence that learning, not instinct, supplies the tune.
why.B: No month appears anywhere in that statement, so the stated reason does not match it.
why.C: The single bird is exactly what explains how a boundary can move at all.
why.D: The opening paragraph describes the ridge and never mentions an isolated male.

context: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence beginning "But the ridge itself is only a few hundred metres high" belongs:

choices.text: after the two slopes and their two songs have both been described.
at the very start of the essay, before either dialect is introduced.
in the final paragraph, after the account of how fast a song can change.
immediately before the explanation of how a young male learns his song.

why.A: Correct — the objection only lands once the reader knows a ridge divides the two.
why.B: Opening with an objection to a claim the reader has not yet met would only confuse.
why.C: By the final paragraph the ridge has dropped out of the discussion entirely.
why.D: The learning of the song is a separate thread, and the ridge interrupts it there.

context: The library, which had charged ten cents a day since «1971 stopped» charging anything in 2016.

why.A: A non-essential clause needs a comma at both ends, and the closing one is missing here.
why.B: Correct — the clause beginning "which" is fenced off by a comma at each end.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and the left side is not one.
why.D: A colon delivers what an independent clause has promised, and none is promised here.

context: Since the amnesty took effect, circulation «has risen» in every branch but one.

why.A: Correct — "since" plus a result that still stands calls for the present perfect.
why.B: The past perfect would place the rise before some other past event, and none is given.
why.C: A simple past closes the rise off, but "since" keeps it running up to the present.
why.D: The present progressive drops the link back to the moment the amnesty took effect.

context: The staff «had expected in advance to anticipate» a wave of books that never came home.

why.A: "In advance" and "anticipate" both repeat what "expected" has already said.
why.B: Correct — one verb carries the whole meaning without saying it twice.
why.C: The present tense "expect" clashes with "never came home," which places the whole episode in the past.
why.D: Expecting also happens beforehand, which makes the added phrase redundant.

context: «Overdue for eleven years, a woman returned a field guide» in the second week.

choices.text: A woman returned a field guide that had been overdue for eleven years
Overdue for eleven years, the second week brought back a field guide
Returning a field guide, eleven years overdue was the woman

why.A: The opening phrase describes the field guide, but a woman is what follows the comma.
why.B: Correct — the eleven years attach to the guide, the only thing that was overdue.
why.C: This hands the overdue years to the second week, which cannot itself be overdue.
why.D: Inverting the clause leaves the phrase attached to nothing and the sentence unreadable.

context: The board’s first objection «, that the fines paid for something —» turned out to be the weaker one.

choices.text: — that the fines paid for something —
, that the fines paid for something;
: that the fines paid for something,

why.A: An interrupter has to open and close with the same mark, and a comma cannot close a dash.
why.B: Correct — the aside is fenced by a dash at each end, so the pair finally matches.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and neither side here is one.
why.D: A colon introduces what an independent clause has promised, which this aside is not.

context: The board asked the director and «I» to prepare a report on the first year.

why.A: The pronoun is the object of "asked", and "I" can only ever be a subject.
why.B: Correct — drop "the director and" and "asked me" is what remains.
why.C: A reflexive has to match the subject, and the board is the subject of this sentence.
why.D: "Mine" is a possessive form and cannot stand as the object of a verb.

context: Return rates barely moved. «Therefore,» the number of reinstated cards tripled in six months.

why.A: "Therefore" claims the flat return rate caused the tripling, which nothing supports.
why.B: Correct — the two facts run alongside each other, which is what "meanwhile" marks.
why.C: "In other words" would make the tripling a restatement of the flat return rate, and it is a separate result.
why.D: The reinstated cards are a second result rather than an instance of the return rate.

context: The report tracked how many books came back, how many cards were reopened, and «the rise in circulation».

why.A: A noun phrase breaks a series whose first two members are clauses beginning "how".
why.B: Correct — all three items now open with "how", so the series matches itself.
why.C: A gerund phrase is a third different shape, which leaves the list uneven.
why.D: An infinitive turns the third item into a purpose rather than a third thing tracked.

context: Neither the fine schedule nor the reminder letters «was» changed during the first year.

why.A: With "neither ... nor" the verb matches the nearer subject, and "letters" is plural.
why.B: Correct — "letters" sits closest to the verb, so the verb has to be plural.
why.C: This is singular as well as perfect, so it disagrees with the nearer subject.
why.D: A singular present-tense verb misses both the number and the past time frame.

context: The writer is considering adding a sentence naming the architecture firm that designed the library building. Should the sentence be added?

choices.text: No, because the essay is about the fines policy rather than the building.
No, because the firm is already named earlier in the same paragraph.
Yes, because it explains why the board was reluctant to lose the revenue.
Yes, because it shows that the library has served the city for a long time.

why.A: Correct — the architect has no bearing on what the fines did or on whom they fell.
why.B: No firm is named anywhere in the essay, so nothing would be repeated.
why.C: A design credit says nothing about revenue or about the board’s reasoning.
why.D: Length of service is not at issue, and the sentence would still change the subject.

context: The «librarians» objections were heard at three meetings before the vote.

why.A: With no apostrophe the word is a plain plural and shows no ownership at all.
why.B: Correct — several librarians own the objections, so the apostrophe follows the s.
why.C: The singular possessive would mean one librarian raised every objection.
why.D: A plural already ending in s never takes a second s after the apostrophe.

context: The amnesty had no «effect» on how quickly borrowed books came back.

why.A: Correct — the noun after "no" is "effect", and a result is exactly what is meant.
why.B: "Affect" is the verb form, and a verb cannot follow "no" in this position.
why.C: An affectation is a put-on manner, which has nothing to do with return times.
why.D: An -ing form cannot serve as the noun the sentence needs after "no".

context: Suppose the writer wanted to close the essay by stressing that the question is still open. Which of the following would best accomplish that goal?

choices.text: The board votes on the policy each year and has not yet voted the same way twice.
The library holds about four hundred thousand items across its seven branches.
Fines had been charged at ten cents a day without interruption since 1971.
The director keeps the first amnesty poster framed behind her office door.

why.A: Correct — a vote that keeps changing is the clearest sign the question is still open.
why.B: The size of the collection is a fact about the library, not about the argument.
why.C: The old fine rate is background and says nothing about what happens next.
why.D: A framed poster suggests the matter was closed, which is the opposite of the goal.

context: Three branches reported the same three problems«:» damaged spines, missing discs and unshelved returns.

why.A: Correct — an independent clause promises three problems, and a colon delivers the list.
why.B: A semicolon separates independent clauses, and a bare list of nouns is not one.
why.C: A comma is too weak to introduce a list the clause has just announced.
why.D: "Namely" duplicates the work the colon is already doing before it.

context: The reminder letters went out every Friday. «Although nobody on the staff expecting a reply.»

choices.text: Nobody on the staff expected a reply.
Although nobody on the staff expecting a reply,
Nobody on the staff, expecting a reply.

why.A: This has a subordinator and no finite verb, so it never becomes a sentence.
why.B: Correct — a subject and a finite verb turn the fragment into a real sentence.
why.C: A comma at the end leaves the clause subordinate and just as dependent as before.
why.D: The participle still supplies no finite verb, so these words cannot stand alone.

context: My aunt Verity, who had worked the board for thirty-one «years kept» a clock in the same room.

why.A: A non-essential clause needs a comma at both ends, and the closing one is missing.
why.B: Correct — the clause beginning "who" is fenced off by a comma at each end.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and the left side is not one.
why.D: A colon delivers what a full clause has promised, and nothing has been promised here.

context: The automatic equipment was «faster, nobody in Ardnew has ever argued otherwise».

choices.text: faster; nobody in Ardnew has ever argued otherwise
faster nobody in Ardnew has ever argued otherwise
faster, and, nobody in Ardnew has ever argued otherwise

why.A: Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone make a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon is strong enough to join two clauses that could each stand alone.
why.C: Removing the punctuation leaves the two clauses fused, which is worse than the splice.
why.D: The comma after "and" separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

context: She let me plug the easy calls. «Although never the ones going out of the county.»

choices.text: She never let me plug the ones going out of the county.
Although never the ones going out of the county,
Never the ones going out of the county.

why.A: A subordinator with no subject and no finite verb cannot stand as a sentence.
why.B: Correct — a subject and a finite verb turn the fragment into a sentence.
why.C: A comma at the end leaves the clause subordinate and still dependent on something.
why.D: Dropping "although" removes the subordinator but supplies no verb, so it is still a fragment.

context: By the time the automatic equipment arrived, Verity «had worked» the board for thirty-one years.

why.A: Correct — the past perfect places the thirty-one years before the equipment arrived.
why.B: The present perfect runs up to now, but the arrival is finished and in the past.
why.C: A present-tense verb puts the work in the reader’s own time rather than in the past.
why.D: The past progressive describes something under way and does not total the years.

context: The row of small hinged shutters «drop» open whenever anyone lifts a receiver.

why.A: The subject is "row", which is singular; "of shutters" cannot change its number.
why.B: Correct — a singular subject takes the singular verb "drops".
why.C: This is plural as well as perfect, so it matches neither the subject nor the time frame.
why.D: A plural progressive still fails to agree with the singular subject "row".

context: Verity apologised to the man on the line for «myself» and then took the cord back.

why.A: A reflexive has to match the subject, and Verity rather than the narrator is the subject.
why.B: Correct — the object of "for" is the plain object pronoun.
why.C: "I" is a subject form and cannot follow a preposition.
why.D: "My" is possessive and needs a noun after it, which the sentence does not supply.

context: The «Cassidys» telephone rang at half past six on a morning in August.

why.A: Without an apostrophe the word is a plain plural and marks no ownership.
why.B: Correct — the family is plural and already ends in s, so the apostrophe follows it.
why.C: The singular possessive would mean one Cassidy rather than the household.
why.D: A plural already ending in s never takes a second s after the apostrophe.

context: «Hanging on their weighted pulleys, I could see the cords» from the doorway.

choices.text: I could see the cords hanging on their weighted pulleys
Hanging on their weighted pulleys, the doorway showed the cords
The cords, I could see hanging on their weighted pulleys,

why.A: The opening phrase describes the cords, but "I" is what follows the comma.
why.B: Correct — the phrase now sits beside the cords, which are the things hanging.
why.C: This hands the pulleys to the doorway, which is not hanging from anything.
why.D: Fencing the clause off in the middle leaves the sentence without a main verb.

context: Verity knew the hours, knew the names, and «was aware of every routine» in Ardnew.

choices.text: the routines were known to her

why.A: The first two items share the verb "knew", so a different verb breaks the pattern.
why.B: Correct — all three items now run "knew the ___", which is what a series needs.
why.C: A passive clause changes who is doing the knowing and no longer matches.
why.D: This swaps the verb for a noun phrase, which is a fourth shape rather than the same one.

context: The new equipment connected a call in under a second. «Likewise,» it knew nothing about the town.

why.A: "Likewise" claims the two sentences agree, and the second one takes something back.
why.B: Correct — speed and ignorance pull against each other, which is what "but" marks.
why.C: "Therefore" would make the ignorance a consequence of the speed, which it is not.
why.D: "In addition" stacks a second point of the same kind, and this one runs the other way.

context: The board held a hundred jacks «— one for every line in Ardnew,» and a hundred cords.

choices.text: — one for every line in Ardnew —
, one for every line in Ardnew —
; one for every line in Ardnew;

why.A: An interrupter cannot open with a dash and close with a comma; the marks must match.
why.B: Correct — a pair of dashes fences off the aside with the same mark at each end.
why.C: This mixes the two marks in the other order, which fails for the same reason.
why.D: Semicolons separate independent clauses and cannot fence off a phrase like this.

context: The job came down to one thing that no wire carried«,» knowing the town.

why.A: A comma is too weak to deliver the thing the clause has just promised to name.
why.B: Correct — a colon introduces what an independent clause has announced is coming.
why.C: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and "knowing the town" is not one.
why.D: "That is" needs punctuation of its own and still leaves the introduction undone.

context: Verity was never impatient «of» a caller who could not remember a number.

why.A: "Impatient of" is used for things one refuses to tolerate, not for people one waits on.
why.B: Correct — English pairs "impatient" with "with" when the object is a person.
why.C: "Impatient from" is not an English pairing in any sense of the adjective.
why.D: "Against" suggests opposition rather than the strain of waiting for someone.

context: The shutter dropped and «made an audible clicking sound that could be heard» in the kitchen.

why.A: "Audible" and "could be heard" say the same thing twice over in one phrase.
why.B: Correct — one plain verb carries the meaning and names the noise exactly.
why.C: "Sounded" drops the particular noise the shutter makes, which is the point of the line.
why.D: "Emitted a sound" is both longer and vaguer than the verb the sentence wants.

context: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence beginning "None of that was written anywhere" belongs:

choices.text: after the list of what Verity knew about the town.
in the opening paragraph, before the board is described.
in the final paragraph, after the clock is mentioned.
before the sentence explaining that the narrator was thirteen.

why.A: Correct — "that" has nothing to point back to until the list of what she knew has run.
why.B: In the opening paragraph there is no knowledge yet for the sentence to be about.
why.C: By the final paragraph the exchange is closed and the knowledge is no longer the subject.
why.D: The narrator’s age comes before any of the knowledge, so the reference would be empty.

context: Suppose the writer wanted to add a sentence stressing how little public recognition the job carries. Which of the following would best accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Nobody applauds a vowel, and no award exists for the work.
Rehearsal rooms are usually booked in blocks of six weeks at a time.
Fennelly has coached productions in three different countries.
A vowel chart maps the position of the tongue inside the mouth.

why.B: Booking practice describes the schedule and says nothing about who notices the work.
why.C: Working in three countries suggests a career in demand rather than one overlooked.
why.D: The chart is a technical tool and carries no claim about recognition at all.

context: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to argue that dialect coaches deserve more prominent credit in theatre programmes. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it notes that a coach is credited in six-point type on the last page.
Yes, because it observes that nobody in the audience applauds a vowel.
No, because it is concerned with what the coach protects, not with how she is credited.
No, because it never says where a coach’s name appears in the programme.

why.A: The small credit sets up the essay’s subject; the writer never asks for it to be changed.
why.B: That line describes how unnoticed the work is, which is the premise of the essay rather than a proposal.
why.C: Correct — the essay moves from the size of the credit to Fennelly’s method and the audience member she coaches for.
why.D: It does: in six-point type on the last page.

context: The writer is considering deleting the statement that the cast listens for a week without trying to imitate anything. Should it be kept?

choices.text: Kept, because it is the step that makes the imitation come out right.
Kept, because it names the recordings Fennelly plays to her casts.
Deleted, because the essay is about accents rather than about rehearsal.
Deleted, because the paragraph has already described her method in full.

why.A: Correct — the next sentence says imitation goes wrong when it starts early.
why.B: No particular recording is named there, so the stated reason does not match.
why.C: Rehearsal is where the accent is built, so the two cannot be separated.
why.D: The sentence is the method; without it the paragraph describes nothing in particular.

context: The writer is considering adding a sentence listing the awards given each year for stage design and lighting. Should the sentence be added?

choices.text: No, because the essay is about a job that those lists leave out.
No, because stage design has already been discussed in an earlier paragraph.
Yes, because it would show that the theatre recognises technical crafts.
Yes, because it explains why Fennelly has lost jobs over her refusals.

why.A: Correct — a list of other awards pulls the paragraph away from the job it describes.
why.B: Stage design is never mentioned, so nothing would be repeated by adding this.
why.C: Recognition of other crafts is a separate subject and not what the paragraph is about.
why.D: Her refusals turn on flattering the audience and have no bearing on any award.

context: Broadcasters’ speech has been «sanded down» by years of professional work.

why.A: Correct — sanding smooths a surface deliberately, which is what the training does.
why.B: Erosion is slow and accidental, and nobody is training a river.
why.C: "Abraded" is a clinical term for scraping and carries none of the smoothing.
why.D: "Diminished" says the speech got smaller rather than that it lost its edges.

context: Fennelly «refutes» the request whenever a director asks for a thicker accent.

why.A: "Refutes" means to disprove a claim, and a request is not a claim to be disproved.
why.B: Correct — "declines" is the plain verb for turning down something that was asked.
why.C: "Rebukes" is aimed at a person for wrongdoing, not at a request.
why.D: "Renounces" means giving up something one already holds or believes.

context: Ita Fennelly, who has coached in three «countries holds» that the job is misnamed.

why.A: A non-essential clause needs a comma at both ends, and the closing one is missing.
why.B: Correct — the clause beginning "who" is fenced off by a comma at each end.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and the left side is not one.
why.D: A colon delivers what a full clause has promised, and nothing has been promised.

context: Before she took her first coaching job, Fennelly «had studied» phonetics for four years.

why.A: Correct — the past perfect puts the four years before the first coaching job.
why.B: The present perfect runs up to now, but the first job is finished and in the past.
why.C: A present-tense verb puts the study in the reader’s own time rather than earlier.
why.D: The present progressive describes something under way now, which this is not.

context: «Sitting at the side of the rehearsal room, the notebook records» every vowel that slips.

Sitting at the side of the rehearsal room, every slipped vowel is recorded

why.A: The opening phrase describes someone sitting, and a notebook does not sit at a side.
why.B: Correct — the coach is the one sitting, so the coach follows the comma.
why.C: The passive supplies no one for the phrase to describe, so it still dangles.
why.D: Moving the phrase into the middle leaves it attached to the notebook as before.

context: Each of the three directors had «their» own reason for wanting the accent thickened.

why.A: "Each" is singular, so a plural pronoun does not agree with it in formal usage.
why.B: Correct — a singular pronoun matches the singular subject "each".
why.C: This is the contraction of "they are" and cannot show possession at all.
why.D: "Its" is used for things rather than for the people being referred to here.

context: The vowel chart can be learned in a week. «Similarly, the habits» behind it take much longer.

why.A: "Similarly" claims the two facts agree, and the second one sets against the first.
why.B: Correct — the contrast is clear without a connector, and no false agreement is claimed.
why.C: "Consequently" would make the slow habits a result of the quick chart, which they are not.
why.D: The habits are not an example of the chart; they are the thing the chart leaves out.

context: She listens for where the weight falls, how long a pause runs, and «which consonants get dropped».

why.A: Correct — all three items are clauses opening with a question word, so the series matches.
why.B: A noun phrase breaks a series whose first two members are clauses.
why.C: A gerund phrase is a third shape again, which leaves the list uneven.
why.D: An infinitive turns the third item into a purpose rather than a third thing listened for.

context: A «coachs» credit appears in six-point type on the last page of the programme.

why.A: Without an apostrophe there is no possessive, and "coachs" is not a word in any case.
why.B: Correct — one coach owns the credit, so the apostrophe goes before the s.
why.C: The plural of "coach" is "coaches", so this cannot be its plural possessive.

context: Fennelly is not interested «on» flattering an audience she thinks can hear perfectly well.

context: She has lost «jobs over it, she has never lost one» over an accent that was too subtle.

why.A: Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone make a comma splice.

context: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence "The first dozen were unusable." belongs:

choices.text: after the two ways in which a mix can go wrong.
in the opening paragraph, before the riverbank is described.
in the final paragraph, beside the shelf of dated blocks.

context: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence "None of that survives in a photograph." belongs:

at the start of the second paragraph, before any comparison is drawn.
in the third paragraph, after the plaster is mixed too thin.

context: A good track «lasts for a period of about a day» before the weather takes it.

choices.text: has a duration of about a day

why.A: "For a period of" says nothing that "about a day" has not already said.
why.B: Correct — the verb and the span of time are all the sentence needs.
why.C: Dropping "about" turns an estimate into an exact figure; the writer is approximating how long a track survives.

context: He «came to the realization that he had learned» the consistency by ruining things.

choices.text: came to realize that he had learned

why.A: "Came to the realization" is a four-word way of saying one verb’s worth of meaning.

why.C: Trimming the noun still leaves "came to" doing work the verb can do alone.
why.D: "Had the realization of" is the same noun phrase with a different preposition.

context: Pryce will not say why the badgers went «— that is somebody else’s work —» and he says so early.

why.A: Correct — paired dashes can enclose a full clause dropped into another sentence.
why.B: Commas around an independent clause inside another sentence make a splice.
why.C: An opening dash with no closing mark leaves the interruption hanging open.
why.D: Semicolons join independent clauses in sequence; they cannot bracket an aside.

context: The shelf of dated blocks «— twenty years of them,» stands in an unheated outbuilding.

why.A: A dash opens the interruption, and a comma cannot close what a dash began.
why.B: Correct — the same mark closes the interruption that the opening dash began.
why.C: Adding "and" leaves the sentence with an interruption that never closes at all.
why.D: With no closing mark the subject runs straight into its verb without a break.

context: The depth of the toe prints «tell» how the animal put its weight down.

why.A: "Tell" agrees with "prints", which sits in a phrase and is not the subject.
why.B: Correct — the subject is "depth", a singular noun, so the verb is singular.
why.C: "Have told" is plural as well, and it moves the sentence into a finished past.
why.D: "Are telling" is plural and turns a standing fact into something in progress.

context: Neither the stones nor the root «was» visible under the mud he was working.

why.A: Correct — after neither/nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "root".
why.B: "Were" agrees with "stones", which is the further of the two subjects here.
why.C: "Have been" is plural and also pulls the sentence out of the past it describes.
why.D: "Are" is wrong in number and puts a finished afternoon into the present tense.

context: He goes out in the worst weather for a plain reason«;» the short life of a track.

why.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and "the short life of a track" is a phrase.
why.B: Correct — a colon follows a complete clause and delivers what it announced.
why.C: ", and" adds the short life of a track as a second thing he goes out for, rather than naming the reason.
why.D: "Namely" after a semicolon still leaves an incomplete clause on the right.

context: The three things a cast cannot report «are:» health, hunger and age.

why.A: A colon after "are" cuts a linking verb off from the complement it needs.
why.B: Correct — the list completes the verb directly, so nothing belongs between them.
why.C: "Namely" adds a signpost and keeps the same break between verb and complement.
why.D: A dash makes the same interruption a colon does, only with a different mark.

context: He still loses one in five. «Usually to a stone he did not see under the mud.»

choices.text: A stone he did not see usually takes it.
Usually to a stone he did not see under the mud,
Usually a stone under the mud he did not see.

why.A: A prepositional phrase on its own has no subject and no verb to run on.
why.B: Correct — a subject and a finite verb turn the phrase into a sentence.
why.C: A comma at the end leaves the phrase attached to nothing that follows it.
why.D: Dropping "to" produces a noun phrase, which is still not a sentence.

context: The plaster sets in twenty minutes. «Which is long enough for the light to go.»

choices.text: That is long enough for the light to go.
Long enough for the light to go.
Which is long enough, the light goes.

why.A: A clause opening with "which" attaches to a sentence rather than standing as one.
why.B: Correct — "that" is a subject pronoun, so the clause has a subject and a verb.
why.C: Dropping "which" removes the relative but supplies no subject and no verb.
why.D: A comma between two statements makes a splice on top of the original fragment.

context: Pryce is careful «about» what a cast can be asked to prove.

why.A: Correct — English pairs "careful" with "about" before a subject of concern.
why.B: "Careful for" is not an English pairing after this adjective in any sense.
why.C: "Careful on" names a surface underfoot rather than a matter under thought.
why.D: "Careful at" is not an English pairing before a matter being weighed.

context: The deer that arrived eight years ago show no sign «on» leaving the crossing.

why.A: "Sign on" is not an English pairing before a word ending in -ing.
why.B: Correct — "sign" takes "of" before the thing the sign is evidence for.
why.C: "For" would name a purpose, and no purpose is being reported here.
why.D: "To" would need an infinitive after it rather than the -ing form.

context: He goes out «in the cold and, the wet» rather than on the pleasant mornings.

choices.text: in the cold and the wet
in the cold, and the wet
in the cold, and, the wet

why.B: Correct — two items joined by "and" take no comma between them.
why.C: A comma before "and" is for two independent clauses, and "the wet" is not one.

context: Before the committee met, the developer «submits» a list of forty possible names.

why.A: A present-tense verb cannot report something finished before a past meeting.
why.B: Correct — the past perfect places the list before the meeting the sentence names.
why.C: "Submit" is plural as well as present, and the developer is one party.

context: The fire officer «has sat» on the committee since the radio system was replaced.

why.A: Correct — "since" plus a past starting point calls for the present perfect.

context: Hard to spell over a radio«, the officer rejected the name» at the first meeting.

why.C: A participle leaves the officer as the thing that is hard to spell.
why.D: A rejection is not hard to spell over a radio, so the phrase still dangles.

context: Walking the new estate with a map, «the names seemed» interchangeable to the clerk.

why.A: Names cannot walk an estate with a map, so the opening phrase has no owner.

context: The committee gave the clerk and «I» the list of forty names to sort.

context: Every one of the forty names had «their» own objection attached to it.

why.A: "Their" is plural, and the subject of the sentence is "every one", not "names".
why.B: Correct — "every one" is singular, so the singular possessive is the match.

context: The officer’s rules are practical. «However,» they decide more names than the historian’s do.

why.A: "However" promises a reversal, and the second sentence extends the first instead.
why.B: Correct — the second sentence presses the first one further, which "in fact" signals.
why.C: "Nevertheless" concedes something, and nothing here is being conceded.

context: Renaming a street costs the people who live on it. «Meanwhile,» the committee renames almost nothing.

context: The committee checks a name for spelling, for length, and «whether it sounds like another street.»

choices.text: for its likeness to another street.
if it sounds like another street.

why.A: A clause cannot sit in a list whose other members are prepositional phrases.
why.B: Correct — a third "for" phrase matches the two that come before it.
why.C: Swapping "whether" for "if" leaves a clause where a phrase is needed.
why.D: A bare participle still does not match the "for" pattern the list has set.

context: A good name is easy to say, easy to spell, and «easy to hear» over a radio.

why.A: Correct — the third item repeats the "easy to" pattern the first two set.
why.B: A full clause breaks a list whose other members are adjective phrases.
why.C: A gerund subject turns the third item into a sentence of its own shape.
why.D: An adverb and participle drop the "easy to" frame the other two items share.

context: The «officers» objection was that two streets in the estate sounded alike.

why.A: Without an apostrophe the word is a plural noun and cannot own the objection.

why.D: Dropping the ending leaves two nouns in a row with no possession marked.

context: The committee rejected the name on «it’s» third reading, without a vote.

why.A: "It’s" expands to "it is", which cannot stand before "third reading".
why.B: Correct — the possessive of "it" carries no apostrophe in any position.

context: The clerk types the minutes«, the historian checks the dates» before the file closes.

why.D: A second comma brackets the clause without fixing the join at the front.

context: Nobody watches the committee«,» its decisions surface only when a sign goes up.

why.A: Two complete statements joined by a comma alone make a splice.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon links two related independent clauses without a conjunction.
why.C: "However" is a conjunctive adverb and cannot join clauses across a comma.
why.D: "Then" is likewise an adverb, so the comma is still carrying the whole join.

context: The committee can «refuse» a name, but it cannot make a street worth living on.

why.A: Correct — to refuse something is to decline to accept it, which is what happens.
why.B: "Refute" means to disprove a claim, and a proposed name makes no claim.
why.C: "Repulse" means to drive back an attack, which no list of names amounts to.

context: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence "Nobody ever thanked her for a correct number." belongs:

choices.text: at the opening of the final paragraph, ahead of the reflection.
in the first paragraph, before the hut and the plate are described.
in the second paragraph, after the docket is filled in triplicate.
in the fourth paragraph, before the unfamiliar driver arrives.

why.A: Correct — it sets up the point about a job made of unremarked repetition.
