context: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence "The difference is what the quarry sells." belongs:

choices.text: after the two weighings the sentence is drawing a difference between.
at the start of the second paragraph, before either weighing is named.
in the third paragraph, beside the complaint about the Dunmore road.
in the final paragraph, after the narrator says she was twelve.

why.A: Correct — "the difference" has nothing to subtract until both weights are given.
why.B: At the paragraph’s start no weight has been taken, so there is no difference yet.
why.C: The state of the road is a grievance of the regulars and not part of the arithmetic.
why.D: The closing reflection is about repetition rather than about how the sum works.

context: The writer is considering deleting the phrase "with a crossword in between" from the final paragraph. Should it be kept?

choices.text: Kept, because it keeps the nineteen years ordinary rather than heroic.
Kept, because it shows that the weighbridge was quiet for most of the day.
Deleted, because the crossword has already been mentioned once before.
Deleted, because it makes the mother seem inattentive to her own job.

why.A: Correct — the crossword is what stops the summary from turning into a tribute.
why.B: How busy the hut was is never the point, and the phrase does not measure traffic.
why.C: An earlier mention is a reason the echo lands, not a reason to cut the phrase.
why.D: She returns to the crossword after writing the true weight, which shows the opposite.

context: At this point the writer is considering adding: "Quarry lorries in the county carried an average of eighteen tonnes." Should this be added?

choices.text: No, because a county average pulls away from one hut and one dial.
No, because the passage has already given the exact weight of the load.
Yes, because it lets the reader judge how large the driver’s request was.
Yes, because it explains why the Dunmore road was being wrecked by traffic.

why.A: Correct — the passage works at the scale of one window and one docket.
why.B: No weight is ever given in the passage, exactly or otherwise.
why.C: The size of the request is beside the point; the refusal is not about the amount.
why.D: The road is a subject of complaint in the hut and not something the essay explains.

context: Suppose the writer wanted to add a sentence showing that the mother treated every driver alike. Which choice best accomplishes that?

choices.text: She was pleasant to the ones who tried it on in exactly the same way.
She could tell from the engine which lorry was coming up the hill.
The regulars talked to her through the window while the needle settled.
She had run the weighbridge on the Dunmore road for nineteen years.

why.A: Correct — the same manner extended to the worst of them is the point exactly.
why.B: Recognising an engine shows familiarity with the lorries, not evenness with people.
why.C: Talk through the window describes the regulars only and leaves the others out.
why.D: Length of service says how long she did the job, not how she treated anyone.

context: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to show that ordinary work can carry a moral weight its doer never names. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because the refusal is folded back into nineteen years of routine.
Yes, because the mother explains to her son what the refusal meant to her.
No, because the passage treats the August afternoon as an isolated event.
No, because the narrator never describes what the job actually involved.

why.A: Correct — the closing paragraph refuses to let the refusal stand as a separate act.
why.B: She says nothing about it; she turns the docket over and returns to the crossword.
why.C: The final paragraph states plainly that the afternoon was not the exception.
why.D: The second paragraph sets out the two weighings and the triplicate docket in full.

context: He leaned on the sill and «exclaimed» about his load and the kind of day he had.

why.A: "Exclaimed" reports a sudden cry, and he is talking at the window steadily.
why.B: Correct — he is setting out reasons at length, which is what explaining is.
why.C: "Expounded" suits a doctrine being set out, not a driver making an excuse.
why.D: "Exhorted" means urging someone to act and takes a person as its object.

context: The needle on the dial «settled» before she wrote either number on the docket.

why.A: Correct — a needle settles when it stops swinging and comes to rest on a figure.
why.B: "Settled up" means paying what is owed, not a needle coming to rest.
why.C: "Resolved" would mean the needle answered a question rather than stopped moving.
why.D: "Subsided" describes something sinking or dying away, not coming to rest.

context: The hut «was small in size, being about as big as» a garden shed.

choices.text: was small in size, about the size of

why.A: "Small in size" says twice what "small" says once, and the comparison follows anyway.
why.B: Correct — the comparison carries the smallness without anything said twice.
why.C: "Small in size" says twice what "small" says once, and "size" then comes round a third time in the comparison.
why.D: "Small as" is missing the first "as" the comparison needs ("as small as"), so the phrase does not read as English.

context: Everything leaving the quarry «had to be required to stand» on the plate twice.

choices.text: was required to have to stand

why.A: "Had to" and "required to" state the same obligation one after the other.
why.B: Correct — one statement of the obligation is all the sentence needs.
why.C: Reversing the order keeps both phrases and the doubled obligation with them.
why.D: "Had stood" reports that something once happened and loses the rule: the point is that everything was required to stand on the plate.

context: Outside the hut«, set flush into the road,» lay a steel plate wide enough for a lorry.

why.A: Correct — paired commas close off a descriptive phrase dropped into the sentence.
why.B: Opening the phrase with a comma and never closing it leaves the sentence split.
why.C: Closing without opening does the same damage at the other end of the phrase.
why.D: Semicolons join independent clauses and cannot bracket a descriptive phrase.

context: She wrote the two weights «and, the difference» on a docket in triplicate.

why.A: A comma after "and" cuts the conjunction off from the item it is joining.

why.C: A comma after the pair separates the list from the phrase that completes it.
why.D: A comma before "and" would be for two clauses, and "the difference" is not one.

context: She knew which drivers would try it «at» and was pleasant to them anyway.

why.A: "Try it at" is not an English expression in any region or register.
why.B: Correct — "try it on" is the fixed phrase for attempting a small deception.
why.C: "Try it for" would introduce a purpose and breaks the set expression.
why.D: "Try it about" pairs a verb and preposition that do not go together at all.

context: The complaint about the road was one the regulars never grew tired «from».

why.A: "Tired from" names a cause of exhaustion rather than a subject one is sick of.
why.B: Correct — "tired of" is the pairing English uses for something one has had enough of.
why.C: "Tired on" is not an English pairing in any sense of the adjective.
why.D: "Tired about" pairs the adjective with a preposition it never takes.

context: The docket went three ways«,» the driver, the office and the spike on the wall.

why.A: A comma is too weak to deliver the three ways the clause has just promised.
why.B: Correct — a colon follows a complete clause and hands over the list it announced.
why.C: A semicolon needs a full clause on its right, and a list of three nouns is not one.

choices.text: ; the end of a slow movement.

why.B: A semicolon needs a complete clause after it, and this phrase has no verb.

why.D: The comma at the end brackets a phrase that runs to the full stop instead.

context: The convention that governs concert audiences «have» changed twice in two centuries.

why.C: "Were" is plural as well and pushes the sentence into a different tense.

context: Neither the critics nor the conductor «were» willing to wait for the habit to form.

why.A: "Were" agrees with the critics, who are the further of the two subjects here.

why.C: "Have been" is plural and moves a finished episode into the present perfect.

why.A: A prepositional phrase standing alone has neither a subject nor a verb.
why.B: Correct — a subject and a finite verb make the phrase a sentence.
why.C: A comma at the end leaves the phrase leaning on something that never comes.
why.D: Adding words to a noun phrase does not supply the verb it still lacks.

context: What the older audience gave a composer was information. «It is not available now.»

why.A: Correct — a subject pronoun and a finite verb make this a complete sentence.
why.B: A relative clause opening with "which" has to attach to a sentence, not be one.
why.C: An adjective phrase on its own supplies neither a subject nor a verb.

context: By the time the critics took up the cause, audiences «have been» clapping between movements for a century.

context: Between the critic and «he», the habit was settled inside a single decade.

context: The convention was made by critics, by conductors, and «by publishers» in one decade.

why.A: Correct — the third item repeats the "by" that the first two items both carry.

why.B: A comma after the adverb does nothing about the comma splice ahead of it.
why.C: A participle leaves the second half without a finite verb and so without a clause.
why.D: Correct — a semicolon joins the clauses and "moreover" adds the second to the first.

context: Roughly a third of proposed commemorations rest on a claim that «nobody can source or find the origin of».

choices.text: nobody can source or locate the origin of
no one person is able to source

why.A: "Source" and "find the origin of" say the same thing twice in the same clause.
why.B: Correct — one verb carries the whole meaning the pair was splitting between them.
why.C: Swapping "find" for "locate" keeps the repetition and only changes its wording.
why.D: This runs longer than the original and adds "one person", which narrows nothing.

context: The modern hall returns one «single undifferentiated verdict, a verdict that is not broken down,» at the end of forty minutes.

choices.text: single, undifferentiated verdict that is whole,

why.A: "One", "single" and "not broken down" all repeat what "undifferentiated" says.
why.B: Moving the adjective into a relative clause keeps "single" and spends words saying it.
why.C: Correct — a single adjective carries what the original spread across three phrases.
why.D: "Whole" repeats "undifferentiated" a third time rather than replacing anything.

context: When the clerk handed the historian the brochure, «she» returned it without an argument about merit.

why.A: "She" could be the clerk or the historian, and the sentence never settles which.
why.B: An object form cannot serve as the subject of "returned" in this clause.
why.C: "They" is plural and leaves the same ambiguity it was brought in to clear up.
why.D: Correct — naming the historian removes an ambiguity no pronoun can resolve here.

context: Neither the critic nor the publishers thought «their» work was finished that decade.

why.A: Correct — after neither/nor the pronoun matches the nearer subject, which is plural.
why.B: A singular pronoun would agree with the critic, who is the further of the two.
why.C: "Its" would treat a group of people as a thing rather than as persons.
why.D: "One's" is indefinite and points to nobody actually named in the sentence.

context: The gauge, «which his father had bought secondhand,» stood in the same corner for forty-seven years.

choices.text: which his father had bought secondhand
that his father had bought secondhand,
which his father, had bought secondhand,

why.A: Correct — a non-essential clause opening with "which" takes a comma at both ends, and both are here.
why.B: Dropping the closing comma leaves the clause open at one end while the other end is still punctuated.
why.C: "That" introduces an essential clause, which takes no commas at all, so the one left behind is stranded.
why.D: This puts a comma between the subject of the clause and its verb, which separates two words that belong together.

context: Each book held «two columns; a date and a measurement in millimetres.»

choices.text: two columns: a date and a measurement in millimetres.
two columns, a date: and a measurement in millimetres.
two columns a date and a measurement in millimetres.

why.A: A semicolon joins two things that could each stand alone, and "a date and a measurement in millimetres" could not.
why.B: Correct — the colon introduces the list that spells out what the two columns were.
why.C: The colon has landed inside the list rather than in front of it, splitting the first item from the second.
why.D: With no mark at all the list runs straight into the clause and the reader has to guess where it starts.

context: The twenty-three exercise books on the shelf above his desk «was» the whole record.

why.A: The subject is "books," which is plural; the shelf is only where they sit.
why.B: This is singular as well, and it adds a present-perfect sense the sentence has no use for.
why.C: Correct — the plural subject "books" takes the plural verb "were."
why.D: This is singular and present tense, while the record is being described in the past.

context: By the time the office wrote to him in 1979, Pym «keeps» the record for forty-five years.

why.A: A present-tense verb cannot describe something finished before a past event.
why.B: A bare participle leaves the sentence with no main verb for its subject.
why.C: The future tense points past 1979, while the forty-five years lie behind it.
why.D: Correct — the past perfect places the forty-five years of keeping before the letter of 1979.

context: «Standing in the lee of a rising hedge, the record was compromised by the gauge.»

choices.text: Standing in the lee of a rising hedge, the gauge compromised the record.
The record, standing in the lee of a rising hedge, was compromised.
Compromised by the gauge, the record stood in the lee of a rising hedge.

why.A: The opening phrase describes whatever follows the comma, and a record does not stand in the lee of anything.
why.B: Correct — the gauge is the thing that stands in the hedge’s lee, and it now follows the phrase directly.
why.C: Moving the phrase into the middle does not change what it attaches to; the record is still doing the standing.
why.D: This keeps the same mismatch and adds a second one, since the gauge has become the thing doing the compromising to itself.

context: The dates ran without a gap. «Likewise,» eleven of them were written by his daughter.

why.A: "Likewise" says the second fact matches the first, but an unbroken run and a change of hand are not the same kind of fact.
why.B: Nothing about an unbroken run of dates causes somebody else to have written eleven of them.
why.C: Correct — the second sentence qualifies the first, which is the job of a contrasting transition.
why.D: The eleven days are an exception to the claim rather than an instance of it.

context: His «daughters» handwriting was larger and rounder than his own.

why.A: Without an apostrophe this is a plain plural, and the handwriting is not being said to belong to anyone.
why.B: A plural already ending in s never takes a further s after the apostrophe.
why.C: This would mean two or more daughters, and the passage gives Pym one.
why.D: Correct — one daughter possesses the handwriting, so the apostrophe goes before the s.

context: He copied the remaining books out before sending them. «A job that took him a year and a half.»

choices.text: It was a job that took him a year and a half.
a job that took him a year and a half.
Taking him a year and a half to do.

why.A: This is a noun with a clause hanging off it and no verb of its own, so it cannot stand as a sentence.
why.B: Correct — "It was" gives the group of words a subject and a verb, which is what it lacked.
why.C: Lowercasing the first word does not supply the missing verb; it only hides the seam.
why.D: A participle is still not a main verb, so this remains a fragment.

context: The correction was large, «it was larger than any single day’s rainfall he had recorded.»

choices.text: it was larger than any single day’s rainfall he had recorded;
larger than any single day’s rainfall he had recorded.
and larger, than any single day’s rainfall he had recorded.

why.A: A comma alone cannot hold two complete sentences together.
why.B: This moves the mark to the end, where it separates the clause from the full stop rather than from the clause before it.
why.C: Correct — dropping "it was" turns the second half into a phrase that the comma can properly attach.
why.D: The comma now falls between "larger" and the comparison it governs, splitting the phrase it should join.

context: The rarest thing about the record «— that one man took it at one spot by one method —» is also what made the hedge matter so much.

choices.text: — that one man took it at one spot by one method,
, that one man took it at one spot by one method —
that one man took it at one spot by one method

why.A: Correct — a pair of dashes sets off the interruption, and a pair is what is here.
why.B: A dash at the front and a comma at the back is a mismatched pair, and a mismatched pair reads as one mark gone missing.
why.C: This is the same mismatch the other way round, opening with a comma and closing with a dash.
why.D: With nothing setting it off, the inserted clause runs into the subject and the reader loses the main verb.

context: The office had to «work backwards in a reverse direction from the record itself» to find the error.

choices.text: work backwards, going in reverse, from the record itself
work backwards from the record itself

why.A: "Backwards" and "in a reverse direction" say the same thing twice over.
why.B: This is the shortest choice, but it cuts the phrase naming what the office worked back from, which the sentence needs.
why.C: Setting the repetition off in commas makes it more prominent rather than less.
why.D: Correct — this keeps the whole meaning and drops the phrase that only repeats "backwards."

context: A gauge in the lee of a tall hedge «hoards» less rain than one standing clear.

why.A: "Hoards" attributes an intention to the instrument, which nothing in the passage supports.
why.B: Correct — "collects" is the plain word for what a gauge does and matches the register of the passage.
why.C: "Amasses" implies a great quantity gathered up, which overstates a few millimetres.
why.D: "Absorbs" is what soil or a sponge does, taking water into itself, while a gauge catches rain to be measured.

context: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence "Nothing in twenty-three exercise books says when a hedge got tall." belongs:

choices.text: after the hedge is introduced and before the office works backwards.
in the opening paragraph, beside the description of the brass gauge.
in the paragraph about the eleven days his daughter covered.
at the very end, after the reader has been told this was not a defeat.

why.A: Correct — it explains why the record cannot answer the question itself, which is exactly what sends the office to the other stations.
why.B: The hedge has not been mentioned at that point, so the sentence would be about a thing the reader does not yet know exists.
why.C: That paragraph is about a gap in who took the readings, not about what the readings fail to record.
why.D: Placed last it becomes an afterthought, arriving after the problem it creates has already been settled.

context: At this point the writer is considering adding: "Sheffield is about fifteen miles from the Pym house by road." Should this be added?

choices.text: No, because the passage has already given the distance to the two stations.
No, because the distance to the hospital has no bearing on the record.
Yes, because it explains why his daughter rather than his wife took the readings.
Yes, because it shows how far the correction the office applied had to reach.

why.A: The twelve miles the passage gives belongs to the comparison stations, not to Sheffield, so this is not a repetition.
why.B: Correct — the paragraph is about who wrote eleven figures down, and a road distance does nothing for that.
why.C: The passage never raises the question of which member of the household went out, only that the daughter did.
why.D: The correction was worked out from two stations twelve miles away, which has nothing to do with the hospital.

context: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to show that a careful record can be undone by something its keeper never thought to record. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because the hedge is exactly the fact the exercise books do not hold.
Yes, because the eleven missing days are what forced the office to correct it.
No, because the office was able to correct the record from other stations.
No, because the passage says the column of figures was sound throughout.

why.A: Correct — the closing paragraph turns on the hedge being both the cause and the thing no column recorded.
why.B: The eleven days are covered in the record, by a different hand, and the passage says the dates run without a gap.
why.C: The correction confirms the problem rather than removing it; the office still had to reach outside the record.
why.D: The figures being sound is the point: a sound column still produced a record that needed correcting.

context: Pym had been fond «for» the hedge long before it began to cost him anything.

why.A: "Fond for" is not an English pairing; the adjective does not take "for."
why.B: "Fond with" is not idiomatic in any sense of the word.
why.C: Correct — "fond of" is the fixed pairing.
why.D: "Fond about" is likewise not a pairing English uses.

context: He emptied the gauge, «wrote down the figure, and was returning» to the house.

choices.text: writing down the figure, and returning
was writing down the figure, and returned
wrote down the figure, and returned

why.A: The third verb shifts into a different form from the two simple past verbs beside it.
why.B: Two participles against one past-tense verb leaves the series uneven and the sentence without a clear main verb.
why.C: This fixes the third verb by breaking the second, leaving the series mismatched in a new place.
why.D: Correct — "emptied," "wrote" and "returned" are all simple past, so the three match.

context: Neither the office nor the surrounding stations had kept «its» instruments in one place for as long.

why.A: After neither/nor the pronoun agrees with the nearer subject, and "stations" is plural.
why.B: Correct — the nearer subject is plural, so the plural pronoun is the one that agrees.
why.C: A masculine singular pronoun points at a person, and neither subject in the sentence is one.
why.D: "It’s" is the contraction of "it is" and cannot show possession at all.

context: He owned three pen nibs «a fine one, a medium one and a broad one,» and one bottle of ink.

choices.text: a fine one a medium one and a broad one,
— a fine one, a medium one and a broad one —
, a fine one, a medium one and a broad one

why.A: The list is closed off at the end but not opened at the front, so it runs straight into "nibs."
why.B: Removing the commas inside the list makes the three items run together.
why.C: Correct — a pair of dashes sets off a list that already contains commas of its own.
why.D: This opens the list without closing it, which is the same fault as the original in reverse.

context: He was particular about which nib did which job «; the fine one for streams, the medium for paths.»

choices.text: , the fine one for streams: the medium for paths.
the fine one for streams, the medium for paths.
: the fine one for streams, the medium for paths.

why.A: A semicolon joins two things that could each stand alone, and what follows is a list of examples, not a clause.
why.B: This puts the colon between the two items of the list instead of in front of them.
why.C: With no punctuation, the list runs straight into "job" and the reader cannot tell where the sentence turns.
why.D: Correct — the colon sits tight against "job" and introduces the two examples that follow.

context: He «will not draw» a path he had not walked, and he never announced this as a rule.

why.A: The future tense clashes with "had not walked" and "never announced," both of which are in the past.
why.B: Correct — "would not draw" is the past habitual, which is what the rest of the sentence is in.
why.C: The present tense describes a man still at the board, and the passage has him finished.
why.D: The present perfect reaches up to now, which conflicts with a habit described as having ended.

context: «Pushing a measuring wheel ahead of him, the count went onto the back of an envelope.»

choices.text: The count, pushing a measuring wheel ahead of him, went onto an envelope.
Pushing a measuring wheel ahead of him, he wrote the count on the back of an envelope.
Pushed ahead of him, the measuring wheel wrote the count on an envelope.

why.A: The opening phrase needs a person after the comma, and a count cannot push a wheel.
why.B: Moving the phrase inside the sentence leaves it attached to the count just as before.
why.C: Correct — "he" now follows the phrase, and he is the one doing the pushing.
why.D: This makes the wheel do the writing, which is a new mismatch in place of the old one.

context: The envelopes with the count written on the back of each one «goes» into a tin.

why.A: The subject is "envelopes," which is plural; everything between it and the verb is description.
why.B: This is singular as well, and the present perfect turns a repeated action into a finished one.
why.C: This is singular, and it also shifts the habit into something happening at this moment.
why.D: Correct — the plural subject takes the plural verb "go."

context: Everyone in the parish had used the way for years. «As a result,» there was no right of way.

why.A: Long use is not what produced the absence of a right of way; the two facts pull against each other.
why.B: Correct — the second fact sits awkwardly beside the first, which is what a concessive transition marks.
why.C: This presents the two as facts stacking up in the same direction, when they point opposite ways.
why.D: The absence of a right of way is not an example of everyone having used the path.

context: Both «gates were» chained by the end of that August.

why.A: Correct — "gates" here is a plain plural subject and owns nothing, so it takes no apostrophe.
why.B: This makes one gate the owner of something, and nothing in the sentence is being owned.
why.C: This makes several gates the owners of something, with the thing owned never named.
why.D: An apostrophe after a verb has no function in English punctuation.

context: The club printed the map anyway. «Four hundred copies going out in the spring.»

choices.text: four hundred copies going out in the spring.
Four hundred copies went out in the spring.
Four hundred copies, going out in the spring.

why.A: "Going" is a participle rather than a main verb, so this group of words has no verb to call its own.
why.B: Joining it to the previous sentence with a lowercase letter and a full stop still leaves it standing alone.
why.C: Correct — "went" is a main verb, which is what turns the phrase into a sentence.
why.D: Adding a comma changes the pacing but not the grammar; there is still no main verb.

context: Ronan left the field off the map, «the club added it themselves.»

choices.text: so the club added it themselves.

why.A: Two complete sentences are being held together by a comma, which cannot do that job alone.
why.B: A semicolon would work in place of the comma, but here it has been put at the end instead.
why.C: The added comma falls between the subject and its verb and does nothing about the splice.
why.D: Correct — "so" is a conjunction, and a comma before a conjunction is the standard way to join two clauses.

context: The path was inked in badly «— with the medium nib where the fine one was wanted —» and the sheet went out.

choices.text: , with the medium nib where the fine one was wanted —
— with the medium nib where the fine one was wanted,
with the medium nib — where the fine one was wanted

why.A: Correct — the aside is set off by a matched pair of dashes, which is what an interruption of this length wants.
why.B: Opening with a comma and closing with a dash is a mismatched pair; an interruption takes the same mark at both ends.
why.C: Opening with a dash and closing with a comma is a mismatched pair.
why.D: This puts one dash in the middle of the aside, cutting it in two rather than fencing it off.

context: He walked «each and every one of the paths personally himself» before drawing them.

why.A: "Each and every" doubles one idea and "personally himself" doubles another.
why.B: Correct — this keeps the whole meaning with neither pair of repeated words.
why.C: This clears the second redundancy but leaves "each and every" standing.
why.D: Placed before the object, "himself" reads as the thing walked, as though he walked himself, and the emphasis on doing it in person is lost.

context: A path on a printed map, he said, stops being a favour and becomes a «complaint».

why.A: A complaint is an expression of grievance, and the map is not grumbling about anything.
why.B: Correct — a claim is an assertion of a right, which is precisely what the printed path asserts without asking.
why.C: A demand is addressed to someone, and the map addresses no one in particular.
why.D: A proposal invites an answer, and the objection is that nobody was asked.

context: He went on drawing, the club went on printing, and «the gates stayed chained».

why.A: Correct — all three are clauses with a subject and a past-tense verb, which is as parallel as they need to be.
why.B: A relative clause leaves "the gates" without a main verb of its own, while the first two members each have one.
why.C: A bare noun phrase cannot sit in a series whose other two members are full clauses.
why.D: A participle leaves the third member without a main verb while the first two have one.

context: Between Ronan and «I», only one of us had walked the field in question.

why.A: "I" is a subject pronoun, and a word governed by "between" is an object.
why.B: A reflexive pronoun needs a subject earlier in the clause to point back at, and there is none.
why.C: Correct — "between" takes an object, and "me" is the object form.
why.D: "Mine" is possessive, and nothing in the sentence is being said to belong to the narrator.

context: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence "This was not a rule he announced." belongs:

choices.text: in the final paragraph, beside the map the narrator still keeps.
in the opening paragraph, after the three nibs have been described.
in the paragraph about Colm Tarry’s field and the missing right of way.
immediately after the statement that he would not draw an unwalked path.

why.A: Placed at the end it would refer back across four paragraphs to a rule the reader has long since absorbed.
why.B: No rule has been stated at that point, so "this" would have nothing to refer back to.
why.C: That paragraph is about a rule he did announce, out loud, to the club.
why.D: Correct — it qualifies the rule the sentence before it states, and the story of the moor then shows how it was learned.

context: At this point the writer is considering adding: "The club had two hundred members when Ronan first drew for it." Should this be added?

choices.text: No, because the passage has already given the number of members in the spring.
No, because the growth of the club is not what the paragraph is weighing.
Yes, because it shows how far the printed map travelled once it went out.
Yes, because it explains why the club overruled him about the field.

why.A: The passage gives four hundred members in the spring the map went out; a figure from when Ronan started is a different fact, so it would repeat nothing.
why.B: Correct — the paragraph is about what a printed path does to a landowner, and a membership figure does not bear on that.
why.C: A figure from years earlier says nothing about the reach of the sheet that actually went out.
why.D: The passage gives the club’s reason as wanting the path on the map, and size is never offered as part of it.

context: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to show that being proved right can be worth less than what it cost. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because the parish lost the path that Ronan’s refusal was meant to protect.
Yes, because the club apologised to him once the gates had been chained.
No, because Ronan states plainly at the end that the argument went his way.
No, because the passage never says what happened after the map went out.

why.A: Correct — he was right about what a printed path would do, and the field closed anyway, to everyone.
why.B: No apology appears anywhere; the passage says only that the club went on printing.
why.C: The passage says the opposite, that Ronan never claimed he had been right.
why.D: The fourth paragraph follows the map through June and August to the chained gates.

context: The club insisted «in» putting the path on the map.

why.A: "Insisted in" is not an English pairing, though it is a common slip.
why.B: "Insisted for" is not idiomatic in any sense of the verb.
why.C: Correct — "insist on" is the fixed pairing before a thing insisted upon.
why.D: "Insisted about" is likewise not a pairing English uses.

context: From below, it is something «stranger, its» skin and muscle are so clear that a person looking up can watch the heart beating.

why.A: A comma alone is holding two independent clauses together, which makes a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — a complete clause comes before the colon, and what follows it explains the "something stranger" the clause promised.
why.C: With no mark at all, the two clauses run straight into each other.
why.D: The semicolon already joins the clauses, so adding "and" after it joins them twice.

context: Skin and muscle can be made nearly clear. «Blood, however, packed» with a red protein that absorbs light.

why.A: "Packed" is a participle here, so the word group has a subject but no main verb.
why.B: Correct — "is packed" gives "blood" a finite verb, so the word group becomes a sentence.
why.C: "Being" is not a finite verb either, so the sentence still has none.
why.D: "Which" turns the verb into part of a relative clause and leaves "blood" without a verb of its own.

context: A frog with clear skin and red blood should still show a red line wherever its vessels «ran».

why.A: The past tense clashes with "should still show," which describes what is generally true of any such frog.
why.B: Correct — the sentence states a general truth in the present, so the vessels "run" wherever they are.
why.C: The past perfect places the vessels before some past moment the sentence never names.
why.D: The future perfect describes something finished by a future time, which has nothing to do with where vessels lie.

context: As it falls asleep, it pulls most of its red cells out of «circulation, it packs» them into its liver.

why.A: Two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone, which is a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — dropping the second "it" makes "packs" a second verb for the same subject, so no clause joint is needed.
why.C: A semicolon needs a complete clause after it, and "packs them into its liver" has no subject.
why.D: "Then" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so the comma is still joining two clauses on its own.

context: The liver, along with a reflective membrane that wraps it, «hold» the cells there for hours.

why.A: "Hold" is plural, but "along with a reflective membrane" does not add to the subject; the subject is the singular "liver."
why.B: Correct — the subject is "the liver," and a phrase beginning "along with" sits outside the subject, so the verb stays singular.
why.C: "Are" is plural, which treats the membrane as part of the subject.
why.D: "Have" is plural, and the present perfect also breaks the present tense of the paragraph.

context: In a human, red cells crowded together tend to stick and form clots, and a clot in the wrong place can be fatal. The frog«, however,» does it every day and suffers no harm.

why.A: Correct — the frog is set against the human case just described, and "however" marks that contrast.
why.B: "Therefore" claims the frog’s safety follows from the danger to humans, which reverses the logic.
why.C: The frog is not an example of clotting; it is the exception to it.
why.D: "Similarly" promises a likeness, and the frog’s case is the opposite of the human one.

stem: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after “Medical researchers would very much like to know how”: “Clots are behind a large share of strokes and heart attacks in people.” Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: Yes, because it shows why the frog’s trick matters to medical researchers.
Yes, because it suggests that glass frogs themselves are at risk of strokes.
No, because it merely repeats the earlier statement that a clot can be fatal.
No, because the paragraph is about how the frog hides from predators.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph ends by saying researchers want to know how, and this sentence supplies the human stakes that explain why.
why.B: The paragraph says the frog suffers no harm, and the sentence is about people, not frogs.
why.C: The earlier sentence says a clot can kill; this one says how common clot-related illness is, which is what makes the research worth doing.
why.D: Hiding from predators is the subject of the next paragraph; this one is about blood.

context: «Researchers suspect this, is why» the frogs choose the undersides of leaves.

why.A: The comma splits "this" from its verb "is," the two halves of the clause the researchers suspect.
why.B: Correct — "this is why" is the thing suspected, and nothing inside it needs to be set off.
why.C: A comma between a subject and its verb separates two words that belong together.
why.D: The comma cuts the verb "suspect" off from the clause that is its object.

context: Light comes through from above, and the edges of a «frogs» body all but disappear.

why.A: "Frogs" is a plain plural, but the body belongs to the frog, so the word needs to be possessive.
why.B: Correct — "a" marks a single frog, and the apostrophe before the "s" shows the body is its.
why.C: The apostrophe after the "s" makes a plural possessive, which cannot follow "a."
why.D: This adds a possessive to a plural and then another "s," which is never a correct form.

context: «Lit from the side, a predator would find a frog on top of a leaf far easier to see.»

choices.text: Lit from the side, a frog on top of a leaf would be far easier for a predator to see.
Lit from the side, it would be far easier for a predator to see a frog on top of a leaf.
A predator, lit from the side, would find a frog on top of a leaf far easier to see.

why.A: The opening phrase describes the frog, but the subject that follows it is "a predator," which is not the thing lit.
why.B: Correct — "a frog" now follows the opening phrase, and the frog is the thing lit from the side.
why.C: "It" is an empty subject, so the opening phrase has nothing to describe.
why.D: Moving the phrase beside "a predator" makes the hunter the one being lit.

context: Transparency «also explains where the frogs sleep.»

choices.text: also explains and accounts for where the frogs sleep.
also explains the location of where the frogs sleep.
also explains where it is that the frogs go to sleep.

why.A: Correct — the sentence says what the paragraph will show in five plain words.
why.B: "Explains" and "accounts for" mean the same thing here.
why.C: "The location of where" says the place twice.
why.D: "Where it is that" and "go to" add words without adding meaning.

context: Predators that hunt by sight look for an «outlay», and a clear body lets the green of the leaf show through.

why.A: An "outlay" is money spent, which has nothing to do with what a hunter sees.
why.B: Correct — an outline is the edge of a shape, which is what the clear body blurs.
why.C: An "outcome" is a result, not something a predator can look for on a leaf.
why.D: An "outlet" is an opening or a place to plug something in.

context: What the frog has is not a disguise so much as a «delay — the» few seconds a hunter spends deciding whether the green smudge is a leaf or a meal.

why.A: Correct — a single dash at the end of a clause introduces the phrase that says what the delay is.
why.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and "the few seconds a hunter spends" is a phrase.
why.C: With no mark, "a delay the few seconds" jams the definition against the word it defines.
why.D: A full stop leaves "The few seconds a hunter spends deciding" standing alone without a main verb.

context: What the frog has is a delay — the few seconds a hunter spends «to decide» whether the green smudge is a leaf or a meal.

why.A: "Spend time" is followed by an -ing verb, not by an infinitive.
why.B: Correct — English says a person spends time doing something.
why.C: "Spends seconds for deciding" puts a preposition where the idiom takes none.
why.D: "At deciding" names a skill, as in "good at deciding," rather than how time is used.

stem: The writer wants the essay’s final sentence to connect the frog’s survival to a detail from the first paragraph. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

choices.text: For an animal the size of a thumbnail, a few seconds is often enough.
For a predator, those few seconds are simply part of the hunt.
Glass frogs are found in the forests of Central and South America.
Scientists hope to learn much more about these frogs in the coming years.

why.A: Correct — "the size of a thumbnail" returns to the opening image and ties the frog’s small size to why a short delay can save it.
why.B: This turns to the hunter’s point of view and never returns to anything in the first paragraph.
why.C: A range fact connects to nothing in the opening and does not say whether the delay helps.
why.D: A general hope for more research neither concerns survival nor echoes the opening.

context: The first lesson lasted forty «minutes, and covered» roughly forty feet.

why.A: "Lasted" and "covered" share one subject, so a comma before "and" splits a single compound verb.
why.B: Correct — two verbs with one subject are joined by "and" with no comma.
why.C: A second comma after "and" cuts the conjunction off from the verb it introduces.
why.D: A semicolon separates independent clauses, and "covered roughly forty feet" has no subject.

context: Each time I let the clutch out, the truck lurched, shuddered, and «died».

why.A: Correct — "lurched, shuddered, and died" are three past-tense verbs in the same form.
why.B: The progressive form breaks the pattern of two simple past verbs before it.
why.C: Adding "it" gives the third item a subject the first two do not have.
why.D: The past perfect puts the last action before the first two, which reverses the order.

context: She reached over, turned the key, and «waits» for me to try again.

why.A: The present "waits" breaks the past tense of "reached" and "turned" in the same sentence.
why.B: Correct — the third verb matches the simple past of the two before it.
why.C: The future tense does not fit an action that happened during the lesson.
why.D: The present perfect shifts out of the past narrative the sentence has set up.

context: She reached over, turned the key, and waited «for» me to try again.

why.A: Correct — English pairs "wait" with "for" before the person or event awaited.
why.B: "Waited at" names a place, as in waiting at the gate, not what she was waiting for.
why.C: "Waited about" is not an English pairing.
why.D: "Waited of" is not an English pairing either.

context: The trick, she finally explained, is that the clutch and the gas are not two «pedals, they are» one conversation.

why.A: A comma alone joins two independent clauses, which makes a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon joins two independent clauses without a conjunction.
why.C: Removing the comma fuses the two clauses with no punctuation at all.
why.D: "However" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so the clauses are still spliced.

context: Neither my aunt nor my cousins «was» able to explain it any better than that.

why.A: With "neither ... nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, and "cousins" is plural.
why.B: Correct — the verb agrees with "cousins," the part of the subject closest to it.
why.C: "Is" is singular and present, and the narrative is in the past.
why.D: "Has" is singular and shifts the tense to the present perfect.

context: By the second week I could get the truck moving on flat ground. «Hills were another matter.»

why.A: Correct — "hills" is the subject and "were" is the verb, so this short sentence is complete.
why.B: Removing "were" leaves a noun and a phrase with no verb.
why.C: "Being" is not a finite verb, so the word group is a fragment.
why.D: "Which" turns the sentence into a relative clause that cannot stand alone.

context: That meant stopping on a slope and «starting again once more» without rolling back into the ditch.

why.A: "Again" and "once more" say the same thing side by side.
why.B: Correct — "again" alone says the truck had to start a second time.
why.C: Reversing the order keeps both words that say the same thing.
why.D: "Restarting again" is still redundant: the "re-" already means again.

context: «Stalled halfway up the hill for the third time, the gate looked impossibly far away.»

choices.text: Stalled halfway up the hill for the third time, I thought the gate looked impossibly far away.
The gate looked impossibly far away to me, stalled halfway up the hill for the third time.
Stalled halfway up the hill for the third time, the gate’s distance looked impossible.

why.A: The opening phrase describes the driver who stalled, but the subject that follows it is "the gate."
why.B: Correct — "I" follows the opening phrase, and the narrator is the one who stalled.
why.C: At the end of the sentence the phrase still sits closest to the gate, which did not stall.
why.D: The subject is now "distance," which stalled no more than the gate did.

context: «It’s» the same sound, she admitted, but it means something different once you stop being afraid of it.

why.A: Correct — "it’s" is short for "it is," which is what the sentence says: it is the same sound.
why.B: "Its" is a possessive, and nothing here belongs to anything.
why.C: An apostrophe after "its" is never a correct form.
why.D: The apostrophe after "is" has nothing to mark.

context: I have not driven a stick shift in years. «But» when I pull away from a stoplight, there is still a small part of my left leg that reaches for a pedal.

why.A: Correct — the habit that remains is set against the years without driving, and "but" marks that contrast.
why.B: "Therefore" claims the leg reaches for the pedal because the narrator has not driven, which reverses the point.
why.C: The reaching leg is not an example of not driving a stick shift.
why.D: "Likewise" promises a similar point, and this one runs against the sentence before it.

context: There is still a small part of my left leg that «attains» for a pedal that isn’t there.

why.A: "Attain" means to achieve a goal, and it does not take "for."
why.B: Correct — to "reach for" something is to stretch toward it, which is what the leg does.
why.C: "Achieves" means succeeds at, and the pedal is not there to be achieved.
why.D: "Accesses" means gets into or opens, which is not what a foot does to a pedal.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence “By the end of that first lesson, I had stalled it eleven times.” Where would it most logically be placed?

choices.text: After “the truck lurched, shuddered, and died.”
After “the full weight of my left leg.”
At the end of the essay, after “a pedal that isn’t there.”

why.A: Correct — "that first lesson" points back to the forty-minute lesson, and the stalls count the deaths the sentence just described.
why.B: At that point no lesson has started, so "that first lesson" has nothing to point back to.
why.C: The hill stalls happen weeks later, not during the first lesson the sentence names.
why.D: Ending on a count from the first day would pull the essay back years after it has moved on.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to show how a relative’s unusual way of teaching helped the narrator master a difficult skill. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because Delia’s advice to listen to the truck gets the narrator up the hill.
Yes, because it compares manual and automatic transmissions in technical detail.
No, because the narrator ended up taking the driving test in an automatic.
No, because the essay is more concerned with the farm than with the aunt.

why.A: Correct — the essay builds to the advice about listening, calls it "the one thing that finally helped," and ends with the license.
why.B: The essay mentions both kinds of car but explains neither mechanically.
why.C: The test car is a closing detail; the skill the essay tracks is the clutch, which the narrator did learn.
why.D: The farm is only the setting; Delia’s teaching drives every paragraph.

context: «Built for cars rather than voices, the choir found the garage surprisingly generous.»

choices.text: Built for cars rather than voices, the garage proved surprisingly generous to the choir.
The choir, built for cars rather than voices, found the garage surprisingly generous.
Built for cars rather than voices, the choir was surprised by how generous the garage was.

why.A: The opening phrase describes the garage, but the subject that follows it is "the choir," which was not built for cars.
why.B: Correct — "the garage" follows the opening phrase, and the garage is what was built for cars.
why.C: Moving the phrase beside "the choir" still says the singers were built for cars.
why.D: The subject is still "the choir," so the phrase still describes the singers.

context: Concrete is hard and flat, and «it» reflects nearly everything that strikes it.

why.A: Correct — "concrete" is singular, so the pronoun that stands for it is "it."
why.B: "They" is plural, and the only noun it could refer to, "concrete," is singular.
why.C: "Which" needs a noun directly before it to attach to, and "and" leaves it with nothing to start a clause.
why.D: "This one" suggests a choice among several materials, and only one has been named.

context: Farris calls this effect “free harmony”«:» every note you sing is still sounding when you sing the next one.

why.A: Correct — a complete clause comes first, and the colon introduces the explanation of what "free harmony" means.
why.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses makes a comma splice.
why.C: "Because" makes the second half a dependent clause, and a semicolon needs an independent clause after it.
why.D: "That" attaches the explanation to "harmony" as though it were part of the name.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence “Churches built of stone produce the same effect, which is partly why so much early choral music was written for them.” Should the writer make this deletion?

choices.text: Yes, because the passage is about a parking garage and has no reason to mention churches.
No, because it ties the garage’s echo to an old tradition of singing in stone rooms.
Yes, because it contradicts Farris’s description of free harmony.
No, because it explains why the choir sings only hymns.

why.A: The passage is about the garage’s sound, and the comparison shows that sound is not a novelty.
why.B: Correct — it shows that the effect Farris prizes is the one choral music was long written for.
why.C: The churches produce "the same effect," so the sentence supports her description.
why.D: The choice of music is explained in the next paragraph, by the blurring of fast passages.

context: Consonants, the sounds that make words understandable, «turns» to mush.

why.A: "Turns" is singular, and the subject is the plural "consonants."
why.B: Correct — the plural "consonants" takes the plural "turn"; the phrase between commas renames the subject without changing it.
why.C: "Is" is singular, which agrees with nothing in the subject.
why.D: "Has" is singular and shifts the tense away from the present of the paragraph.

context: Farris chooses the music «accordingly slow» hymns, rounds, and chords held for eight or ten beats.

why.A: With no mark, "accordingly" seems to describe "slow," and the list runs into the clause that announces it.
why.B: Correct — the clause is complete at "accordingly," and a colon introduces the list of what she chooses.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and a list of music is not one.
why.D: "And" makes the list a second thing she does rather than the music she chooses.

context: Farris chooses the music to suit the room. «Nobody sings anything quick.»

choices.text: Which means nobody sings anything quick.

why.A: Correct — "nobody" is the subject and "sings" the verb, so the short sentence is complete.
why.B: Without a verb the word group cannot stand as a sentence.
why.C: "Singing" is a participle, not a finite verb.
why.D: "Which" makes this a relative clause, and it has nothing to attach to after a full stop.

context: The night attendant spent the «choirs» first month asking them to leave.

why.A: "Choirs" is a plain plural, but the month belongs to the choir, so the noun must be possessive.
why.B: Correct — there is one choir, and the apostrophe before the "s" shows the month is its.
why.C: An apostrophe after the "s" marks a plural possessive, and there is only one choir.
why.D: A second apostrophe has nothing to mark.

context: The night attendant spent the choir’s first month asking them to «leave, the garage, he pointed out, was» for cars.

choices.text: leave; the garage, he pointed out, was
leave the garage, he pointed out, was
leave, however, the garage, he pointed out, was

why.A: A comma alone joins two independent clauses, which makes a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon joins the two clauses, and the commas around "he pointed out" set off the aside.
why.C: Removing the comma makes "the garage" the object of "leave," which changes the meaning and leaves "was for cars" with no subject.
why.D: "However" is not a conjunction, so a comma is still joining the two clauses.

context: He now keeps the ramp barrier raised on Thursdays «so that latecomers who arrive after the start can walk up».

choices.text: so that latecomers can walk up
so that late arrivals arriving can walk up
so latecomers who are late can walk up

why.A: A latecomer is someone who arrives after the start, so the clause repeats the noun.
why.B: Correct — "latecomers" already says they arrive after the start.
why.C: "Arrivals arriving" repeats the same idea in two forms.
why.D: "Latecomers who are late" says the same thing twice.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence “It took him a month to notice that the ramp was empty anyway.” Where would it most logically be placed?

choices.text: After “chose the garage for its sound.”

why.A: Correct — "him" is the attendant just named, and noticing the empty ramp explains the change of mind reported next.
why.B: No man has been mentioned in the first paragraph, so "him" has nothing to refer to.
why.C: The person named there is Farris, a woman, so "him" cannot refer back to her.
why.D: By then he has already changed his mind and sung along, so noticing the ramp comes too late to explain anything.

context: «A garage — Farris says, is» the only room in town that nobody has tried to make pretty.

why.A: The aside opens with a dash and closes with a comma; an interruption takes the same mark at both ends.
why.B: Correct — a matched pair of commas sets off "Farris says" from the sentence around it.
why.C: This opens with a comma and closes with a dash, which mismatches the pair the other way round.
why.D: The opening dash is never closed, so "Farris says" runs into the rest of the sentence.

context: A garage, Farris says, is the only room in town that nobody has «tried at making» pretty.

why.A: "Try at" is not how English introduces the thing attempted.
why.B: Correct — "try" takes an infinitive when it names an attempt: tried to make.
why.C: "Tried for" names a goal to be won, as in trying for a prize.
why.D: "Tried in" is not an English pairing for an attempt.

context: Carpet, curtains, and «seats that are upholstered» swallow sound; bare concrete gives it back.

why.A: The first two items are single nouns, and the third becomes a noun with a clause after it.
why.B: Correct — a short noun phrase matches "carpet" and "curtains."
why.C: A participial phrase does not match the plain nouns before it.
why.D: An infinitive is a verb phrase and cannot sit in a list of materials.

context: The vehicles came in whatever color the seller happened to have, and a bus in one county looked nothing «as» a bus in the next.

why.A: "Look nothing as" is not English; "as" introduces a clause or a role, not a likeness.
why.B: Correct — "looked nothing like" is the fixed phrase for complete unlikeness.
why.C: "Alike" follows the things being compared, as in "they looked alike," and cannot take an object.
why.D: "Looked nothing similar to" mixes two phrases; "nothing" pairs with "like."

context: The person who changed this was Frank «Cyr a» professor of rural education at Columbia University.

why.A: Without a comma, "Cyr a professor" runs the name straight into the phrase that describes him.
why.B: Correct — a comma sets off the phrase that tells the reader who Cyr was.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and a descriptive phrase is not one.
why.D: "Being" turns the description into a participle that reads as a reason rather than an identification.

context: Cyr «has spent» a year surveying how children in rural districts got to school.

why.A: The present perfect reaches into the present, but the survey was finished before the events of 1939.
why.B: Correct — the past perfect places the survey before the conference the essay goes on to describe.
why.C: The present tense breaks the past narrative of the paragraph.
why.D: The future perfect points forward from now, and the survey happened decades ago.

context: Cyr had spent a year surveying how children in rural districts got to school. «Finding conditions that alarmed him.»

why.A: "Finding" is a participle with no subject, so the word group has no main clause.
why.B: Correct — "what he found" is the subject and "alarmed" the verb.
why.C: A clause beginning with "which" cannot stand alone after a full stop.
why.D: A noun with a relative clause after it still has no main verb.

context: Buses varied in size, in safety, and «how they were built».

why.A: The first two items repeat "in," and the third drops it, so the series breaks.
why.B: Correct — "in" is repeated before each item, so the third matches "in size" and "in safety."
why.C: "By" changes the preposition the first two items share.
why.D: The word order is garbled, and "how built they were" is not an English phrase.

context: A driver approaching one on a country road had no way of recognizing «it» as a vehicle full of children.

why.A: Correct — "one" stands for a single bus, and "it" refers back to that bus.
why.B: "Them" is plural, and the bus the driver approaches is one.
why.C: "Him" refers to a man, not a vehicle.
why.D: "Those" is plural and has no plural noun nearby to point to.

context: The group, which included engineers, paint experts, and school administrators, «were» asked to agree on standards.

why.A: "Were" is plural, but the subject is the singular "group"; the plural list sits inside a clause set off by commas.
why.B: Correct — the subject is "the group," acting as one body, so the verb is singular.
why.C: "Are" is plural and present, and the paragraph is in the past.
why.D: "Have" is plural and shifts the tense to the present perfect.

context: They settled dozens of questions about size, construction, and signaling equipment. The most famous decision«, though,» was the color.

why.A: Correct — "though" sets the one famous decision apart from the many technical ones before it.
why.B: "Therefore" claims the color decision follows from settling the other questions.
why.C: "In other words" promises a restatement, and the color is a separate decision.
why.D: "Similarly" promises a likeness, and the sentence is singling the color out.

context: They wanted a color that would stand out against almost any landscape «and also in addition in» the half-light of early morning.

why.A: "Also" and "in addition" say the same thing side by side.
why.B: Correct — "and" alone adds the second setting to the first.
why.C: Without "and," the second setting is tacked on with no conjunction to join it.
why.D: Commas around "in addition" do not stop it repeating "also."

context: «Its» since been known by various names, but the shade itself has changed remarkably little.

why.A: "Its" is a possessive, but the sentence needs "it has."
why.B: Correct — "it’s" is short for "it has" here: it has since been known.
why.C: An apostrophe after "its" is never a correct form.
why.D: "It is since been known" is not a grammatical verb phrase.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence “They also wanted black lettering to be easy to read against it.” Should the writer make this deletion?

choices.text: No, because it gives a second reason for the choice, one that bears on why yellow won.
Yes, because the lettering on a bus has nothing to do with the color of its paint.
Yes, because it only repeats the point about visibility in the early morning.
No, because it explains why buses are no longer painted blue.

why.A: Correct — the delegates wanted both visibility and readable lettering, and the sentence supplies the second requirement.
why.B: Lettering has to be read against the paint, which is why the delegates cared about it.
why.C: The earlier point is about seeing the bus; this one is about reading what is written on it.
why.D: The essay mentions blue only as a thought experiment in the last paragraph.

context: Part of the color’s success is that it became a «symptom».

why.A: A symptom is a sign of illness, and the color is a message to drivers, not evidence of a disease.
why.B: Correct — the next sentence explains that drivers learned what the color warns them of, which is what a signal does.
why.C: A signature identifies who made something; the color tells drivers what the vehicle might do.
why.D: A slogan is a phrase, and a color cannot be one.

context: A school bus painted blue would be just as easy to «see, however, it» would be far harder to understand.

why.A: "However" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so the comma in front of it leaves two clauses spliced.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon joins the clauses, and the comma after "however" sets the adverb off.
why.C: Moving the comma changes nothing about the join; a comma alone still holds the clauses together.
why.D: With no mark before "however," the first clause runs straight into the second.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence “Nearly every state had its own rules, and some had none at all.” Where would it most logically be placed?

choices.text: At the end of the first paragraph
After “The most famous decision, though, was the color.”
After “a deep yellow with a slight orange tint.”
At the beginning of the last paragraph

why.A: Correct — the first paragraph shows how buses differed from county to county, and the sentence gives the reason: there were no common rules.
why.B: By that point the conference has written common rules, so saying there were none contradicts the paragraph.
why.C: The color has already been chosen there, and the lack of rules belongs before the conference, not after its result.
why.D: The last paragraph is about what the color means to drivers, not about the situation before 1939.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to argue that yellow is the most visible color a vehicle can be painted. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: No, because the essay says the color works mainly because drivers know what it means.
Yes, because the delegates chose the color for how it looks in the early morning.
Yes, because it describes delegates comparing dozens of shades on a wall.
No, because the essay is mainly about how buses were built before 1939.

why.A: Correct — the last paragraph says a blue bus would be just as easy to see, which is the opposite of the stated goal.
why.B: Visibility was one reason for the choice, but the essay denies that yellow is uniquely visible.
why.C: Comparing shades shows a choice was made, not that the winner is the most visible color there is.
why.D: The years before 1939 take up one paragraph; most of the essay is about the color.

context: Its two diesel engines «was» replaced only once, in 1958.

why.A: "Was" is singular, and the subject right beside it, "engines," is plural.
why.B: Correct — the plural "engines" takes the plural "were."
why.C: "Has" is singular, and the present perfect does not fit a single event dated 1958.
why.D: "Is" is singular and puts an event from 1958 in the present.

context: The ferry moved «steady», and nobody seemed to mind.

why.A: "Steady" is an adjective, and the word here describes how the ferry moved, which takes an adverb.
why.B: Correct — the adverb "steadily" modifies the verb "moved."
why.C: "Steadier" is a comparative adjective with nothing to compare against, and it still cannot modify a verb.
why.D: "Steadiness" is a noun and cannot describe the way something moves.

context: She was in charge «with» everything on board: the engines, the cable, the tickets, and the patience of the passengers.

why.A: "In charge with" is not English; the phrase that names what a person runs is "in charge of."
why.B: Correct — "in charge of" is the fixed phrase.
why.C: "In charge for" is not an English pairing.
why.D: "In charge about" is not an English pairing.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence “Marsh’s brother owned a hardware store in the county seat for many years.” Should the writer make this deletion?

choices.text: Yes, because it says nothing about the ferry or about Marsh’s work on it.
Yes, because it contradicts the claim that Marsh ran the ferry until it closed.
No, because it explains how Marsh came to work on the river.
No, because it shows that Marsh’s family was well known in Oakford.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph is about what Marsh ran on board, and her brother’s store has no bearing on it.
why.B: A brother’s store in another town does not contradict anything about Marsh’s job.
why.C: The sentence gives no reason for Marsh’s job; it is about a different person’s business.
why.D: The store was in the county seat, not Oakford, and nothing says the family was well known.

context: The ferry — officially Ferry No. «3, never» had a name painted on its hull, but everyone in Oakford called it the Halloran.

why.A: The aside opens with a dash and closes with a comma; an interruption takes the same mark at both ends.
why.B: Correct — a second dash closes the aside that the first dash opened.
why.C: A semicolon cannot close an aside, and it leaves "The ferry" cut off from its verb.
why.D: With nothing closing the aside, "Ferry No. 3 never had a name" reads as one run of words.

context: The cable that pulled the «ferry, was» replaced every ten years.

why.A: The comma separates the subject, "the cable that pulled the ferry," from its verb, "was."
why.B: Correct — no punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb.
why.C: A semicolon splits the subject from its verb, leaving neither half a sentence.
why.D: A single dash also cuts the subject off from its verb.

context: Each new cable was «to» heavy for a crew to lift, so it arrived on a flatbed truck and was unrolled by a winch.

why.A: "To" is a preposition or part of an infinitive; the word meaning "excessively" is "too."
why.B: Correct — "too heavy for a crew to lift" means heavier than a crew could manage.
why.C: "Two" is the number and makes no sense before "heavy."
why.D: "That heavy" points back to a weight already described, and none has been.

context: The ferry lost «their» cable twice in floods, in 1973 and again in 2003, and both times the landing washed out.

why.A: "Their" is plural, and the only antecedent, "the ferry," is singular.
why.B: Correct — the singular possessive "its" refers to the ferry.
why.C: "It’s" means "it is," which makes no sense before "cable."
why.D: "They’re" means "they are," which is neither possessive nor singular.

context: Rebuilt twice, «Oakford residents never thought of the landing as permanent».

choices.text: the landing never struck Oakford residents as permanent
residents of Oakford never considered the landing permanent
Oakford residents never thought the landing was permanent

why.A: The opening phrase describes the landing, but the subject after the comma is "Oakford residents," who were not rebuilt.
why.B: Correct — "the landing" comes right after the phrase, and the landing is what was rebuilt.
why.C: Rewording the subject does not change it; the phrase still describes the residents.
why.D: The subject is still "Oakford residents," so the phrase still says they were rebuilt.

context: Every crossing went into «it the» time, the number of vehicles, and the height of the river on the gauge by the landing.

why.A: With no mark, "it the time" runs the pronoun straight into the list.
why.B: Correct — the clause is complete at "it," and a colon introduces the list of what went into the logbook.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and a list is not one.
why.D: "And" makes the time a second thing the crossing went into rather than the first item recorded.

context: The logbooks now fill eleven «shelves, they» are the only complete record of traffic on that stretch of road.

why.A: Two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone, which is a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — a full stop separates the two complete sentences.
why.C: With no punctuation at all, the two clauses are fused.
why.D: Swapping the pronoun leaves a comma splice; "these are the only complete record" is still a full clause.

context: The records of every crossing «are» kept in the county library, where a historian from the state university has begun to read them.

why.A: Correct — the subject is the plural "records," and the phrase "of every crossing" between them does not change it.
why.B: "Is" agrees with "crossing," the noun inside the prepositional phrase, not with the subject.
why.C: "Has" is singular and also does not agree with "records."
why.D: "Was" is singular, and the past progressive suggests the records are no longer there.

context: When the new bridge «opens» in the fall of 2019, the ferry made its last crossing the same week.

why.A: The present tense clashes with "made" and with a date in the past.
why.B: Correct — the simple past matches "made" and the year 2019.
why.C: The future tense puts a finished event from 2019 ahead of us.
why.D: The present perfect cannot sit with a specific past date like "the fall of 2019."

context: The bridge takes forty seconds to cross. «Therefore,» people in Oakford still drive down to the old landing on summer evenings, just to look at the water.

why.A: "Therefore" says the quick crossing causes the visits, but the visits happen despite it.
why.B: Correct — people keep going to the old landing although the bridge has made it unnecessary.
why.C: "Similarly" signals a second example of the same thing, and the two sentences point in opposite directions.
why.D: The visits are not an example of how long the bridge takes to cross.

context: She says the ferry ran «every single day without fail, daily,» for ninety-one years, and she would rather remember that than the bridge.

why.A: "Every single day" and "daily" say the same thing side by side, and "without fail" adds nothing to either.
why.B: Correct — the phrase says it once.
why.C: This still says the same thing twice in a row.
why.D: "Ran days" means it ran in the daytime, which changes the claim instead of trimming it.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence “Most of them were once her passengers.” Where would it most logically be placed?

choices.text: After “just to look at the water.”

why.A: Correct — "them" refers to the people who drive down to the landing, and "her" to Marsh, who has already been named.
why.B: Marsh has not been introduced yet, so "her" has no one to refer to.
why.C: The nearest plural there is the floods, which cannot be anyone’s passengers.
why.D: "Them" would refer to the records, which were never passengers.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to explain why the state decided to replace the ferry with a bridge. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it notes that the bridge takes forty seconds to cross.
Yes, because it describes the floods that twice cost the ferry its cable.
No, because it reports that the bridge opened but gives no reasons.
No, because it never mentions the bridge at all.

why.A: That is a comparison with the ferry, not a reason the state gave for building the bridge.
why.B: The floods are never connected to any decision about a bridge.
why.C: Correct — the essay is about the ferry and Marsh, and the bridge appears only as the thing that ended them.
why.D: The bridge is mentioned in the final paragraph, with its opening date.

context: The glaciers «that she studies» all end in the sea.

why.A: Correct — the clause says which glaciers are meant, so it is essential and takes no commas.
why.B: "That" introduces an essential clause, and commas would mark it as removable.
why.C: A single comma splits the subject from the clause that identifies it and leaves nothing to close it.
why.D: A comma inside the clause separates "that" from the words it introduces.

context: As the ice melts, each of the «bubbles burst» with a small crack.

why.A: "Burst" agrees with "bubbles," but the subject is "each," which is singular.
why.B: Correct — "each" is the subject, so the verb is singular; "of the bubbles" only says each of what.
why.C: "Have" is plural, and the present perfect also breaks from "melts."
why.D: "Are" is plural and still agrees with the wrong noun.

stem: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after “some of them hundreds of years ago”: “The bubbles are under pressure, squeezed for centuries by the weight of the ice above them.” Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: Yes, because it explains why a bubble cracks instead of simply escaping as the ice melts.
Yes, because it tells the reader how many bubbles are in each liter of ice.
No, because the essay is about Sato rather than about the physics of ice.
No, because it contradicts the claim that the bubbles were trapped when snow fell.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph says the bubbles burst with a crack, and pressure is what makes that happen.
why.B: The sentence gives no count; the number of bubbles comes up only later, in the model.
why.C: The whole first paragraph explains what she hears, so a sentence on why it sounds is on topic.
why.D: Being squeezed afterward is consistent with being trapped when the snow fell.

context: Sato first noticed the roar in «2009, the year she initially heard it,» while recording harbor seals for another project.

choices.text: 2009, hearing it for the first time,

why.A: "Initially heard it" repeats "first noticed," which is already at the start of the sentence.
why.B: "When she first heard it" still says what "first noticed" has already said.
why.C: The participle repeats the same idea in different words.
why.D: Correct — "first noticed" already says this was the first time, so the date needs nothing after it.

context: The «seal’s» calls kept disappearing under a hiss that she assumed was a fault in her equipment.

why.A: "Seal’s" is a singular possessive, but she was recording harbor seals, plural, and no single seal has been named.
why.B: Correct — the calls belong to the seals she was recording, so the plural possessive puts the apostrophe after the "s."
why.C: A plain plural cannot show that the calls belong to the seals.
why.D: A plural ending in "s" takes an apostrophe alone, not a second "s."

context: The seals’ calls kept disappearing under a hiss that she assumed was a fault in her equipment. «Which it was not.» The hiss was the glacier.

why.A: "Which" makes this a relative clause, and after a full stop it has no noun to attach to.
why.B: Correct — "it" is the subject and "was" the verb, so the short sentence stands on its own.
why.C: Still a relative clause with no main clause to hang from.
why.D: "Being" is a participle, and the word group has no subject.

context: Since then, Sato «learned» to read the sound.

why.A: "Since then" reaches from 2009 up to the present, which the simple past cannot do.
why.B: Correct — the present perfect covers something that began in the past and still holds.
why.C: The present tense cannot take "since then," which needs a stretch of time behind it.
why.D: The future perfect points to some later moment, and the learning has already happened.

context: Warm ocean water reaching the face of a glacier «excels» the melting, so the fjords where that water arrives are the loudest.

why.A: "Excel" means to do very well, and it cannot take "the melting" as its object in this sense.
why.B: Correct — warm water speeds up the melting, which is why those fjords are loudest.
why.C: "Exceeds" means goes beyond, which would compare the water with the melting.
why.D: "Accede to" means to agree to a demand, which water cannot do.

context: Sediment in the water muffles the «sound; a» fjord clouded with silt can seem quieter than it is.

why.A: Correct — a semicolon joins two independent clauses that are closely linked.
why.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
why.C: With no punctuation, the two clauses are fused.
why.D: "Which a fjord clouded with silt can seem" does not make sense; the second clause has no place for "which."

context: Neither the tides nor the temperature of the water «explains» all of the change from one week to the next.

why.A: Correct — with "neither . . . nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "the temperature," which is singular.
why.B: The plural "tides" comes first, but the verb follows the nearer noun, which is singular.
why.C: "Are" is plural and agrees with neither the nearer subject nor the tense of the passage.
why.D: "Have" is plural, and the nearer subject is singular.

context: Sato is «as interested in the quiet fjords than in» the loud ones.

choices.text: as interested in the quiet fjords as in
more interested in the quiet fjords as in
as interested in the quiet fjords like

why.A: "As . . . than" mixes two comparisons; "as" must be answered by a second "as."
why.B: Correct — "as interested . . . as" is the complete comparison of equals.
why.C: "More" must be answered by "than," not by "as."
why.D: "Like" cannot complete an "as" comparison, and it drops the "in" the second item needs.

context: Sato shared her recordings with a physicist, Grace Obi, and «she» built a model.
