why.A: "She" could mean Sato or Obi, so the reader cannot tell who built the model.
why.B: Correct — naming her removes the doubt about who built the model.
why.C: "They" suggests both women built it, which the sentence does not claim, and it is still unclear.
why.D: "Her" is an object pronoun and cannot be the subject of "built."

context: The model links the loudness of the roar to three things: the temperature of the water, «how fast the ice is moving», and the number of bubbles in each liter of ice.

choices.text: how fast is the ice moving

why.A: The other two items are nouns followed by "of" phrases, and this one is a clause.
why.B: Correct — "the speed of the ice" matches "the temperature of the water" and "the number of bubbles."
why.C: A noun with a participle after it does not match the "the ___ of ___" pattern.
why.D: This is a question in the middle of a list, and it still does not match the other items.

context: The roar is a rough measure of «melting, however, it» cannot tell anyone exactly how much ice is being lost.

why.A: "However" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma is still the only thing joining the two clauses.
why.B: Correct — the semicolon joins the clauses, and "however" then signals the contrast.
why.C: Dropping the second comma leaves the same comma splice.
why.D: With no mark before "however," the two clauses run together.

context: Satellites can measure how much a glacier has shrunk over a year. «For example,» they cannot see through cloud, and southeast Alaska is under cloud most of the time.

why.A: Being unable to see through cloud is not an example of measuring a glacier; it is a limitation.
why.B: Correct — the second sentence names what satellites cannot do, against what the first says they can.
why.C: "Likewise" signals a similar point, and the two sentences contrast.
why.D: The second sentence does not restate the first; it adds a limitation.

context: Sato’s goal is «modest:» a cheap way to watch glaciers that no satellite can see.

why.A: Correct — the clause is complete at "modest," and the colon introduces what the goal is.
why.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and "a cheap way to watch glaciers" is a phrase.
why.C: "Such as" introduces examples, and the phrase that follows is the goal itself, not an example of modesty.
why.D: "Modest that is a cheap way" has no grammatical reading.

context: Her hydrophones — which cost about as much as a used «bicycle, are» cheap enough to lose, and she loses several every summer.

why.A: The aside opens with a dash but closes with a comma; both ends need the same mark.
why.B: Correct — a second dash closes the aside the first one opened.
why.C: A semicolon cannot close an aside, and it cuts "hydrophones" off from its verb.
why.D: Without a closing mark, the aside runs straight into the main verb.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to explain how scientists measure the total amount of ice a glacier loses each year. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it describes the hydrophone that Sato lowers into the fjords.
Yes, because it explains that the roar grows louder as melting speeds up.
No, because it says the roar cannot measure how much ice is lost.
No, because it never mentions melting at all.

why.A: The hydrophone records sound; the essay says the sound cannot measure how much ice is lost.
why.B: The essay calls the roar only a rough measure and says it cannot give an exact amount.
why.C: Correct — the one method that measures shrinkage gets a single sentence, and the essay’s subject is listening.
why.D: Melting is discussed in several paragraphs, including what speeds it up.

context: For most of my life I had arranged things so that the question never «came up or arose».

why.A: "Came up" and "arose" mean the same thing, side by side.
why.B: Correct — one verb says it.
why.C: Reversing the pair still says the same thing twice.
why.D: "The question never came" drops the "up" that gives the phrase its meaning.

context: I sat at the edge at pool parties, I volunteered to watch the bags at the beach, and I «choosing» hotels by whether they had a gym rather than a pool.

why.A: "Choosing" is a participle, and the first two items set the pattern "I sat," "I volunteered."
why.B: Correct — the simple past matches "sat" and "volunteered."
why.C: The progressive breaks the pattern of three simple-past verbs.
why.D: This makes the third item hypothetical, though the first two report what actually happened.

context: Nobody noticed, or, if they «noticed nobody» said anything.

why.A: The comma after "or" opens the clause "if they noticed," and nothing closes it.
why.B: Correct — a second comma closes the "if they noticed" clause that the first one opened.
why.C: A semicolon cannot close a clause that a comma opened, and "or, if they noticed" is not a sentence.
why.D: A dash does not match the comma that opened the clause.

context: By thirty I had become an expert at a skill nobody knew I «needed: looking» relaxed near water.

why.A: Correct — the clause is complete at "needed," and the colon introduces the skill it names.
why.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and "looking relaxed near water" is a phrase.
why.C: Without a mark, "needed looking" reads as though the narrator needed to be looked at.
why.D: A comma alone joins two independent clauses here, which is a comma splice.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence “The pool had been built in 1962 with money from a local bond.” Should the writer make this deletion?

choices.text: Yes, because the pool’s history has no bearing on the class or on the narrator.
Yes, because it contradicts the statement that the pool belongs to the city.
No, because it explains why the class met so early in the morning.
No, because it shows that the narrator researched the pool before joining.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph is about the class and its first lesson, and the bond interrupts it.
why.B: A pool paid for with a local bond is consistent with its being municipal.
why.C: The date of construction says nothing about the time of the class.
why.D: Nothing in the sentence connects it to anything the narrator did.

context: There were six of us in the class, all adults, and we «was» all embarrassed.

why.A: "Was" is singular, and "we," right before it, is plural.
why.B: Correct — the plural "we" takes "were."
why.C: "Is" is singular and also shifts the past narrative into the present.
why.D: "Has" is singular and does not agree with "we."

context: Our instructor — a retired lifeguard named Pearl «Oduya, did» not waste time on reassurance.

why.A: A dash opens the description, so a dash has to close it; a comma does not match.
why.B: Correct — the pair of dashes sets off the description of the instructor.
why.C: With the aside left open, "Pearl Oduya did not waste time" swallows the rest of the sentence.
why.D: A semicolon splits "Our instructor" from its verb.

context: Her first lesson had nothing to do with «swimming. It» was about breathing.

why.A: Correct — each sentence is complete, and the full stop keeps them apart.
why.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
why.C: With no punctuation, the two clauses are fused.
why.D: "However" is not a conjunction, so a comma is still the only thing joining the clauses.

context: We stood in the shallow end, put our faces in the water, and «breathe» out through our noses until the bubbles stopped.

why.A: The present tense breaks from "stood," "put," and "stopped."
why.B: Correct — the simple past matches the other verbs in the sentence.
why.C: The future tense does not fit an account of something that already happened.
why.D: The present perfect reaches into the present and breaks the past narrative.

context: The body does not want to breathe out underwater; every instinct says to hold «on at» whatever air it has.

why.A: "Hold on at" is not an English phrase.
why.B: Correct — "hold on to" means to keep hold of something.
why.C: "Hold up to" means to measure against a standard, as in holding a paper up to the light.
why.D: "Hold out for" means to wait for something better.

context: Breathing out, she said, is how you «ensure» your body that you are not drowning.

why.A: "Ensure" means to make certain of something, and it cannot take a person as its object followed by "that."
why.B: Correct — to "assure" someone is to tell them something so as to remove their doubt.
why.C: "Insure" means to protect against loss, as with a policy.
why.D: "Assume" means to take something as true without proof, which reverses who is being convinced.

context: Breathing out, she said, is how you assure your body that you are not drowning. «Taking me four mornings to believe her.»

choices.text: It took me four mornings to believe her.
Four mornings, which it took me to believe her.
Because it took me four mornings to believe her.

why.A: "Taking" is a participle, and the word group has no subject or main verb.
why.B: Correct — "it" is the subject and "took" the verb.
why.C: A noun followed by a relative clause still has no main verb.
why.D: "Because" makes this a dependent clause with nothing to attach to.

context: Holding one hand under the small of my back, «I was told by Pearl» to lie still, look at the ceiling, and let the water hold me up.

why.A: The opening phrase describes Pearl, but the subject that follows it is "I," and the narrator was not holding her own back.
why.B: Correct — "Pearl" comes right after the phrase, and she is the one holding her hand under the narrator.
why.C: The subject is still "I," so the phrase still describes the narrator.
why.D: Now the phrase describes "my instructions," which cannot hold a hand anywhere.

context: Each time she took her hand away, I «sank — not» because I was too heavy but because I tensed every muscle I had.

why.A: Correct — the dash sets off the explanation of why the narrator sank.
why.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and "not because . . ." is not one.
why.C: The full stop leaves "Not because I was too heavy . . ." as a fragment.
why.D: A colon cannot be followed by "and," which leaves the explanation hanging off a conjunction.

context: «As far as Pearl was concerned», the trick was to do nothing.

choices.text: As much as Pearl was concerned
So far as Pearl had concern

why.A: Correct — "as far as [someone] is concerned" is the fixed phrase for "in someone’s view."
why.B: "As much as" measures an amount and turns the phrase into a claim about how worried Pearl was.
why.C: Dropping "was" breaks the phrase; "concerned" here needs its verb.
why.D: "Had concern" is not part of the idiom and reads as though Pearl were anxious.

context: One morning in the third week, I lay back «perfect still» and looked at the ceiling.

why.A: "Perfect" is an adjective, and a word that intensifies the adjective "still" has to be an adverb.
why.B: Correct — the adverb "perfectly" modifies "still."
why.C: "Perfection" is a noun and cannot modify "still."
why.D: "Stilled" means made still by something else, which changes what the sentence says.

context: After a while I noticed that «Pearls» hand was gone.

why.A: "Pearls" is a plain plural, but the hand belongs to Pearl, so the name needs a possessive.
why.B: Correct — one person owns the hand, so the apostrophe comes before the "s."
why.C: An apostrophe after the "s" marks a plural possessive, and there is only one Pearl.
why.D: Without the "s" and apostrophe, "Pearl hand" does not show possession at all.

stem: For the sake of logic, the sentence “Nobody clapped, which I appreciated.” should be placed:

choices.text: at the beginning of the paragraph.
after the sentence about how long the narrator had been floating.
at the end of the paragraph.

why.A: Here the narrator reports that nobody clapped before saying that anyone was watching.
why.B: At the start, nothing has happened yet that anyone could clap for.
why.C: That still puts the clapping before the reader learns that the other five were watching.
why.D: Correct — the other five are watching, and only then does it make sense to say none of them clapped.

context: The other five, who had been practicing at the far wall, «was» watching.

why.A: "Was" is singular, but the subject, "the other five," is plural; the clause in between does not change it.
why.B: Correct — the plural subject takes "were."
why.C: "Is" is singular and shifts the account into the present.
why.D: "Has" is singular and does not agree with "the other five."

context: I can manage four lengths of the pool before I need to rest, and my stroke would not impress anyone. «Therefore,» I go in the deep end without checking where the ladder is.

why.A: A weak stroke is not a reason to go into the deep end; the second sentence is in spite of the first.
why.B: Correct — the narrator is still not a strong swimmer, yet now goes into the deep end.
why.C: "Similarly" introduces a matching point, and these two sentences contrast.
why.D: "In addition" adds another limitation, but the second sentence reports progress.

context: The raft had lost «it’s» ladder years ago, so I climbed up the side.

why.A: "It’s" means "it is," which makes no sense before "ladder."
why.B: Correct — "its" is the possessive, showing that the ladder belonged to the raft.
why.C: "Its’" is not a word; the possessive of "it" has no apostrophe.
why.D: "Their" is plural, and the raft is one thing.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to show that adults learn to swim faster than children do. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because the narrator learns to float within three weeks.
Yes, because every student in the class is an adult.
No, because children never appear in the essay.
No, because the narrator never manages to float on her own.

why.A: The essay gives her time, but never sets it against how long a child takes.
why.B: An all-adult class shows who took the class, not how fast adults learn compared with children.
why.C: Correct — children never appear, so no comparison of speed can be drawn.
why.D: She does, in the third week, when she notices the instructor’s hand is gone.

context: It comes from Hollis «Mayberry who» sits at an upright piano just below the left edge of the screen.

why.A: A named person is already identified, so the "who" clause is extra information and must be set off with a comma.
why.B: Correct — a comma sets off the nonessential clause that describes him.
why.C: "That" does not introduce a clause set off by commas, and it is not used for a named person here.
why.D: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and a "who" clause is dependent.

context: It comes from Hollis Mayberry, who sits at an upright piano just below the left edge of the screen and plays for the entire length of the picture, sometimes for more than two hours «without a break».

choices.text: without a break or pause in between
without a break of any kind or length

why.A: Correct — the phrase says it once, with nothing extra.
why.B: "A break" and "a pause in between" are the same thing.
why.C: "Of any kind or length" is filler; "without a break" already rules out every break.
why.D: "Nonstop" and "without a break" say the same thing twice.

context: Silent films were never meant «for being» watched in silence.

why.A: "Meant for being" is not how English names what something was intended to do.
why.B: Correct — "meant to be" is the fixed pairing.
why.C: "Meant of being" is not an English pairing.
why.D: "Meant at being" is not an English pairing.

context: In the 1920s, even a small-town theater «employs» at least a pianist.

why.A: The present tense clashes with "in the 1920s" at the start of the sentence.
why.B: Correct — the simple past fits a statement about the 1920s.
why.C: The future tense cannot describe the 1920s.
why.D: The present perfect reaches into the present, and the sentence is about a closed period.

context: The grand movie «palace’s» in large cities kept full orchestras.

why.A: The palaces own nothing here; the word is a plain plural and takes no apostrophe.
why.B: Correct — the plural subject of "kept" needs no apostrophe.
why.C: An apostrophe after the "s" makes a plural possessive, and no noun follows for the palaces to own.
why.D: The singular does not fit "the grand movie palaces in large cities," which are many.

context: In fact, there «was» more musicians working in movie theaters than in concert halls.

why.A: In a "there" sentence the subject comes after the verb, and the subject here is the plural "musicians."
why.B: Correct — "musicians" is the subject, so the verb is plural.
why.C: "Was" is still singular and does not agree with "musicians."
why.D: "Has" is singular, and the subject is plural.

context: Studios sometimes sent out cue «sheets. Lists» of suggested pieces keyed to the scenes.

why.A: "Lists of suggested pieces keyed to the scenes" has no verb, so it cannot stand as a sentence.
why.B: Correct — joined with a comma, the phrase explains what cue sheets were.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and a noun phrase is not one.
why.D: Adding "These" still leaves a phrase with no verb.

context: Studios sometimes sent out cue sheets, lists of suggested pieces keyed to the scenes. «As a result,» most accompanists ignored them and improvised.

why.A: Sending out cue sheets would not cause accompanists to ignore them.
why.B: Correct — the accompanists improvised although the studios had supplied suggestions.
why.C: Ignoring the sheets does not restate sending them out.
why.D: Like "as a result," this makes the cue sheets the cause of their own neglect.

context: Very little of that music was written «down, so almost» none of it survives.

why.A: Correct — a comma followed by "so" properly joins two independent clauses.
why.B: Without "so," a comma alone joins two independent clauses.
why.C: The comma after "so" leaves nothing but "so" joining the clauses, and it cuts the conjunction off from its clause.
why.D: "Therefore" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so this is a comma splice.

stem: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after “so almost none of it survives”: “What audiences hear at the Crescent is therefore something new each night rather than a reconstruction.” Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: Yes, because it links the lost music to the improvising described next.
Yes, because it names the pieces the studios suggested on their cue sheets.
No, because it contradicts the claim that Mayberry improvises.
No, because the essay is about film history rather than about Mayberry.

why.A: Correct — it explains why every performance at the Crescent is new and leads into "Mayberry improvises too."
why.B: The sentence names no pieces at all.
why.C: Something new each night is exactly what improvising produces.
why.D: Mayberry is the subject from the first paragraph to the last.

context: Pen in hand, «the scene changes get marked» in a small notebook.

choices.text: the scene changes are marked by him
the notebook fills with scene changes

why.A: "Pen in hand" describes whoever is writing, but the subject after it is "the scene changes."
why.B: Correct — "he" follows the phrase, and he is the one holding the pen.
why.C: The subject is still "the scene changes," so they are the ones holding the pen.
why.D: Now the notebook is the one with a pen in hand.

context: He also notes which characters need a theme of «their» own.

why.A: Correct — "characters" is plural, so the plural possessive "their" refers to it.
why.B: "His" is singular, and "characters" is plural.
why.C: "Its" is singular and is not used for people.
why.D: "They’re" means "they are," which makes no sense before "own."

context: He watches the screen and plays what the screen seems to ask for: a rolling figure in the bass for a train, a thin, high melody for a letter being read, «and for the moment before a kiss, nothing at all».

choices.text: and nothing at all for the moment before a kiss
and nothing at all is played for the moment before a kiss
and the moment before a kiss gets nothing at all

why.A: The first two items put the music first and "for" the scene second; this one reverses the order.
why.B: Correct — like the others, this item names the music and then says what it is for.
why.C: "Is played" turns the last item into a clause in a list of noun phrases.
why.D: This makes the scene the subject, which breaks the pattern the first two items set.

context: Silence, Mayberry says, is louder «then» any chord a pianist can play, and it only works if it is rare.

why.A: "Then" refers to time; a comparison takes "than."
why.B: Correct — "louder than" introduces the thing being compared.
why.C: "Louder that" has no grammatical reading.
why.D: "Louder as" mixes a comparative with "as," which belongs to comparisons of equals.

context: A film that has music under every frame teaches «it’s» audience to stop hearing it.

context: «That last choice is the one audiences ask about most.»

That last choice, which audiences ask about most.
Because audiences ask about that last choice most.

why.A: Correct — "choice" is the subject and "is" the verb, so the sentence is complete.
why.B: "Being" is a participle, which leaves the word group without a main verb.

context: The job’s three hazards — the length of the films, the hard piano stool, and the light from the «screen — have» never changed.

why.A: Correct — the list contains commas of its own, so a pair of dashes sets it off.
why.B: A comma cannot close an aside opened by a dash, and it blurs where the list ends.

context: The last is the «worst, flickering» blues and grays fall across the keys and make it hard to see his own hands.

why.A: A comma alone joins two independent clauses, which is a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — the first clause is complete, and the colon introduces the explanation of why the light is worst.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence “The audience, mercifully, did not notice.” Where would it most logically be placed?

context: Younger musicians occasionally «asks» Mayberry to teach them.

context: He tells each of «they» to start by watching films with the sound off and humming along.

context: It is a lichen, Rhizocarpon «geographicum and it» grows so slowly that geologists have learned to use it as a clock.

why.A: The comma before the name opens an appositive that is never closed, and the comma that would close it is also the one the "and" needs.

context: The method, called lichenometry, was developed in the 1950s by an Austrian botanist named Roland Beschel, who noticed that the largest lichens «on a surface» seemed to say something about how long the surface had been exposed.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence “Beschel also played the cello in an amateur orchestra.” Should the writer make this deletion?

No, because it explains how Beschel came to be in the mountains where he saw the lichens.
No, because it shows that lichenometry was invented by an amateur.

context: The «principal» behind it is simple.

context: When a glacier retreats or a rockfall exposes fresh stone, the surface «started» bare.

why.A: The past tense does not match "retreats" and "exposes," which describe what always happens.
why.B: Correct — the present tense matches the general process that the rest of the sentence describes.

context: Within a few decades the first lichens arrive on the wind, take hold, and «they begin» to spread outward in a rough circle.

why.C: A participle breaks the pattern of present-tense verbs.

context: Because the growth is slow and fairly steady, the diameter of the largest lichen on a surface gives an estimate of how long ago that surface was «uncovered in the past».
