why.D: "Then" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so the comma is still splicing two clauses.

context: Tudor lost money on that trip and on several after it, and his partners withdrew and left the debts to «him» alone.

why.A: Correct — "him" is the object form, which the preposition "to" requires.
why.B: "He" is a subject pronoun and cannot follow the preposition "to."
why.C: A reflexive pronoun has to point back to the subject of its clause, and the subject here is "his partners."
why.D: "His" is possessive and needs a noun after it; "to his alone" does not work.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence “He spent time in debtors’ prison.” Should the writer make this deletion?

choices.text: No, because it shows how far the early losses carried him.
Yes, because it turns from the ice trade to Tudor’s private life.
Yes, because the essay never says Tudor owed money.
No, because it explains why his friends thought the idea was a joke.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph is about how badly the first voyages went, and prison measures how badly: the debts left to him were real enough to jail him.
why.B: The prison term is a direct result of the trade’s losses, so it is not a detour into private life.
why.C: The sentence before it says his partners left the debts to him.
why.D: His friends mocked the idea before the first voyage; the prison term came afterward.

context: What he learned from those failures was that selling ice meant selling the habit «to use» it.

why.A: The idiom is "the habit of" followed by an -ing form, not an infinitive.
why.B: Correct — "the habit of using" is the standard phrase.
why.C: "Habit for" is not idiomatic; "for" suggests a purpose.
why.D: "Habit in" is not idiomatic English.

context: Each of the ports he shipped to got an insulated icehouse of «its» own, and he taught bartenders to chill drinks.

why.A: Correct — the subject is "each," which is singular, so the singular "its" agrees with it.
why.B: "Ports" sits right before the verb, but the subject is "each," so the plural "their" does not agree.
why.C: "It’s" means "it is," which makes no sense before "own."
why.D: "His" would mean Tudor’s own icehouse, but each port received one.

context: He also offered ice «free. Until» customers came to expect it.

why.A: "Until customers came to expect it" is a dependent clause and cannot stand as a sentence.
why.B: Correct — the clause beginning with "until" attaches to the sentence it depends on.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and the "until" clause is dependent.
why.D: "And" promises a second main clause, but what follows is still dependent, so the sentence never finishes.

context: By the 1830s his ships were carrying ice as far as «India. A voyage» of four months.

why.A: "A voyage of four months" has no verb, so it cannot stand as a sentence.
why.B: Correct — the phrase becomes an appositive describing the trip to India.
why.C: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and this phrase has no verb.
why.D: "Being" is not a main verb, so the second part is still a fragment.

context: «Even so,» a surprising share of the cargo arrived frozen.

why.A: Correct — a four-month voyage would be expected to melt the ice, so "even so" marks the surprise that much of it survived.
why.B: A long voyage is not a reason ice would arrive frozen; it works against it.
why.C: The ice arriving frozen is not an example of the voyage being long.
why.D: Nothing before this sentence is similar to ice surviving the trip.

context: «First, horses pulling» a plow fitted with steel blades that scored the ice into a grid.

why.A: "Pulling" is not a main verb, and "scored" belongs to the blades, so the sentence has no main verb.
why.B: Correct — "pulled" gives the subject "horses" a main verb.
why.C: "That pulled" turns the verb into a description of the horses, and the sentence still has no main verb.
why.D: The commas do not help; "pulling" is still not a main verb.

context: The blocks, each weighing a hundred pounds or more, «was» floated down a channel to the icehouse and pushed up a ramp.

why.A: "Each" sits in the interrupting phrase, but the subject is "blocks," which is plural.
why.B: Correct — the plural "were" agrees with "blocks" and keeps the past tense of the passage.
why.C: "Are" agrees with "blocks," but the present tense does not fit a trade the passage describes in the past.
why.D: "Is" is singular, drawn to "each," and it is also in the wrong tense.

context: A thaw at the wrong moment could «totally trash» a season’s crop in a day.

why.A: "Totally trash" is slang and does not fit the essay’s plain, informative tone.
why.B: Correct — "ruin" is precise and matches the essay’s tone.
why.C: "Abolish" means to formally end a law or practice, not to spoil a crop.
why.D: "Overthrow" describes removing a ruler or government.

context: The trade peaked near the end of the nineteenth century, when millions of tons «were» cut each winter.

why.A: Correct — the subject "millions of tons" is plural, and the past tense fits the nineteenth century.
why.B: "Was" is singular, but "millions" is plural.
why.C: "Is" is singular and in the present tense.
why.D: "Has been" is singular, and the present perfect does not fit a past century.

context: «Similarly,» it collapsed.

why.A: A collapse is the opposite of a peak, not similar to it.
why.B: Correct — "then" marks the next event in time, the fall that followed the peak.
why.C: "Thus" says the peak caused the collapse, but the passage blames mechanical plants.
why.D: The collapse does not restate the peak; it reverses it.

context: «Able to run in any season, mechanical ice plants could make ice anywhere», without depending on the weather.

choices.text: Able to run in any season, ice could be made anywhere by mechanical plants
Able to run in any season, anyone could buy ice from mechanical plants
Able to run in any season, the weather no longer mattered to mechanical ice plants

why.A: Correct — the opening phrase describes the plants, and "mechanical ice plants" comes right after it.
why.B: The opening phrase now describes "ice," which does not run.
why.C: The opening phrase now describes "anyone," but it is the plants that could run.
why.D: The opening phrase now describes "the weather."

context: Home refrigerators finished the «job: within» a generation, the icebox was an antique.

why.A: Correct — the colon introduces a clause that explains what "finished the job" means.
why.B: A comma cannot join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
why.C: Without punctuation "within a generation" attaches to "finished the job," and the rest of the sentence is left hanging.
why.D: "Because" reverses cause and effect: refrigerators made the icebox obsolete, not the other way around.

stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence after “Men with long saws finished the cuts”: “The grid mattered, because square blocks could be stacked tightly, with no gaps for warm air.” Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: Yes, because it explains why the ice was scored into a grid.
Yes, because it shows how dangerous the harvest was.
No, because it repeats what the paragraph already says about the grid.
No, because it moves the focus from the harvest to the icehouses.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph says the plow cut a grid but never says why; square blocks that stack without gaps are the reason.
why.B: The sentence is about stacking blocks, not about danger to the workers.
why.C: The paragraph mentions the grid but says nothing about its purpose.
why.D: The sentence explains a step in the harvest by what it made possible later; it stays on the harvest.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence “Once people had tasted a cold drink in July, few of them wanted to go back.” Where would it most logically be placed?

why.A: Correct — the sentence explains why giving ice away worked: once people had tried it, they kept wanting it.
why.B: At that point Tudor has not shipped any ice, so nobody has tasted a cold drink yet.
why.C: That paragraph is about cutting the ice, not about the customers who bought it.
why.D: That sentence is about a thaw ruining the crop; a sentence about customers does not follow from it.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to show how a business can create the demand for its own product. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because Tudor builds icehouses and gives ice away until people expect it.
Yes, because it explains how mechanical plants replaced the pond ice trade.
No, because most of the essay describes how ice was cut rather than sold.
No, because the trade Tudor built eventually collapsed anyway.

why.A: Correct — the third paragraph shows Tudor making customers before selling to them.
why.B: Replacing a trade is not the same as creating demand for a product.
why.C: Only the fourth paragraph describes the cutting; the second and third are about selling.
why.D: The later collapse does not undo the demand Tudor created.

stem: The writer wants to end the sentence “Today the old icehouses are mostly gone, though …” with a detail that connects the present day to the harvest described in the fourth paragraph. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

choices.text: a few ponds are still cut by hand each winter, with the old saws, for visitors to watch.
a few have become small museums that tell the story of Tudor’s trade.
most people now alive have never seen a block of ice cut from a pond.
mechanical plants now make ice more cheaply than ever before.

why.A: Correct — hand cutting with the old saws echoes the fourth paragraph’s saws and blocks and brings it into the present.
why.B: This links the present to Tudor’s selling, described earlier, rather than to the harvest itself.
why.C: This describes the present but connects to nothing the fourth paragraph shows.
why.D: This returns to the mechanical plants of the final paragraph, not to the harvest.

context: On a clear night far from any town, a person with ordinary «eyesight, can see» a few thousand stars at once.

why.A: A comma should not separate the subject, "a person with ordinary eyesight," from its verb, "can see."
why.B: Correct — the subject runs straight into its verb with no comma between them.
why.C: A semicolon separates independent clauses, and it cuts the subject off from its verb.
why.D: "And" needs a verb before it to join, but "a person with ordinary eyesight" has none, so the sentence falls apart.

context: The difference «lays» not in the sky but in the air above the city.

why.A: "Lays" means puts something down and needs an object; the sentence means "is located."
why.B: Correct — "lies" means is found or is located, and it agrees with "difference."
why.C: "Lain" is a past participle and cannot serve as the main verb without a helper like "has."
why.D: "Laying" is an -ing form of the wrong verb, and it leaves the sentence without a main verb.

context: That air scatters the light of «streetlamp’s», signs, and windows back toward the ground.

why.A: Nothing belongs to the streetlamp here; the word is simply plural, like "signs" and "windows."
why.B: Correct — a plain plural matches "signs" and "windows" in the list.
why.C: A plural possessive needs something owned after it, and "signs" is not owned by the streetlamps.
why.D: A singular noun with no article does not fit a list of plurals.

context: Astronomers call this glow skyglow, and it «has been growing» for more than a century.

why.A: Correct — "for more than a century" describes something that began in the past and continues now, which the present perfect progressive expresses.
why.B: The simple past suggests the growth is over, but the essay later shows it continuing.
why.C: The past perfect needs a later past moment to be earlier than, and there is none.
why.D: The future tense cannot go with "for more than a century."

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence “Astronomy is one of the oldest of the sciences.” Should the writer make this deletion?

choices.text: Yes, because it says nothing about skyglow or how it is measured.
No, because it explains why astronomers were the first to notice skyglow.
No, because it introduces the scientists the essay goes on to discuss.
Yes, because it contradicts the claim that skyglow has grown for a century.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph defines skyglow, and a remark on the age of astronomy is a detour from it.
why.B: The sentence says nothing about who noticed skyglow first.
why.C: The essay goes on to discuss volunteers, not astronomers.
why.D: The age of a science has no bearing on how long skyglow has been growing.

context: «The act of measuring it» is harder than it sounds.

why.A: "The act of" is filler; the gerund "measuring" already names the act.
why.B: Correct — the gerund phrase serves as the subject with nothing wasted.
why.C: "Measuring of it" is not idiomatic; the gerund takes its object directly.
why.D: A prepositional phrase cannot be the subject, so "is harder" has nothing to agree with.

context: Satellites can photograph cities from above, «but» they see light going up, not the glow a person sees looking up.

why.A: Correct — the second clause sets a limit on the first, which is a contrast.
why.B: "So" makes the second clause a result, but photographing from above does not cause the problem; it is the problem.
why.C: "Or" offers the clauses as alternatives, but both are true at once.
why.D: "Because" makes the second clause a reason for the first, which reverses their relation.

context: Some satellites «also blind» to the bluish light of modern LED lamps.

why.A: The sentence has no verb, so it is a fragment.
why.B: Correct — "are" gives "satellites" a verb.
why.C: "Being" is not a main verb, so the sentence is still a fragment.
why.D: A comma does not supply the missing verb.

stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence after “the bluish light of modern LED lamps”: “LED lamps use far less electricity than the sodium lamps they replaced.” Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: No, because it turns from measuring skyglow to the cost of electricity.
Yes, because it explains why the satellites cannot see the light.
Yes, because it shows that LED lamps are the main cause of skyglow.
No, because it contradicts the claim that satellites see light going up.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph explains why satellites are a poor measure of skyglow, and energy savings have nothing to do with that.
why.B: Electricity use says nothing about what a satellite can detect.
why.C: The sentence compares energy use; it makes no claim about skyglow.
why.D: The two statements are about different things and do not conflict.

context: «Nevertheless,» for a picture of the sky as people actually experience it, researchers have turned to people.

why.A: "Nevertheless" signals that researchers acted despite the satellites’ limits, but they turned to people because of those limits.
why.B: Correct — the researchers turned to people in place of the satellites just described.
why.C: Turning to people is not an example of the satellites’ limits.
why.D: Nothing before this sentence is similar to turning to people.

context: Since 2006, a program called Globe at Night has asked volunteers to step outside, find a familiar «constellation and, compare» what they see with a set of charts.

why.A: The comma belongs before "and," which joins the last item of the list; after it, it cuts the conjunction off from its verb.
why.B: Correct — the comma comes before the conjunction that introduces the last item.
why.C: The second comma separates "and" from the verb it introduces.
why.D: A semicolon separates independent clauses, not items in a simple list.

context: Each of the charts «shows» the constellation as it would appear under a different level of skyglow.

why.A: Correct — the subject is "each," which is singular, so "shows" agrees with it.
why.B: "Charts" sits right before the verb, but the subject is "each," which takes a singular verb.
why.C: "Are" is plural and does not agree with "each."
why.D: "Have" is plural, and the present perfect also suggests the charts have finished showing it.

context: The charts range «from: a handful» of bright stars to a crowded field.

why.A: A colon cannot come between a preposition and its object.
why.B: Correct — "from" leads straight to its object with no punctuation.
why.C: A comma splits the preposition from its object.
why.D: A semicolon separates independent clauses, and nothing here is one.

context: The volunteer picks the closest match and «submitting it» along with the time and place.

why.A: "Submitting" does not match "picks," the verb it is paired with.
why.B: Correct — "submits" matches "picks" in form and tense.
why.C: The present perfect breaks the match with the simple present "picks."
why.D: An infinitive does not match "picks."

context: No telescope is «needed — just» patience and about ten minutes for the eyes to adjust to the dark.

why.A: Correct — the dash sets off what is needed in place of a telescope.
why.B: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and "just patience and about ten minutes" has no verb.
why.C: The period leaves "Just patience and about ten minutes…" as a fragment.
why.D: Without a break, "needed just patience" reads as though patience, too, is not needed.

context: A volunteer may choose the wrong chart, or a thin cloud may hide the fainter «stars, however, tens» of thousands of observations begin to average out such mistakes.

why.A: "However" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so commas around it still leave two independent clauses spliced together.
why.B: Correct — the semicolon joins the two clauses, and "however" introduces the second.
why.C: This is still a comma splice, and "however" now runs into the clause it introduces.
why.D: With no punctuation before "however," the two clauses are fused.

context: Analyzing more than fifty thousand of them in 2023, «the sky was found by researchers to be brightening» by nearly ten percent a year.

choices.text: researchers found that the sky had been brightening
the sky, researchers found, had been brightening
it was found by researchers that the sky had been brightening

why.A: The opening phrase describes whoever did the analyzing, but the subject right after it is "the sky."
why.B: Correct — "researchers" follows the opening phrase, and they are the ones who analyzed the observations.
why.C: The subject is still "the sky," so the sky is still doing the analyzing.
why.D: The subject is now "it," which cannot analyze anything.

context: «It» was far faster than satellite data had suggested.

why.A: "It" could mean the sky, the most recent singular noun, and a sky cannot be fast.
why.B: Correct — "that rate" names what was faster than expected: the brightening of nearly ten percent a year.
why.C: "They" would point to the researchers, who were not what was fast.
why.D: The sky was brightening; it is the rate of brightening, not the sky, that can be fast.

context: A sky that shows 250 stars when a child is born would show fewer than half as many «by the time» that child turns eighteen.

why.A: Correct — "by the time" marks the point at which the change will have happened.
why.B: "Until" says the sky would show fewer stars only up to the child’s eighteenth birthday, which reverses the meaning.
why.C: "For the time" is not an idiom that marks a deadline.
why.D: "On the time" is not idiomatic English.

context: The cost is not «born» only by astronomers.

why.A: "Born" refers to birth; the sentence means carried or paid.
why.B: Correct — "borne" is the past participle of "bear," to carry or endure.
why.C: "Bourne" is an old word for a boundary or a stream.
why.D: "Bore" is the simple past tense and cannot follow "is."

context: Migrating birds navigate partly by the stars, and a sea turtle «hatchlings’» first crawl is toward the brightest horizon, which should be the sea.

why.A: "A" marks a single hatchling, so the plural possessive does not fit.
why.B: Correct — the singular possessive matches "a" and shows the crawl belongs to one hatchling.
why.C: The plain plural shows no possession, and it clashes with "a."
why.D: A plural ending in s takes an apostrophe alone; "-s’s" is never correct, and the plural still clashes with "a."

context: Yet the remedy is «unusually simple and not complicated».

why.A: "Not complicated" repeats "simple."
why.B: Correct — "simple" says it once.
why.C: "Not complex" repeats "simple."
why.D: "Uncomplicated" repeats "simple," and dropping "unusually" loses the writer’s point that this is rare.

context: Light that is shielded, aimed downward, and turned off when nobody needs it «do not reach» the sky.

why.A: The subject is "light," which is singular; the long clause after it does not change that.
why.B: Correct — "does" agrees with the singular subject "light."
why.C: "Are" is plural and does not agree with "light."
why.D: "Have" is plural and does not agree with "light."

context: «Unlike most kinds of pollution, this one disappears» the moment its source is switched off.

choices.text: Unlike most kinds of pollution, you can make this one disappear
Unlike most kinds of pollution, switching off the source makes this one disappear
Unlike most kinds of pollution, the source of this one can be switched off, and it disappears

why.A: Correct — the comparison sets one kind of pollution beside other kinds.
why.B: The comparison now sets "you" against kinds of pollution.
why.C: The comparison now sets "switching off the source" against kinds of pollution.
why.D: The comparison now sets "the source" against kinds of pollution.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence “Orion, for example, is easy to find in a winter sky, even from a city.” Where would it most logically be placed?

why.A: Correct — the previous sentence asks volunteers to find a familiar constellation, and Orion is one; the next sentence goes on to "the constellation."
why.B: That paragraph is about how many stars can be seen, and constellations have not come up yet.
why.C: The program and its constellations have not been introduced yet, so "for example" has nothing to be an example of.
why.D: The essay’s closing point is about the remedy, and a detail about finding Orion would trail off after it.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to explain why ordinary people’s observations can be scientifically useful. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it shows that many rough observations can add up to a reliable measurement.
No, because it admits that a single observation is not worth much.
No, because most of the essay is about the harm skyglow does to animals.
Yes, because it shows that volunteers need no telescope to take part.

why.A: Correct — the fourth paragraph shows single errors averaging out across tens of thousands of observations.
why.B: The essay admits this only to show how many observations overcome it.
why.C: Only one sentence mentions animals.
why.D: That explains why taking part is easy, not why the results are useful.

stem: The writer’s main purpose in ending the essay with the sentence “Unlike most kinds of pollution, this one disappears the moment its source is switched off” is to:

choices.text: stress how quickly the problem could be undone.
suggest that skyglow does less harm than other pollution.
admit that the remedy may be too simple to work.
introduce a comparison the essay goes on to develop.

why.A: Correct — after the harms, the essay ends on the point that the remedy works the moment it is applied.
why.B: The sentence compares how quickly each kind disappears, not how much harm each does.
why.C: The sentence claims the remedy works immediately; it expresses no doubt.
why.D: It is the last sentence; the essay does not go on.

context: For more than three hundred years, anyone who needed to multiply large numbers quickly «reaches» for the same tool.

why.A: The present tense clashes with "needed" and with a practice the essay says has ended.
why.B: Correct — the simple past matches "needed" and describes a finished era.
why.C: The future tense cannot describe three centuries that are already over.
why.D: The present perfect suggests the practice continues, but "needed" and the rest of the essay place it in the past.

context: The slide «rule, a» ruler with a second ruler sliding inside it — was marked with scales that grew more crowded toward one end.

why.A: The aside closes with a dash, so it has to open with one; a comma and a dash cannot form a pair.
why.B: Correct — the opening dash matches the closing one and sets off the description of the tool.
why.C: With no mark to open the aside, the closing dash has nothing to pair with.
why.D: A colon would make the rest of the sentence an explanation, and the verb "was marked" is left with no subject.

context: It was invented in England in the 1620s, shortly after John Napier published his work on «logarithms and» by the twentieth century it hung from the belt of nearly every engineer.

why.A: The phrase "shortly after … logarithms" is set off at its start but not its end, and "and" joins two independent clauses, which needs a comma before it.
why.B: Correct — the comma both closes the phrase and comes before "and" joining two independent clauses.
why.C: The phrase opened with a comma after "1620s" has to close with a comma; a semicolon cannot complete the pair.
why.D: A comma after "and" separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

context: The idea behind it is «elegant».

why.A: Correct — "elegant" means simple and clever, which is what the next sentences show the idea to be.
why.B: "Eloquent" describes persuasive speech or writing, not an idea for a tool.
why.C: "Elegiac" means mournful, which does not fit a description of how the tool works.
why.D: "Elongated" means stretched out; it describes a shape, not an idea.

context: «Logarithms, which turn» multiplication into addition, the kind a ruler can do with lengths.

why.A: "Which turn" makes the verb part of a clause describing logarithms, and the sentence never gets a main verb.
why.B: Correct — "turn" becomes the main verb of the subject "logarithms."
why.C: "Turning" is not a main verb, so the sentence is still a fragment.
why.D: "That turn" still describes logarithms without giving them a main verb.

context: To multiply two numbers, «the first number is lined up by a user» on one scale with the start of the other, then reads the answer beneath the second number.

choices.text: a user lines up the first number
the first number gets lined up
lining up the first number is done

why.A: The subject is "the first number," so it is the number that seems to multiply, and "then reads" has no sensible subject.
why.B: Correct — "a user" is the one multiplying, and the same subject goes on to read the answer.
why.C: The number is still the subject, and it cannot read the answer.
why.D: The subject is now an action, which can neither multiply nor read.

context: The whole operation takes «a few seconds of time».

why.A: Seconds are already a measure of time, so "of time" repeats it.
why.B: Correct — the phrase says it once.
why.C: Every second is equally long, so "brief" adds nothing.
why.D: "In duration" repeats what "seconds" already says.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence “Multiplying 6 by 7, for example, takes one movement of the slide.” Where would it most logically be placed?

choices.text: After “The idea behind it is elegant.”
After “the user had to know which.”

why.A: Correct — the sentence before describes the method in general, the example applies it, and the next sentence says how long the operation takes.
why.B: The method has not been described yet, so "one movement of the slide" would mean nothing.
why.C: The number 42 appears there, but that paragraph is about the decimal point, not the motion of the slide.
why.D: That paragraph is about the calculator replacing the slide rule, not about how to use one.

context: The slide rule had limits that its users learned to live «by».

why.A: "Live by" means to follow a rule or principle; the sentence means tolerating the limits.
why.B: Correct — "learn to live with" means to accept something one cannot change.
why.C: "Live for" means to be devoted to something, which does not fit limits.
why.D: "Live at" names an address, not a way of coping.

context: It gave answers to about three digits, which was enough to build a bridge but not «for balancing» a bank account.

why.A: "For balancing" does not match "to build," the infinitive it is set against.
why.B: Correct — "to balance" matches "to build" on the other side of "but not."
why.C: An -ing form does not match the infinitive "to build."
why.D: A prepositional phrase does not match "to build."

context: «Also nothing» about where the decimal point went.

why.A: The sentence has no subject and no verb.
why.B: Correct — "it said" supplies a subject and a verb.
why.C: "Saying" is not a main verb, and there is still no subject.
why.D: A comma does not supply the missing subject and verb.

context: A reading of 42 might mean 4.2, 420, or «42,000; the» user had to know which.

why.A: Correct — the semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses.
why.B: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.
why.C: With no punctuation, the two clauses are fused.
why.D: "However" is not a conjunction, so the commas still splice the clauses, and there is no contrast to signal.

context: Trained to expect this, «engineers learned to estimate every answer in their heads» before calculating it.

choices.text: every answer was estimated in their heads by engineers
estimating every answer in their heads became a habit for engineers
the habit engineers learned was estimating every answer in their heads

why.A: Correct — "engineers" comes right after the opening phrase, and they are the ones who were trained.
why.B: The answers now seem to be the ones trained to expect this.
why.C: The opening phrase now describes "estimating," which cannot be trained.
why.D: The opening phrase now describes "the habit."

stem: The writer includes the sentence “A reading of 42 might mean 4.2, 420, or 42,000; the user had to know which” primarily to:

choices.text: illustrate the problem of the missing decimal point.
show how precise a slide rule could be.
explain how logarithms turn multiplication into addition.
suggest that engineers often made serious mistakes.

why.A: Correct — the previous sentence says the tool gave no decimal point, and the example shows what that meant in practice.
why.B: The sentence shows an uncertainty, not a strength.
why.C: Logarithms were explained in the previous paragraph; this sentence is about reading an answer.
why.D: The next sentences say engineers learned to avoid this mistake by estimating.

context: «Similarly,» the end came quickly.

why.A: Nothing in the previous paragraph is similar to the slide rule’s sudden end.
why.B: Correct — engineers were loyal to the tool and its habits, and "still" marks that the end came quickly in spite of that.
why.C: The end of the slide rule is not an example of anything in the previous paragraph.
why.D: The sentence does not restate the previous one; it starts a new stage of the story.

context: In 1972 Hewlett-Packard released the HP-35, «a calculator small enough to fit in a shirt pocket that could do everything a slide rule could», and it worked to ten digits.

choices.text: a calculator that could fit in a shirt pocket and do everything a slide rule could
a calculator small enough to fit in a shirt pocket, which could do everything a slide rule could
a calculator that could do everything a slide rule could in a shirt pocket

why.A: "That could do everything" sits right after "a shirt pocket," so it seems to be the pocket that could do everything.
why.B: Correct — both "fit" and "do" now belong to "a calculator that."
why.C: The comma does not help; "which" still follows "a shirt pocket" and seems to describe it.
why.D: "In a shirt pocket" now says where it did its calculating, not how small it was.

context: It cost $395, more than a «weeks» pay for a young engineer.

why.A: The pay belongs to a week, so the word needs a possessive apostrophe.
why.B: Correct — "a week’s pay" is the singular possessive, matching "a."
why.C: The plural possessive clashes with "a," which marks one week.
why.D: "Weeks’s" is never a correct form.

context: Within a few years the price «has fallen» to a fraction of that.

why.A: The present perfect connects to the present, but the fall happened in the 1970s, before the events that follow.
why.B: Correct — the past perfect places the price drop before the manufacturers stopped, both in the past.
why.C: The present tense does not fit events of the 1970s.
why.D: The future perfect looks ahead from now, but the events are long past.

context: The major manufacturers of slide rules soon stopped making «it».

why.A: "It" is singular, but what the manufacturers made is "slide rules," which is plural.
why.B: Correct — the plural "them" refers to "slide rules."
why.C: "Stopped making one" says they stopped making a single slide rule.
why.D: "Him" refers to a male person, and there is none in the sentence.

context: Keuffel & Esser, the best-known American maker, produced «its» last one in 1975 and gave it to the Smithsonian.

why.A: Correct — the company is a single maker, as the appositive "the best-known American maker" confirms, so the singular "its" fits.
why.B: Two names make the company sound plural, but it is one maker and takes a singular pronoun.
why.C: "It’s" means "it is," which makes no sense before "last one."
why.D: "His" would refer to a man, and the subject is a company.

stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence after “gave it to the Smithsonian”: “The Smithsonian, founded in 1846, is the largest group of museums in the world.” Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: No, because it turns from the end of slide rules to the history of a museum.
Yes, because it explains why the slide rule was given to a museum.
Yes, because it shows how important the last slide rule was.
No, because the essay has already said the Smithsonian is a museum.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph is about the slide rule’s decline, and the museum’s founding date and size are beside the point.
why.B: A museum’s age and size do not explain why a company gave it anything.
why.C: The sentence describes the museum, not the slide rule.
why.D: The essay never says so, and that would not be the reason to leave the sentence out anyway.

context: Slide rules «has» not disappeared entirely.

why.A: "Has" is singular, but the subject "slide rules" is plural.
why.B: Correct — "have" agrees with the plural subject.
why.C: "Is" is singular, and "is not disappeared" is not a correct verb form.
why.D: "Having" is not a main verb, so the sentence becomes a fragment.

context: Collectors buy them, repair them, and «they display them» in glass cases.

why.A: The first two items are bare verbs, "buy them" and "repair them," so the third should not add a subject.
why.B: Correct — "display them" matches "buy them" and "repair them."
why.C: An -ing form does not match the two plain verbs before it.
why.D: This changes the form of the verb and suggests someone else does the displaying.

context: There «is» still a few pilots who carry a circular version, called a flight computer, to work out fuel and wind.

why.A: In a sentence beginning with "there," the subject comes after the verb, and here it is "pilots," which is plural.
why.B: Correct — "are" agrees with "a few pilots."
why.C: "Was" is singular, and the past tense does not fit a practice that continues today.
why.D: "Has been" is singular and does not agree with "pilots."

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence “Apollo astronauts carried slide rules to the Moon as a backup.” Should the writer make this deletion?

choices.text: Yes, because the Apollo flights came before the slide rule’s decline, so they do not show it surviving.
No, because it shows that slide rules were trusted even in spaceflight.
No, because it explains why pilots still carry flight computers.
Yes, because it contradicts the claim that the calculator did everything a slide rule could.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph lists ways slide rules survive today, and missions flown before the HP-35 do not belong on that list.
why.B: The detail is striking, but it does not support the paragraph’s point that slide rules survive.
why.C: The sentence says nothing about pilots or their reasons.
why.D: Carrying a backup does not contradict what a calculator could do.

context: For most people, though, the slide rule is a puzzle found in a grandparent’s desk «drawer: a» ruler that does not seem to measure anything.

why.A: Correct — the colon introduces a phrase that explains why the slide rule is a puzzle.
why.B: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and "a ruler that does not seem to measure anything" is not one.
why.C: "Which" now refers to the drawer, so the drawer becomes the ruler.
why.D: The period leaves "A ruler that does not seem to measure anything" as a fragment.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to describe how one technology replaced another. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it shows the HP-35 doing more than the slide rule until makers stopped.
No, because most of the essay explains how slide rules worked.
No, because the essay admits that slide rules have not disappeared entirely.
Yes, because it explains how logarithms turn multiplication into addition.

why.A: Correct — the fourth paragraph traces the replacement from the HP-35’s release to the last slide rule made.
why.B: The explanation of the slide rule sets up the replacement; the essay still describes the replacement in full.
why.C: A few survivors do not change the fact that one technology replaced the other.
why.D: That explains how the slide rule worked, not how it was replaced.

context: In 2016, an octopus named Inky «leaves» his tank at the National Aquarium of New Zealand during the night.

why.A: The present tense does not fit an event dated 2016.
why.B: Correct — the simple past fits a completed event in 2016.
why.C: The present perfect cannot be used with a specific past date like "in 2016."
why.D: The future tense cannot describe something that happened in 2016.

context: «Arriving in the morning, the lid was found slightly open by staff», with a wet trail across the floor leading to a drain.

choices.text: Arriving in the morning, staff found the lid slightly open
Arriving in the morning, the open lid was noticed by staff
Arriving in the morning, a slightly open lid greeted staff

why.A: The opening phrase describes whoever arrived, but the subject right after it is "the lid."
why.B: Correct — "staff" follows the opening phrase, and they are the ones who arrived.
why.C: The subject is still "the open lid," so the lid seems to have arrived.
why.D: The subject is "a slightly open lid," which did not arrive anywhere.

context: «The drain, which emptied» into the sea.

why.A: "Which emptied" makes the verb part of a clause describing the drain, so the sentence has no main verb.
why.B: Correct — "emptied" becomes the main verb of "the drain."
why.C: "Emptying" is not a main verb, and "which" still leaves the sentence unfinished.
why.D: "That emptied" describes the drain but still gives it no main verb.

context: Inky was never seen again, and the people who ran the aquarium «was» more impressed than upset.

why.A: "Aquarium" sits right before the verb, but the subject is "the people," which is plural.
why.B: Correct — "were" agrees with "the people," and the clause about the aquarium does not change that.
why.C: "Is" is singular and in the present tense.
why.D: "Has been" is singular and does not agree with "people."

context: Stories like Inky’s have made octopuses famous as escape artists, but they also «raze» a serious question.

why.A: "Raze" means to tear down a building completely.
why.B: Correct — to "raise" a question is to bring it up.
why.C: "Rise" does not take an object; a question cannot be "risen."
why.D: "Rays" is a noun, not a verb.

context: The question is «simple; how» did an animal so unlike us become so smart?

why.A: A semicolon joins two statements of equal weight; here the second part spells out the question the first part announces, which calls for a colon.
why.B: Correct — the colon introduces the question that "The question is simple" promises.
why.C: A comma alone cannot join the statement to a full question; this is a comma splice.
why.D: With no punctuation, "simple how" runs the statement into the question.

context: An octopus is a mollusk, closer to a clam than to any animal we usually «think of as» clever.

why.A: Correct — "think of something as" is the standard phrase for how we regard it.
why.B: "Think as" is missing "of" and is not idiomatic.
why.C: "Think about as" mixes two phrases and is not idiomatic.
why.D: "Think for" is not idiomatic in this sense.

context: Its brain owes nothing to «ours, therefore, whatever» intelligence it has evolved on its own.

why.A: "Therefore" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so commas around it still splice two independent clauses.
why.B: Correct — a period separates the two clauses, and "therefore" opens the second.
why.C: With no punctuation before "therefore," the two clauses are fused.
why.D: The semicolon is in the wrong place: it cuts "therefore" off from the clause it introduces and leaves a comma splice before it.

context: That intelligence is organized «very differently and in a different way» from ours.

why.A: "In a different way" repeats "differently."
why.B: Correct — "differently" says it once.
why.C: "Different" is an adjective, and the word here describes the verb "is organized," which needs the adverb.
why.D: "In another way" repeats "differently."

context: An octopus has about five hundred million neurons, roughly as many as a dog, but two-thirds of them «is» in its arms rather than its head.

why.A: A fraction takes its number from the noun it is a fraction of, and "them" means the neurons, which are plural.
why.B: Correct — "two-thirds of them" refers to neurons, so the verb is plural.
why.C: "Was" is singular, and the past tense does not fit a fact that is still true.
why.D: "Has been" is singular and does not agree with the plural neurons.

context: Each arm can taste what it touches and «reacting» without waiting for instructions from the brain.

why.A: "Reacting" does not match "can taste," the verb it is joined to.
why.B: Correct — "can react" matches "can taste."
why.C: An infinitive does not match "can taste."
why.D: The present perfect breaks the match with "can taste."

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence “That arm was no longer connected to a brain at all.” Where would it most logically be placed?

choices.text: After “where the mouth would have been.”

why.A: Correct — "that arm" is the severed arm just described, and a severed arm is the one case with no brain attached.
why.B: "That arm" would mean any of the octopus’s arms, which are all connected to its brain; the arms only act without waiting for it.
why.C: No single arm has been mentioned yet, so "that arm" has nothing to point to.
why.D: The final paragraph is about life span, and no arm is mentioned there.

stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence after “rather than its head”: “Octopuses also have three hearts and blue blood.” Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: No, because the paragraph is about how the octopus’s intelligence is organized, not its circulation.
Yes, because it gives another example of how different the octopus is from us.
Yes, because it explains how the severed arm could keep moving.
No, because it contradicts the statement that the octopus is a mollusk.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph opens by saying the intelligence is organized differently, and the heart count is off that topic.
why.B: The paragraph is about a difference in thinking, not any difference at all.
why.C: Hearts and blood do not explain a severed arm, which has neither.
why.D: Having three hearts does not stop an animal from being a mollusk.

context: In the laboratory, octopuses solve problems that were «designated» for mammals.

why.A: "Designated" means officially assigned or named, which is not what was done to the problems.
why.B: Correct — the problems were made, or designed, with mammals in mind.
why.C: "Destined" means fated, which does not fit problems built for a test.
why.D: "Were designing" would make the problems do the designing.

context: They unscrew jar lids to reach a crab inside, learn to navigate simple mazes, and recognize individual «keeper’s».

why.A: Nothing belongs to the keeper here; the word is simply plural.
why.B: Correct — a plain plural, since the octopuses recognize many keepers.
why.C: A plural possessive needs something owned after it, and nothing follows.
why.D: "Individual keeper" with no article reads as a single, unnamed keeper and clashes with the plural sense.

context: Sometimes they squirt water at a keeper «who» they dislike.

why.A: The keeper is the object of "dislike," so the object form is needed.
why.B: Correct — "they dislike whom" shows the pronoun is an object.
why.C: "Whose" is possessive and needs a noun after it.
why.D: "Which" is used for things and animals, not for a person.

context: «Also playing.»

why.A: This has no subject and no main verb.
why.B: Correct — "they" gives the sentence a subject and "play" a verb.
why.C: "Playing" without a helping verb cannot be the main verb.
why.D: This still has no subject and no main verb.

context: Given a floating bottle, some octopuses will push it into the current of their tank again and «again — behavior» that looks like nothing so much as a child with a ball.

why.A: Correct — the dash sets off a phrase that sums up what the octopuses are doing.
why.B: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and "behavior that looks like…" is not one.
why.C: The period leaves "Behavior that looks like…" as a fragment.
why.D: With no mark, "again behavior" runs the summary into the sentence.

context: What puzzles biologists most «is» the short life span.

why.A: Correct — the subject is the clause "what puzzles biologists most," which is singular, and it matches "the short life span."
why.B: "Biologists" is not the subject; it is the object of "puzzles."
why.C: "Were" is plural and in the past tense.
why.D: "Have been" is plural and does not agree with the singular clause.

context: Most octopuses live only a year or «two and they» rarely meet their parents.

why.A: "And" joins two independent clauses here, so a comma belongs before it.
why.B: Correct — the comma comes before the conjunction that joins two independent clauses.
why.C: The second comma cuts "and" off from its clause.
why.D: A comma after "and" separates the conjunction from its clause, and none comes before it.

context: Few of them ever look after «they’re» young once the eggs have hatched.

why.A: "They’re" means "they are," which makes no sense before "young."
why.B: Correct — the possessive "their" shows whose young they are.
why.C: "There" refers to a place.
why.D: "Theirs" stands alone and cannot come before a noun.

context: «After all,» intelligence is usually thought to pay off over a long life, spent learning from others.

why.A: Correct — "after all" introduces the reason the short life span is puzzling.
why.B: The sentence is not an example of the short life span; it explains why that is strange.
why.C: "Nevertheless" signals something true in spite of what came before, but the sentence explains the puzzle rather than setting it aside.
why.D: Nothing before this is similar to a claim about when intelligence pays off.

context: The octopus seems to have built a remarkable mind without either, and scientists «are still trying» to work out why.

why.A: Correct — "still" signals an effort that continues now, which the present progressive expresses.
why.B: The past tense suggests the effort is over, which contradicts "still" and "seems."
why.C: The past perfect needs a later past moment and clashes with "still."
why.D: The future tense says the effort has not yet begun.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to argue that octopuses should not be kept in aquariums. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: No, because it describes what octopuses can do but never argues about keeping them.
Yes, because Inky’s escape shows that octopuses want to be free.
Yes, because it shows octopuses recognizing and disliking their keepers.
No, because the aquarium staff were more impressed than upset by the escape.

why.A: Correct — the essay explains octopus intelligence and never takes a position on aquariums.
why.B: The essay reports the escape but draws no conclusion about what octopuses want.
why.C: Disliking a keeper is offered as evidence of intelligence, not as an argument against captivity.
why.D: How the staff felt has no bearing on whether octopuses should be kept.

stem: Which choice most effectively introduces the main subject of the final paragraph?

choices.text: What puzzles biologists most is the short life span.
Octopuses are found in every ocean on Earth.
Many biologists have studied octopuses in the wild.
Octopuses are also skilled at changing color.

why.A: Correct — the rest of the paragraph is about how short an octopus’s life is and why that is puzzling.
why.B: Where octopuses live has nothing to do with the rest of the paragraph.
why.C: This does not name the paragraph’s subject, the short life span.
why.D: Color is not mentioned anywhere in the paragraph.

context: In the dry country of western India, water has always been worth more «then» shade, and for centuries builders there found ways to provide both.

why.A: "Then" refers to time; a comparison needs "than."
why.B: Correct — "than" introduces the second half of a comparison.
why.C: "More as" is not how English completes a comparison.
why.D: "More that shade" does not complete the comparison.

context: The result was the «stepwell — a» well that a person does not lower a bucket into but walks down into.

why.A: Correct — the dash introduces a phrase that explains what a stepwell is.
why.B: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and "a well that…" is only a noun phrase.
why.C: The period leaves "A well that a person does not lower a bucket into…" as a fragment.
why.D: With no mark, "stepwell a well" runs the name straight into its definition.

context: Instead of a narrow shaft, a stepwell is a wide pit lined with stairs, «descending downward» level by level to wherever the water happens to be.

why.A: "Descending" already means going downward.
why.B: Correct — the word says it once.
why.C: "Lower" repeats the direction that "descending" already gives.
why.D: "Down" and "downward" say the same thing twice.

context: «The most dramatic example is Chand Baori, in the village of Abhaneri, which is more than a thousand years old.»

choices.text: The most dramatic example is Chand Baori, a well more than a thousand years old in the village of Abhaneri.
The most dramatic example, in the village of Abhaneri, which is more than a thousand years old, is Chand Baori.
More than a thousand years old, the village of Abhaneri holds the most dramatic example, Chand Baori.

why.A: "Which" follows "Abhaneri," so the sentence seems to say the village is a thousand years old.
why.B: Correct — "a well more than a thousand years old" sits right beside "Chand Baori," so the age clearly belongs to the well.
why.C: "Which" still follows "Abhaneri," so the age still attaches to the village.
why.D: The opening phrase now plainly describes the village.

context: «It’s» thirteen levels drop about thirty meters, and its three stepped walls hold some 3,500 narrow steps arranged in a zigzag pattern.

why.A: "It’s" means "it is"; "it is thirteen levels drop" makes no sense.
why.B: Correct — the possessive "its" shows the levels belong to Chand Baori, matching the "its" later in the sentence.
why.C: "Its’" is not a word.
why.D: "Their" is plural, but it refers to Chand Baori, a single well.

context: The fourth wall «holds: a» gallery of carved pavilions.

why.A: A colon cannot come between a verb and its object.
why.B: Correct — the verb leads straight to its object with no punctuation.
why.C: A semicolon separates independent clauses, and "a gallery of carved pavilions" is not one.
why.D: A comma splits the verb from its object.

context: Seen from the rim, «the steps seem» to shift and flicker, and photographs rarely make the depth believable.

choices.text: a visitor sees the steps seem
the eye watches the steps seem
it looks as if the steps seem

why.A: Correct — the steps are what is seen from the rim, and "the steps" comes right after the phrase.
why.B: The opening phrase now describes the visitor, who is not the thing seen from the rim, and "sees … seem" is garbled.
why.C: The opening phrase now describes "the eye," and the verbs no longer fit together.
why.D: "It" is not what is seen from the rim, and "looks as if … seem" says the same thing twice.

context: «Visitors, who see it for the first time, often» need a moment to understand what they are looking at.

choices.text: Visitors who see it for the first time often
Visitors who see it for the first time, often
Visitors, who see it for the first time often

why.A: The commas mark the clause as extra information, as though every visitor were seeing it for the first time.
why.B: Correct — the clause tells which visitors are meant, so it is essential and takes no commas.
why.C: A single comma separates the subject from its verb.
why.D: A single comma opens an aside that never closes.

context: «Still,» the design was more than a spectacle; it solved a practical problem.

why.A: Correct — after a paragraph about how striking the well looks, "still" turns to what it was actually for.
why.B: The well’s dramatic look did not cause it to solve a practical problem.
why.C: Solving a practical problem is not an example of the well’s dramatic appearance.
why.D: Being practical is not similar to being dramatic; the sentence marks a turn.

context: Rainfall in the region comes in a few months of monsoon, and the level of groundwater «rise and fall» by many meters over a year.

why.A: The subject is "the level," which is singular; "of groundwater" does not change it.
why.B: Correct — both verbs agree with the singular subject "the level."
why.C: -ing forms without a helping verb leave the clause with no main verb.
why.D: "Have" is plural, and the present perfect does not fit a pattern that repeats every year.

context: A bucket on a rope works only if the rope is long «enough, a staircase» works at any depth.

why.A: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — a period separates the two independent clauses.
why.C: With no punctuation, the two clauses are fused.
why.D: The comma after "and" cuts the conjunction off from its clause, and "and" also blurs the contrast between bucket and staircase.

context: The logic was «simple: in» the wet season, people descended a few flights, and in the dry season, they kept going.

why.A: Correct — the colon introduces the explanation of what made the logic simple.
why.B: A comma cannot join "The logic was simple" to the independent clauses that follow; this is a comma splice.
why.C: With no punctuation, "simple in the wet season" reads as though the logic were simple only in the wet season.
why.D: "Because" says the seasons are the reason the logic was simple, which gets the relation backward: they are the logic.

context: «In contrast, stepwells» were also social places.

why.A: "Also" adds a second role to the first; "in contrast" wrongly says the two roles oppose each other.
why.B: Correct — "also" already connects this paragraph to the last, so no other transition is needed.
why.C: Being practical did not cause stepwells to become social places.
why.D: Being a social place is not an example of solving a water problem.

context: Because the air near the water stayed cooler than the air at the surface — often by several «degrees, villagers» gathered there in the hottest part of the day.

why.A: A dash opened the aside, so a dash has to close it; a comma leaves the pair mismatched.
why.B: Correct — the second dash closes the aside, and the main clause begins.
why.C: With nothing to close the aside, "several degrees villagers" runs together.
why.D: A semicolon cannot close a dash, and it cuts the "because" clause off from the clause it depends on.

context: They came to fetch water, to wash clothes, and «resting» in the cool.

why.A: "Resting" does not match "to fetch" and "to wash."
why.B: Correct — "to rest" matches the two infinitives before it.
why.C: A full clause does not match the two infinitives in the list.
why.D: A prepositional phrase does not match "to fetch" and "to wash."

context: Women, «who» did most of the water carrying, met on the landings and talked.

why.A: Correct — "who" is the subject of "did," so the subject form is right.
why.B: "Whom" is an object form, but the pronoun is the subject of "did."
why.C: "Which" is used for things, not people.
why.D: "Whose" is possessive and needs a noun after it.

context: Many stepwells were decorated with carvings of gods and dancers, and some were built by wealthy women «for» public gifts.

why.A: "Built for public gifts" says the wells were built to hold gifts; the idiom for what something serves as is "as."
why.B: Correct — the wells were built as gifts to the public.
why.C: "Like public gifts" says the wells merely resembled gifts.
why.D: "By" repeats the preposition already used for the builders and makes no sense here.

context: Under British rule, many stepwells «are» closed or filled in.

why.A: The present tense does not fit a period of history that has ended.
why.B: Correct — the simple past matches "under British rule."
why.C: The future tense cannot describe a past period.
why.D: The present perfect connects to the present, but the closures happened during a past period.

context: Officials considered the wells’ standing water unhealthy, and piped water and pumps made «them» seem unnecessary.

why.A: "Them" could mean the officials, the wells, or the pumps, since all three are plural.
why.B: Correct — naming the wells removes the doubt about what seemed unnecessary.
why.C: "It" would point to the standing water, which is not what seemed unnecessary.
why.D: "Themselves" would mean the pumps made themselves seem unnecessary.

context: «Hundreds abandoned» and left to fill with silt.

why.A: Without a helping verb, "abandoned" is only a description, and the sentence has no main verb.
why.B: Correct — "were abandoned … and left" gives the sentence a full verb.
why.C: A comma does not supply the missing verb.
why.D: "Of them" adds words but still no main verb.

context: In recent decades, some have been cleaned and restored, partly for tourists and partly «for the reason that» falling water tables have reminded planners why the wells were built in the first place.

why.A: "For the reason that" is a wordy way to say "because."
why.B: Correct — one word does the work of four.
why.C: "Due to the fact that" is just as wordy as the original.
why.D: "Owing to how" is not idiomatic before a full clause.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence “In a year of drought, they might climb down nearly all thirteen levels.” Where would it most logically be placed?

choices.text: After “met on the landings and talked.”

why.A: Correct — "they" are the people descending in the dry season, and a drought is the dry season at its worst.
why.B: The thirteen levels are mentioned there, but "they" would mean the steps, which cannot climb.
why.C: No people have been mentioned yet in that paragraph, so "they" has no one to refer to, and the seasons have not been explained.
why.D: That paragraph is about social life at the well, not about how far down the water was.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence “Men, meanwhile, were more often at work in the fields.” Where would it most logically be placed?

choices.text: After “met on the landings and talked.”
After “in the hottest part of the day.”

why.A: Correct — "meanwhile" sets the men’s work against what the women were doing, which is described in the sentence just before.
why.B: Women have not been mentioned yet, so "meanwhile" has nothing to contrast with.

why.D: "The hang on" is not idiomatic.

context: A blade that is ground too hard «grows» hot and loses its temper.

why.A: Correct — "grows" is the main verb for "a blade," and the clause "that is ground too hard" sits between them.
why.B: "Growing" is not a main verb, so the sentence becomes a fragment.
why.C: A second "that" clause leaves "a blade" without a main verb.
why.D: "Having grown" is not a main verb, so the sentence becomes a fragment.

stem: The writer is considering adding the sentence “In steel, temper is the hardness that lets an edge hold.” after the sentence that ends “loses its temper.” Should the writer make this addition?

choices.text: Yes, because it explains the meaning of "temper" that the writer’s joke depends on.
No, because the next sentence already explains what "temper" means.
No, because it shifts the focus from the grandfather to the history of steel.
Yes, because it explains why the grandfather charged a quarter a knife.

why.A: Correct — the next sentence plays on two meanings of "temper," and readers need the metal meaning to see the joke.
why.B: The next sentence uses the everyday meaning, not the metal one.
why.C: The sentence gives a definition, not a history, and it serves the point about the grandfather’s lesson.
why.D: The definition has nothing to do with the price.

context: I found that «amusing», since losing your temper was exactly what he told me never to do at the wheel.

why.A: Correct — the adjective "amusing" describes "that," the fact the writer found funny.
why.B: "Amused" describes the person who is entertained, not the thing that is funny.
why.C: A noun cannot describe "that" after "found"; the sentence needs an adjective.
why.D: The adverb "amusingly" cannot describe "that."

context: By noon, the «neighbors’» knives were lined up along the cart, each one tagged with its owner’s name.

why.A: Correct — the knives belong to many neighbors, which is why each had to be tagged with its owner’s name.
why.B: The singular possessive would mean one neighbor’s knives, but then tagging each knife with its owner’s name would be pointless.
why.C: The plain plural shows no possession; the knives belong to the neighbors.
why.D: A plural ending in s takes an apostrophe alone; "-s’s" is never correct.

context: He charged a quarter a knife, and everyone on the street was familiar «to» the price.

why.A: A person is "familiar with" something; "familiar to" works the other way around ("the price was familiar to everyone").
why.B: Correct — "familiar with" is the standard phrase for knowing something.
why.C: "Familiar about" is not idiomatic.
why.D: "Familiar for" is not idiomatic.

context: He never «argued on» it, even when people offered less.

why.A: "Argued on" is not idiomatic for disputing something.
why.B: Correct — people "argue about" a price.
why.C: "Argued at" is not idiomatic.
why.D: "Argued to" is not idiomatic for disputing a price.

context: Some people paid more than he «asked, he» always put the extra in a coffee can for my school shoes.

why.A: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — a comma and "and" properly join the two independent clauses.
why.C: With no punctuation, the two clauses are fused.
why.D: "However" is not a conjunction, so the commas around it still splice two clauses.

context: «Nevertheless,» the can was usually full by the end of August.

why.A: "Nevertheless" signals a contrast, but a full can is what the extra money would lead to.
why.B: Correct — the extra money going into the can is why it was full by August.
why.C: A full can is not an example of the extra money being saved.
why.D: "Instead" signals a replacement, but nothing is being replaced.

context: The last summer I rode with him, the lesson he repeated most «was: a» dull knife is more dangerous than a sharp one, because it slips.

why.A: A colon should not come between a linking verb and what completes it; the clause before it is not complete.
why.B: Correct — "that" introduces the lesson as the complement of "was."
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and "the lesson he repeated most was" is not one.
why.D: A comma should not separate "was" from what completes it.

context: He said that was true of tools «— and of» most other things as well.

why.A: Correct — the dash sets off the added phrase and gives it emphasis.
why.B: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and "and of most other things" is not one.
why.C: The period leaves "And of most other things as well" as a fragment.
why.D: The comma after "and" splits it from the phrase it introduces.

context: The cart «itself, still» stands in my parents’ garage.

why.A: A comma should not separate the subject "the cart itself" from its verb.
why.B: Correct — the subject runs straight into its verb.
why.C: A semicolon cuts the subject off from its verb.
why.D: The comma after "still" splits it from the verb it modifies.

context: Its wheels are cracked and its paint has «diminished», but the bell still works.

why.A: "Diminished" means grown smaller in size or amount, which is not what happens to old paint.
why.B: Correct — paint that has lost its color over time has "faded."
why.C: "Lessened" means reduced in amount or degree, which does not describe paint losing color.
why.D: "Declined" means decreased or refused, and neither fits paint.

context: Sometimes I take it out, «to ring» it once, and put it back.

why.A: "To ring" does not match "take" and "put" in the series.
why.B: Correct — "ring" matches "take" and "put."
why.C: "Ringing" does not match "take" and "put."
why.D: "Rang" is past tense and does not match the present "take" and "put."

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to give readers instructions for sharpening knives at home. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: No, because although it mentions a few techniques, it is a memoir of the writer’s grandfather.
Yes, because it describes holding the blade at a steady angle.
Yes, because it warns that a dull knife is more dangerous than a sharp one.
No, because it says only professionals should sharpen knives.

why.A: Correct — the steps are passing details in a story about summers with the grandfather, not instructions a reader could follow.
why.B: One tip is not a set of instructions, and the essay never explains how to sharpen at home.
why.C: The warning is the grandfather’s lesson, not a step in sharpening.
why.D: The essay never says this.
